title: GxP-Agent: Process-DAG Topology for Reliable Clinical Trial Programming with LLM Agents
comment: Preprint. 9 pages main text, 3 figures, plus references and appendix
summary: Clinical trial programming -- transforming study protocols into analysis-ready datasets under CDISC standards -- is a bottleneck in regulatory submissions, yet LLM-based code generation fails catastrophically on this task: across 11 single-shot attempts with five frontier models, none produces a valid subject-level analysis dataset. We introduce GxP-Agent, a multi-agent system that encodes regulatory process ordering as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), decomposing monolithic dataset generation into 15 domain-specific nodes executed by worker agents with pharmaverse skill context, validation gates, and conditional retry. On CDISC-Bench, a new execution-based benchmark built from the FDA pilot submission CDISCPilot01 (254 subjects, 49 ground-truth ADSL variables), GxP-Agent with Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieves 100% structural match (49/49 variables, 254 correct records) across three independent runs, compared to 59.2% for the best retrieval-augmented baseline and 0% for all single-agent and flat multi-agent approaches. The DAG topology also enables weaker models: GPT-4.1 achieves 59.2% mean structural match under the same DAG, where it scores 0% under every other architecture. The approach generalizes to ADAE (adverse events; 9-node branching DAG, 55 variables, 1,191 records), achieving 100% structural match on the first attempt. These results demonstrate that encoding domain process knowledge as graph topology -- rather than relying on LLM reasoning alone -- is a key enabler for reliable, GxP-compliant clinical trial programming.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GxP-Agent, a DAG-based multi-agent LLM system that reliably generates CDISC-compliant clinical trial analysis datasets, vastly outperforming single-shot and flat multi-agent LLM code generation on a new benchmark (CDISC-Bench).
AI.motivation: Clinical trial programming to produce CDISC-compliant, analysis-ready datasets is a major bottleneck in regulatory submissions. Existing LLM-based code generation approaches fail catastrophically on this highly constrained, regulated task, producing no valid subject-level analysis datasets in extensive testing. There is a need for a more reliable, regulation-aware approach that encodes domain process knowledge rather than relying purely on LLM reasoning.
AI.method: The authors design GxP-Agent, a multi-agent system that represents the regulatory programming workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The monolithic dataset generation task is decomposed into 15 domain-specific nodes, each executed by worker agents equipped with pharmaverse tooling context. The system includes validation gates to check intermediate outputs and conditional retry mechanisms for failed steps. They introduce CDISC-Bench, an execution-based benchmark based on the FDA CDISCPilot01 submission for the ADSL dataset (254 subjects, 49 variables), and extend the approach to the ADAE dataset via a 9-node branching DAG.
AI.result: On CDISC-Bench for ADSL, GxP-Agent with Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieves a 100% structural match with the ground-truth dataset (all 49 variables and 254 records correct) across three independent runs. The best retrieval-augmented baseline attains 59.2% structural match, while all single-agent and flat multi-agent LLM setups achieve 0%. Under the same DAG topology, a weaker model (GPT-4.1) reaches 59.2% mean structural match, despite scoring 0% on all other architectures. For ADAE (55 variables, 1,191 records) with a 9-node branching DAG, GxP-Agent again attains 100% structural match on the first attempt.
AI.conclusion: Encoding domain process and regulatory workflow knowledge explicitly as a graph topology and coordinating LLM agents through this DAG is crucial for achieving reliable, GxP-compliant clinical trial programming. This structured multi-agent approach enables both strong and weaker LLMs to succeed where single-shot, single-agent, and flat multi-agent methods fail, suggesting a promising direction for high-stakes, regulation-heavy data engineering tasks.

title: Runtime Governance for Agentic AI: Action-Boundary Control with Trusted Provenance and Fail-Closed Execution
summary: Agentic AI systems request tool actions that can modify files, send messages, launch jobs, or change workflow state. This shifts the safety problem from harmful text generation to harmful operational side effects. Prompt-level governance can shape model behavior, but it does not create an execution boundary. We introduce Aegis, a runtime governance system that treats model outputs as action proposals and mediates them through a trusted decision layer before tool execution. The model proposes; the trusted runtime decides. Aegis evaluates proposals against active policy state, resolves provenance server-side, fails closed under uncertainty, and routes selected cases through Senate-style settlement, a quorum- based non-unilateral authorization path. We evaluate Aegis on a repeated sandbox corpus spanning five run families, 42 tasks, three conditions, and ten repeats per family. Across 6,300 rows, prompt-policy conditioning produced 79 risky comparator-path leakage rows. Across 2,100 Aegis-governed rows, the system recorded zero governed mock-tool applications and zero governed risky side-effect completions. All 1,832 Aegis-attempted governed rows preserved trusted Aegis-resolved provenance, and all 1,019 Senate-settled rows had quorum and final signed tally evidence. These results do not prove general autonomous-agent safety. They support the narrower systems claim that, in this evaluated sandbox corpus, runtime action-boundary governance prevented observed risky proposals from becoming governed side effects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Aegis, a runtime governance system that mediates AI tool-use actions through a trusted decision layer, preventing risky model proposals from turning into harmful side effects in their sandbox evaluation.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems can execute tools that modify the real world—files, messages, jobs, workflows—so the main safety risk shifts from harmful text to harmful operational side effects. Current prompt-level governance only steers the model’s text output and cannot enforce hard execution boundaries on what tools actually run. The authors want a mechanism that can reliably block or control risky tool executions even when the model proposes them, and that can provide verifiable evidence of how decisions were made.
AI.method: They design Aegis, a runtime governance architecture where model outputs are interpreted as action proposals rather than direct commands. A separate trusted runtime layer evaluates each proposed tool action against a live policy state, performs provenance checks server-side, and defaults to blocking actions when there is uncertainty (fail-closed). For higher-risk or ambiguous cases, Aegis uses a Senate-style settlement mechanism: authorization requires a quorum-based, non-unilateral decision path with signed evidence of the final tally. They then construct a repeated sandbox evaluation corpus covering five run families, 42 tasks, three experimental conditions, and 10 repeats per family, yielding thousands of rows comparing prompt-only governance to Aegis-governed runs.
AI.result: In prompt-policy-only conditions across 6,300 rows, they observe 79 instances of risky leakage along comparator paths, indicating that prompt-level steering alone cannot fully prevent unsafe behavior. Under Aegis governance across 2,100 rows, there were zero executed mock-tool calls and zero risky side-effect completions among governed actions, meaning no risky proposal translated into an actual governed side effect in this setting. Additionally, all 1,832 rows in which Aegis attempted to govern actions preserved trusted server-resolved provenance, and all 1,019 Senate-settled rows included evidence of quorum and a signed final decision tally.
AI.conclusion: Aegis does not solve general autonomous-agent safety or guarantee safety outside the tested environment, but within their sandbox corpus it enforced effective runtime action boundaries. The experiments support a narrower claim: treating model outputs as proposals and mediating them through a trusted, policy-aware, and evidence-preserving runtime can prevent observed risky AI proposals from becoming real governed side effects. This suggests that robust runtime governance is a promising complement to prompt-level controls for tool-using and agentic AI systems.

title: The Price of Thinking: Reasoning Effort as a Model-Specific API Contract
summary: API buyers purchase a dated contract, not a model name alone: the contract includes the requested and served model, reasoning-effort term or its omission, output rail, service product, prompt, and price schedule. We study the reasoning-effort term through a registered paired contrast of Sonnet 5 with explicit high effort against the same model with effort omitted, using 30 AIME 2026 items and five calls per item. Every paid attempt was assigned one frozen terminal category, and inference resampled items while retaining their repeated calls. Mean delivered cost was \$0.01031 per call higher under the explicit-high contract than under the omitted contract [+\$0.00204, +\$0.01974]. The corresponding accuracy contrast was +0.0133 [-0.0267, +0.0467]; we did not detect an accuracy difference, and the interval permits a gain of up to 4.67 percentage points that this design cannot rule out. Cost per correct answer was \$0.08665 under the high-effort contract and \$0.07662 under the omitted contract, as registered point estimates. A dated contract census, Models-API metadata, and preregistered raw-response probes further documented model-specific omission semantics, including within a provider; claims remained at documentation grade when raw structure was indeterminate. The request registry, parser, terminal taxonomy, statistical plan, and analysis pipeline were frozen before outcomes were examined; the resulting claims are bounded to the model, task, and collection date studied.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes API access to AI models as dated contracts and empirically studies how an explicit “high reasoning effort” request affects cost and accuracy compared with omitting such a term, using GPT-style models on AIME math problems.
AI.motivation: API users don’t just buy a model label; they buy a specific contract at a point in time (which model is actually served, options like reasoning-effort flags, output constraints, and pricing). Providers now expose terms like “high reasoning effort / thinking time,” but it’s unclear what these actually do in practice in terms of cost, accuracy, and semantics. There is a need for careful, preregistered measurement of how such contract terms behave, and for documenting the often-opaque mapping between requested options and the underlying models and behaviors that are actually delivered.
AI.method: The authors formalize the notion of an API “dated contract” including model, effort term, rails, product, prompt, and price. They then run a preregistered paired comparison using the same base model (Sonnet 5) on AIME 2026 problems, contrasting two contracts: one with explicit high reasoning effort, and one where the effort term is omitted. For each of 30 items, the model is called 5 times under each contract. All attempts receive frozen terminal outcome labels, and a resampling-based inference procedure is used that preserves per-item repeated calls. They compute contrasts in delivered cost per call, accuracy, and cost per correct answer. In parallel, they run a census of dated contracts and API metadata plus preregistered probes of raw responses to characterize how omission of effort is implemented across models and within a provider, keeping claims at documentation level when the underlying structure is unclear. The entire statistical and analytic pipeline is preregistered and frozen before seeing outcomes.
AI.result: Calls under the explicit high-effort contract cost on average $0.01031 more per call than under the effort-omitted contract, with a confidence interval of about +$0.00204 to +$0.01974. The accuracy contrast between high-effort and omitted-effort contracts is estimated at +0.0133 (about 1.33 percentage points) with a wide interval from -0.0267 to +0.0467, so no accuracy difference is detected, but gains up to 4.67 percentage points are not ruled out. Registered point estimates put cost per correct answer at $0.08665 for high-effort versus $0.07662 for omitted effort. The metadata census and response probes show that what “omitting” effort means is model- and provider-specific, with varying and sometimes indeterminate semantics; such claims are reported only at a documentation level.
AI.conclusion: Specifying an explicit high reasoning-effort term in an API contract for the studied model, task, and time window reliably increases monetary cost per call but does not yield a statistically detected improvement in accuracy on AIME-style problems, though modest gains remain possible within the confidence bounds. On a cost-per-correct basis, the high-effort option appears less efficient at the registered point estimates. More broadly, API access should be viewed as dated contracts whose semantics—including what happens when options like effort are omitted—are model- and provider-specific and must be empirically documented. The preregistered design constrains claims to the particular model, task, and collection date analyzed, underscoring the need for ongoing measurement as APIs and their hidden mappings evolve.

title: FedPref: Federated Preference Learning for Structured Radiology Report Extraction
comment: Accepted at ELAMI 2026, held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026. To appear in the Springer proceedings
summary: Radiology reports describe findings and locations in free text, but downstream search and analysis require these relations in a fixed schema. Learning this extraction requires labels that are unevenly distributed across institutions: smaller hospitals have less local evidence, and pooling data may be infeasible. We introduce FedPref: frozen public language models propose alternative JSON extractions, local annotations rank them, and sites collaboratively train compact Qwen3-8B adapters while sharing only model updates. A heterogeneous teacher pool provides cross-model contrast when repeated single-model samples collapse. On development data from six simulated hospitals with unequal data volume and disease prevalence, FedPref improves client-mean F1 by 2.49 points and worst-site F1 by 9.10 points compared with training each site in isolation, with the largest gains at the sites holding the least data. Central training on the pooled preference-pair union is 2.66 points higher on client-mean F1. On a locked, 400-report manually validated gold test set, FedPref reaches 68.68 F1 and pooled training 71.67, preserving that same ordering. FedPref thus lets institutions with unequal, unpooled data benefit from collaboration without ever sharing reports or annotations.

AI.tldr: FedPref is a federated preference-learning framework that uses public language models and local ranking of candidate JSON extractions to collaboratively train adapters for radiology report information extraction without sharing private data.
AI.motivation: Radiology reports are written in free text, but downstream applications need structured representations (e.g., which finding occurs at which anatomical site). Training extractors to map free text to a fixed schema usually requires large, labeled datasets. However, labels are unevenly distributed: big centers have data and annotations, while small hospitals have few labels. Direct pooling of data is often impossible because of privacy, regulation, or organizational barriers. The paper is motivated by the need for a collaborative approach that lets multiple institutions with heterogeneous data and label distributions jointly improve extraction models without sharing raw reports or annotations.
AI.method: The authors propose FedPref, a federated preference-learning framework. They start with frozen, public large language models that, given a radiology report, generate multiple candidate JSON-structured extractions (e.g., different possible mappings of findings and locations). Local annotators at each site do not create labels from scratch; instead, they rank or choose among these candidate extractions, creating preference pairs. Each institution trains a compact adapter on top of a Qwen3-8B model using these preference signals. Training is done in a federated way: sites send only model updates (e.g., adapter gradients/weights) to a central server for aggregation, never sharing reports or annotations. To avoid collapse when sampling repeatedly from a single model, they use a heterogeneous pool of teacher LMs to propose diverse candidate extractions and provide cross-model contrast. The approach is evaluated on multi-site simulated hospital data with varying data volumes and disease prevalence.
AI.result: On development data from six simulated hospitals with unequal sizes and label distributions, FedPref improves client-mean F1 by 2.49 points and worst-site F1 by 9.10 points compared to training each institution’s model independently. Gains are largest at the smallest, most data-scarce sites, showing effective knowledge transfer. Centralized training on the union of all preference pairs (pooled data) yields an additional 2.66 F1 points on client-mean F1 beyond FedPref, representing an upper bound when pooling is allowed. On a separate, locked gold test set of 400 radiology reports with manual validation, FedPref achieves 68.68 F1, while pooled centralized training reaches 71.67 F1, maintaining the same relative ordering and confirming that FedPref recovers most, though not all, of the pooled-training benefit without data sharing.
AI.conclusion: FedPref enables institutions that cannot share raw radiology reports or annotations to still benefit from collaborative learning for information extraction. By using frozen public LMs to propose structured outputs and local preference-based ranking for supervision, the method substantially improves extraction quality across heterogeneous sites, with particularly large gains for small, data-poor hospitals. While centralized pooled training still performs best, FedPref recovers much of that performance under realistic privacy and data-governance constraints, demonstrating a practical path for privacy-preserving, multi-institutional training of clinical NLP models.

title: Margin-Regularized Structured Semantic Alignment for Brain-Language Correspondence
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models, brain-language decoding has achieved remarkable progress. However, it remains unclear whether decoded content genuinely reflects neural representations or is largely reconstructed by the language model itself. This ambiguity limits interpretability and hinders the investigation of intrinsic brain-language correspondence. To address this challenge, we propose MD-SigLIP. This margin-regularized structured semantic alignment framework directly aligns brain embeddings with text embeddings in a shared semantic space, enabling retrieval-based decoding. This formulation enables explicit modeling of the correspondence between neural representations and language semantics. Building upon duplicate-aware sigmoid contrastive learning, we introduce a listwise margin-regularized term that enforces structured ranking constraints between positive semantic clusters and negative samples. By modeling multi-positive semantic structure and margin-based ordering simultaneously, the method captures the manifold organization of language embeddings reflected in neural signals. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art retrieval performance under both full-vocabulary and subset evaluation settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MD-SigLIP, a margin-regularized semantic alignment framework that aligns brain and text embeddings for retrieval-based brain-to-language decoding, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Although large language models have advanced brain-language decoding, it is unclear whether decoded text truly reflects neural representations or is largely hallucinated/reconstructed by the language model. This ambiguity harms interpretability and understanding of the true brain-language correspondence. The authors aim to build a method that directly links neural signals to language semantics in a transparent and structurally faithful way.
AI.method: The authors introduce MD-SigLIP, a margin-regularized structured semantic alignment framework. Brain activity is mapped to an embedding space that is directly aligned with a text-embedding space, enabling retrieval-based decoding instead of free generation. The method builds on duplicate-aware sigmoid contrastive learning and adds a listwise margin-regularized term that enforces ranking constraints between positive semantic clusters and negative examples. It explicitly models multi-positive semantic structure and margin-based ordering to better capture the manifold geometry of language embeddings reflected in neural signals.
AI.result: MD-SigLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on brain-to-language retrieval tasks, under both full-vocabulary and restricted subset evaluation protocols, outperforming existing decoding approaches.
AI.conclusion: Directly aligning brain embeddings with text embeddings via a margin-regularized, structure-aware contrastive objective improves both performance and interpretability in brain-language decoding. The proposed MD-SigLIP framework better captures the manifold structure of language semantics in neural signals and offers a more faithful way to study intrinsic brain-language correspondence.

title: The Problem Is the Problem: Towards Scalable Mathematical Discovery
summary: AI systems are increasingly capable of contributing to mathematical research. In research practice, frontier-model reasoning is a limited resource, and expert mathematical review is even more sharply constrained. Allocating these scarce resources well is therefore central to making AI-assisted mathematical discovery efficient. In most current AI-for-math workflows, human effort is concentrated at the beginning and end, in selecting suitable research problems and later reviewing the resulting artifacts. These two stages are becoming bottlenecks for research-level mathematics. We address them by proposing a new human-AI discovery paradigm. The human input is no longer a single problem selected in advance, but a research direction in which the experts have interest and expertise. The system then searches a broad literature corpus for candidate problems in that direction. Inspired by search and recommender systems, we build Find, Attempt, and Recommend (FAR), a literature-to-review cascade that automates the search for suitable problems and focuses human attention on artifacts that have passed several stages of filtering. In a combinatorics pilot, the pipeline starts from 5,245 combinatorics papers, recovers 6,453 candidate conjectures or open problems, and filters them to 4,717 apparently well-posed and still-open conjectures. Subsequent reasoning and automated triage stages surface 598 potential resolutions and select 77 items for author-team review. Among them, we identify many interesting discoveries, including results on conjectures and questions of Davies--Jenssen--Perkins--Roberts, Erdős--Straus, Ikenmeyer--Pak--Panova, and Lund--Saraf--Wolf. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of this new mode of human-AI collaboration for mathematical discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FAR, a human-AI pipeline that mines mathematical literature for open problems, filters and attempts them with AI reasoning tools, and recommends the most promising results for expert review, showing it can yield publishable-level discoveries in combinatorics.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly able to contribute to advanced mathematics, but expert attention and top-tier model reasoning are scarce. Current workflows concentrate human effort on picking problems and manually checking AI outputs, both of which are becoming bottlenecks. The authors want a scalable way to: (1) systematically find good research problems aligned with experts’ interests; and (2) filter AI-generated mathematical artifacts so human experts review only the most promising ones.
AI.method:
They propose a new human-AI collaboration paradigm where humans specify a research direction rather than a single problem. The system then:
1. Searches a large corpus of math papers in that direction.
2. Automatically extracts candidate conjectures/open problems from the literature.
3. Filters them to identify those that appear well-posed and still open.
4. Applies AI reasoning and automated triage to attempt resolutions.
5. Recommends a small subset of attempted solutions to human experts for detailed review.

They instantiate this as the FAR (Find, Attempt, and Recommend) pipeline and run a pilot in combinatorics using 5,245 papers as input.
AI.result:
In the combinatorics pilot, starting from 5,245 papers, the system:
- Extracts 6,453 candidate conjectures/open problems.
- Filters these down to 4,717 conjectures that appear well-posed and still open.
- Runs further reasoning and triage, surfacing 598 potential resolutions.
- Narrows these to 77 items selected for detailed review by the author team.

Within this curated set, they find multiple mathematically interesting discoveries, including progress on conjectures and questions by well-known authors and problems (e.g., Davies–Jenssen–Perkins–Roberts, Erdős–Straus, Ikenmeyer–Pak–Panova, Lund–Saraf–Wolf).
AI.conclusion: A literature-to-review pipeline like FAR can effectively allocate scarce expert and frontier-model resources for AI-assisted mathematics. By transforming broad research directions into a curated set of promising, AI-attempted problems, the system yields nontrivial new results and suggests a scalable paradigm for human-AI collaboration in mathematical discovery, at least in domains like combinatorics.

title: Cross-Model Memory Transfer via Target-Side Reader Adaptation
summary: Methods for improving knowledge use in large language models typically fall into two regimes. Non-parametric retrieval offers flexible access to external knowledge, but adds retrieval latency, context overhead, and only shallow integration with the backbone. Parametric adaptation is efficient at inference time, but entangles knowledge with model weights and can be hard to update, audit, or transfer. Engram-style hashed memory occupies a middle regime: it stores learned information in an external, addressable table, yet consumes that table through a small learned reader. This raises a basic question: when such a memory is moved across backbones, what matters more, the frozen memory itself or the target-side reader? We study this question through cross-model frozen-memory extraction, in which a memory trained on a source model is frozen and attached to a different target model, with only a lightweight reader trained. Ablations show that learned memory content and correct addressing both matter, but the transferred table becomes useful only through a reader aligned to the target model. In downstream question answering tasks, a dual-layer, four-branch reader nearly closes the gap between same-model and cross-model reuse, achieving an average score of 38.8 under our controlled evaluation protocol. Moreover, when the provider reader is directly compatible with the target interface, the frozen artifact can provide substantial utility without target-side training, while optional reader adaptation yields further improvement. These results suggest that Engram can serve as a reusable external knowledge artifact, provided that the target has access to a compatible reader interface; target-side adaptation can further improve alignment when direct reader reuse is insufficient.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how "Engram"-style hashed external memories can be reused across different language model backbones, focusing on whether the memory table or the reader module matters more.
AI.motivation: Existing methods to give LLMs access to knowledge either use non-parametric retrieval (flexible but slow, with context overhead and shallow integration) or parametric finetuning (fast at inference but hard to update, audit, or transfer). Engram-style external hashed memories promise a middle ground: they keep knowledge in an external table yet are consumed via a small learned reader. The open problem is how reusable these memories are across different models and what limits that transferability.
AI.method: The authors propose and study "cross-model frozen-memory extraction": they first train an Engram-style memory on a source model, then freeze this memory and attach it to a different target model. Only a lightweight reader is trained on the target side. Through ablation experiments, they separately analyze the roles of learned memory content, correct addressing, and the reader’s alignment with the target backbone. They also design and evaluate more expressive reader architectures, such as a dual-layer, four-branch reader, and test both zero-shot reuse of a provider-supplied reader and optional further adaptation on the target model.
AI.result: Experiments show that both the stored memory contents and accurate addressing are important, but the memory only becomes truly useful when paired with a reader that is well-aligned with the target model. A dual-layer, four-branch reader architecture almost closes the performance gap between using memory with its original model and with a different target model, yielding an average score of 38.8 under their evaluation setup for downstream QA tasks. When the provider’s reader is already interface-compatible with the target, the frozen memory plus reader can give substantial gains without any target-side training, and further target-side reader adaptation improves performance even more.
AI.conclusion: Engram-style hashed memories can function as reusable external knowledge artifacts across different LLM backbones, but their utility depends critically on the reader architecture and its alignment with the target model. If the target model can use a compatible reader interface, it can directly benefit from a frozen, provider-trained memory; lightweight adaptation of the reader further boosts alignment and performance. This positions Engram as a practical middle-ground mechanism for updatable, auditable, and transferable knowledge storage for LLMs.

title: SkillEffect: Checked Lowering for Memory-Bounded Agent Tools
summary: Agent Skills can specify procedural and resource obligations for tool use, and language models instantiate them as concrete programs. However, when models turn this guidance into code for existing tool interfaces, even a semantically correct program may load an entire input and exceed the memory available to one tool call. We present SkillEffect, a checked-lowering runtime for computations with a recoverable source relation, an audited bounded implementation, and a registered output postcondition. Before granting execution authority, an independent checker rebuilds each proposed lowering from the submitted program and immutable input. Every relation plugin supplies a source recognizer, input-fact extractor, bounded-IR constructor, arena-bound function, and postcondition; one common runtime provides checked selection, bounded-VM execution, atomic capacity leasing, and staged publication. Generality in SkillEffect is architectural rather than automatic: each supported computation requires an audited relation plugin, while the dispatch, resource-control, execution, and publication mechanisms are shared across plugins. Across six operator families, bounded access substantially reduces peak memory and improves completion under externally fixed caps. Six plugins instantiate the same contract across five execution patterns, from streaming reduction to bounded-heap Top-k. The XLSX onboarding study and Top-k extension show that a new relation and a new retained-state pattern reuse the same trust boundary, while the checker accepts all evaluated legal configurations and rejects all adversarial proposals. Together, these results show that one checked-lowering architecture can enforce heterogeneous registered memory relations at Agent tool dispatch.

AI.tldr: SkillEffect is a runtime system that safely transforms high-level agent skills into memory-bounded, checkable tool executions.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents often turn high-level skill descriptions into code that calls tools. Even when the code is semantically correct, it can violate resource constraints, such as loading full files and exceeding memory limits for a single tool call. There is a need for a principled way to enforce resource bounds and behavioral contracts at the point where agent-generated programs are lowered to concrete tool executions.
AI.method: The authors design SkillEffect, a checked-lowering runtime based on explicit source–target relations. For each supported computation, developers implement an audited relation plugin that includes: (1) a recognizer for eligible source programs, (2) a way to extract input facts from immutable inputs, (3) a constructor for a bounded intermediate representation (IR), (4) an arena-bound function that respects capacity limits, and (5) a registered postcondition on outputs. A shared runtime then: (a) independently reconstructs and checks each proposed lowering from the original program and inputs, (b) selects appropriate relation plugins, (c) runs the bounded IR on a bounded virtual machine under atomic capacity leasing, and (d) controls staged publication of outputs.
AI.result: They implement six operator families as relation plugins, covering five distinct execution patterns such as streaming reductions and bounded-heap Top-k operations. Experiments show that bounded access significantly reduces peak memory usage and improves task completion rates under fixed external memory caps. In a case study on XLSX onboarding and a Top-k extension, new relations and new retained-state patterns are added without expanding the trusted computing base: they reuse the same trust boundary. The checker correctly accepts all tested legal configurations and rejects all adversarial proposals.
AI.conclusion: A single checked-lowering architecture can enforce diverse, declaratively specified memory and behavioral contracts for tool calls made by agents. By separating audited relation plugins from a common runtime for dispatch, resource control, execution, and publication, SkillEffect enables safe, resource-bounded tool use while preserving flexibility in the computations that can be supported.

title: Institution-Specific LLM Prompting Recovers PHI That De-identification Systems and Their Gold Standards Both Miss
summary:
Secondary use of electronic health records requires de-identification, yet existing systems miss \emph{institutionally situated} protected health information (PHI) such as hospital abbreviations, building names, and internal codes whose status is locally determined. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) with in-context learning (ICL) can close this gap and control the precision--recall trade-off.
  On 100 annotated pediatric oncology notes (5,322 PHI spans) from Texas Children's Hospital, we benchmarked eight LLMs against two purpose-built systems (Stanford TiDE, OpenMed PII) and two pattern-based baselines. Each LLM ran under three prompts of increasing specificity: (1) a HIPAA-aligned baseline, (2) baseline plus the institutional PHI categories it missed, and (3) prompt 2 plus instructions against over-redacting clinical content. We then compared 14~multi-agent and ensemble configurations against the best single prompt, with recall the primary safety metric.
  LLMs outperformed the purpose-built systems (best F1=0.918$\pm$0.001 vs.\ TiDE 0.779), with advantages concentrated in contextual categories. Naming the missed categories recovered 79\% (48/61) of them, and discouraging over-redaction restored precision. No agentic architecture beat calibrated single-pass prompting (F1 0.906--0.907), but LLM outputs surfaced 414~candidate annotation gaps; re-annotation confirmed 227~PHI spans, against which the final prompt reached recall=0.981 (F1=0.907$\pm$0.002).
  Well-calibrated ICL resolves both the institutional PHI gap and the precision--recall trade-off in one LLM call per note. LLMs cost more to run than traditional methods, but that cost buys a way to audit the reference standard.
  LLMs are a legitimate, adaptable alternative to purpose-built de-identification systems; institution-specific prompt development should be the primary adaptation strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) with in-context learning can better de-identify electronic health records—especially local, institution-specific PHI—than existing rule-based and purpose-built systems, while managing the precision–recall trade-off.
AI.motivation: Secondary analysis of electronic health records requires rigorous de-identification to protect patient privacy. Existing de-identification systems, often pattern- or rule-based, systematically miss institution-specific PHI such as local abbreviations, building names, and internal codes, which are not captured in generic PHI taxonomies. This gap creates privacy risks and undermines the safe reuse of clinical text. There is a need to understand whether modern LLMs, guided purely by prompts rather than retraining, can plug this institutional PHI gap and allow practitioners to tune recall and precision to meet safety and utility requirements.
AI.method: Using 100 annotated pediatric oncology notes from Texas Children’s Hospital containing 5,322 PHI spans, the authors benchmark eight LLMs against two specialized de-identification systems (Stanford TiDE, OpenMed PII) and two pattern-based baselines. For each LLM, they test three prompts: (1) a HIPAA-aligned baseline prompt; (2) the baseline plus explicit mention of institution-specific PHI categories previously missed; and (3) prompt 2 plus explicit instructions to avoid over-redaction of clinically relevant content. They additionally construct 14 multi-agent and ensemble configurations (e.g., combining outputs from different prompts or models) and compare them to the best single-prompt configuration, prioritizing recall as the key safety metric. They also use LLM outputs to surface possible gaps in the original human annotations and conduct re-annotation to validate these candidate missing PHI spans.
AI.result: LLMs substantially outperform purpose-built de-identification systems: the best LLM configuration achieves F1=0.918±0.001, compared to TiDE’s 0.779, with most of the advantage in PHI categories that require contextual understanding (e.g., institution-specific identifiers). When the prompt is augmented with the specific institutional PHI categories missed by the baseline, the model recovers 79% (48/61) of those categories. Adding anti-over-redaction instructions restores precision lost from making the prompt more inclusive. None of the 14 multi-agent or ensemble approaches exceed the performance of a well-tuned single-pass prompt, whose F1 plateaus around 0.906–0.907. However, LLM predictions flag 414 possible missing annotations in the gold standard; manual review confirms 227 additional PHI spans, and relative to this updated reference the final prompt reaches recall of 0.981 with F1=0.907±0.002.
AI.conclusion: A carefully designed in-context learning setup allows LLMs to close the institutional PHI gap and manage the precision–recall trade-off in a single de-identification pass per clinical note. Although LLMs are more expensive to run than traditional de-identification tools, they deliver higher accuracy on context-dependent, institution-specific PHI and can also help audit and improve the human reference standard by surfacing missed PHI. The authors argue that LLMs are a viable and flexible alternative to dedicated de-identification systems, and that tailoring prompts to each institution’s local PHI landscape should be the main means of adaptation, rather than building entirely new rule-based systems.

title: Memory Is Communication: The Frontier Between Remembering and Signaling
summary: A bounded agent may obtain information for a decision from its own past, from peers, or from both sources. Retaining task-relevant history can reduce later communication, while a peer message can supply what memory lacks. Under limits on both resources, how should an agent allocate its information budget? Given a fixed task and decision rule, the memory and message rate pairs attaining a performance threshold form an achievable region under specified rules for using history and peer observations. We call its efficient boundary the remembering--signaling frontier. Across conditions where history permits the same maximum reduction in task loss, we hypothesize that a bounded agent will need less peer communication when it obtains a larger loss reduction from history. In preliminary referential games, target repetition coincided with shorter successful messages, while predictability from a hidden cyclic rule did not shorten them. Experiments varying memory and message rates can estimate the frontier and test this prediction across cooperative tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how a bounded agent should optimally trade off using its own memory versus communicating with peers to make good decisions, characterizing the efficient frontier between memory and messaging needs.
AI.motivation: Agents with limited cognitive and communication resources must decide whether to rely more on internal memory (history) or external information (peer messages) for making decisions. Understanding this tradeoff is important for designing efficient multi-agent and human-AI systems, where both storage and bandwidth are constrained. The authors aim to formalize this tradeoff and predict how improving the usefulness of memory affects the need for communication.
AI.method: The authors fix a task and a decision rule, and model an agent that can use two information channels: its own history (memory) and peer messages (communication). They define an “achievable region” of memory–message-rate pairs that reach a given performance (loss) threshold under specified policies for using history and observations. The efficient boundary of this region is termed the remembering–signaling frontier. They propose a hypothesis about the shape of this frontier and run preliminary referential game experiments, manipulating target repetition and hidden cyclic regularities, to see how these affect message lengths as a proxy for communication needs. They also propose future experiments that systematically vary memory and message rates to empirically estimate the frontier.
AI.result: In preliminary referential game experiments, when targets were repeated over time (allowing useful history), successful agents produced shorter messages, indicating reduced communication needs. However, when predictability came from a hidden cyclic rule (which did not translate into effectively usable history for the agent’s policy), message lengths did not become shorter. These findings support the idea that certain forms of historical structure can reduce communication, while others do not automatically do so.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces the concept of a remembering–signaling frontier to capture optimal tradeoffs between memory and communication for bounded agents. It hypothesizes and preliminarily supports the claim that when history yields a larger reduction in task loss, less peer communication is required to reach the same performance level. The referential game results suggest that the kind of structure present in past experience matters: repetition that agents can exploit reduces message length, whereas less accessible regularities do not. The authors argue that more systematic experiments varying memory and message budgets can map out this frontier and test the theory across cooperative tasks.

title: Foundation Agents Meet Agentic Deep Research: Evidence-Grounded Clinical Code Forecasting
summary: Next-encounter ICD forecasting predicts which standardized diagnosis codes will be documented at a future visit from the longitudinal record available beforehand. The task is prospective and multi-label: the target note does not yet exist, and several codes may be correct. Structured EHR foundation models capture recurrence and temporal progression, whereas language foundation models generate flexible diagnostic hypotheses. We introduce ICD-Deepresearch, a DeepResearch workflow that composes these predictive foundation models with medical search and ICD dictionaries. Because no source reveals the future code set, research evaluates candidate transitions by linking patient evidence, external clinical relations, and exact code semantics under a fixed top-K budget. Candidate Generation uses SparseEHR to produce an EHR Prior that initializes two bounded Research Expansion rounds; an independent GPT-5 Direct Forecast supplies complementary candidates. Final Selection validates, deduplicates, and jointly ranks both paths, after which a separate module writes rationales without changing predictions. Finally ICD-Deepresearch achieves patient-averaged precision/recall of 24.60/35.09% on MIMIC-III and 25.14/48.32% on MIMIC-IV. Physicians rate 51% and 68% of its retrieved documents useful, compared with 22% and 39% for standalone GPT-5 web search and 32% and 41% for Medical Deep Research. ICD-Deepresearch therefore improves over the registered local comparators while retrieving evidence with higher physician-rated usefulness than the standalone research systems

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ICD-Deepresearch, a workflow that forecasts which diagnosis codes (ICDs) will appear at a patient’s next visit by combining predictive EHR models, language models, and medical search under a top-K candidate budget.
AI.motivation: Accurately predicting which ICD codes will be documented at a patient’s next encounter can support proactive care, decision support, and billing, but is hard because the target note does not yet exist, multiple labels may be correct, and no single data source reveals the true future code set. Existing structured EHR models capture temporal patterns but lack semantic flexibility, while language models can hypothesize diagnoses but are not tightly grounded in patient data and code semantics. There is a need for a system that prospectively predicts codes while jointly leveraging longitudinal EHR, external medical knowledge, and code dictionaries, and that can be evaluated under realistic constraints on how many candidate codes can be considered (top-K).
AI.method: The authors design ICD-Deepresearch, a multi-stage DeepResearch workflow that composes two kinds of foundation models—structured EHR models (SparseEHR) and a large language model (GPT-5)—with external medical search and ICD code dictionaries. First, Candidate Generation uses SparseEHR to produce an EHR Prior, i.e., an initial set of likely ICD transitions. This prior then seeds two bounded rounds of Research Expansion that retrieve external clinical relations and evidence while staying within a fixed top-K candidate budget. In parallel, an independent GPT-5 Direct Forecast proposes complementary ICD candidates directly from the longitudinal record. In the Final Selection stage, candidates from both paths are validated, deduplicated, and jointly ranked based on how well patient evidence, external relations, and exact ICD semantics support each code. A separate post-hoc module generates natural-language rationales for the final predictions but is explicitly prevented from changing the chosen codes, ensuring a clear separation between prediction and explanation.
AI.result: On the MIMIC-III dataset, ICD-Deepresearch attains patient-averaged precision of 24.60% and recall of 35.09% for next-encounter ICD prediction; on MIMIC-IV it achieves 25.14% precision and 48.32% recall. In physician evaluations of retrieved evidence, 51% (MIMIC-III) and 68% (MIMIC-IV) of the documents surfaced by ICD-Deepresearch are rated useful. These usefulness rates exceed those of two strong baselines: standalone GPT-5 web search (22% and 39%) and Medical Deep Research (32% and 41%). Thus, the method improves both prediction performance relative to local registered comparators and the practical usefulness of supporting evidence according to clinicians.
AI.conclusion: ICD-Deepresearch demonstrates that composing structured EHR foundation models with large language models, medical search, and ICD dictionaries within a controlled DeepResearch workflow yields better prospective multi-label ICD forecasting than existing local baselines. By operating under a fixed top-K candidate budget, the framework reflects realistic clinical decision-support constraints, and its separation of prediction from rationale generation enhances transparency without compromising the underlying predictions. The higher physician-rated usefulness of retrieved documents suggests that the system not only predicts future diagnosis codes more accurately but also surfaces more clinically meaningful evidence, positioning it as a promising approach for next-encounter decision support and coding assistance.

title: DiSCO: Defending text-to-image generation through distribution-guided contrastive prompt optimization
summary: As text-to-image generative models advance, they raise critical safety concerns, particularly the generation of Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content such as violence and nudity, further exacerbated by red-teaming adversarial attacks. Existing defenses predominantly operate under white-box assumptions, relying on text encoder optimization, weight editing, or inference-time intervention, and fundamentally cannot scale to proprietary models. Black-box alternatives based on LLM prompt rewriting offer broader applicability, yet fail in a critical regime we identify as the \textit{benign adversarial} problem: prompts that are linguistically safe but still trigger harmful generation due to the model's learned data distribution. We propose DiSCO, a zero-shot, strictly black-box defense that operates entirely at the prompt level as a plug-and-play module, requiring no model retraining, fine-tuning, or access to model internals. DiSCO performs distribution-guided suffix expansion via beam search, optimized through contrastive scoring over safe and unsafe image pools generated by the target model itself, with iterative adaptive feedback until safe content is produced. We demonstrate that DiSCO consistently enhances the safety of both undefended and defended models on the I2P benchmark under multiple red-teaming attacks, achieving 37.7% and 25.13% ASR reduction, respectively, while maintaining semantic fidelity and improving image coherence. As a black-box, architecture-agnostic module, DiSCO can be readily applied to any text-to-image system without necessitating any changes to the model itself.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DiSCO, a zero-shot black-box prompt-level defense that reduces unsafe image generation (NSFW, violence, nudity) in text-to-image models by adaptively expanding prompts with safe suffixes using contrastive scoring over model-generated image pools.
AI.motivation: Advances in text-to-image models have made it easy to generate high-quality images, but they also increase the risk of generating NSFW content, especially under adversarial (red-teaming) prompts. Existing defenses often assume white-box access (e.g., editing model weights, modifying encoders, or inference-time interventions) which do not scale to proprietary or closed-source models. Black-box methods using LLM-based prompt rewriting are broadly applicable but fail on 'benign adversarial' prompts that look linguistically safe yet still trigger harmful generations due to the model’s learned data distribution. The paper is motivated by the need for a scalable, architecture-agnostic, purely black-box defense that can handle such benign adversarial cases while preserving prompt intent and image quality.
AI.method: The authors propose DiSCO, a zero-shot, strictly black-box, plug-and-play defense operating purely at the text prompt level. DiSCO conducts distribution-guided suffix expansion using beam search: it appends candidate suffixes to the original prompt and evaluates them by generating images from the target model itself. It builds safe and unsafe image pools and applies a contrastive scoring scheme that favors suffixes leading to safe images and penalizes those leading to unsafe ones. The system iteratively refines the suffixes with adaptive feedback until the generated images are deemed safe, without any access to model internals, weight updates, or fine-tuning. The method is architecture-agnostic and works entirely through black-box interaction with the text-to-image model’s input-output behavior.
AI.result: On the I2P benchmark under multiple red-teaming attacks, DiSCO significantly reduces the attack success rate (ASR) for both undefended and previously defended models. Specifically, it achieves a 37.7% reduction in ASR for undefended models and a 25.13% reduction for models that already have built-in safety defenses. In addition to improving safety, DiSCO maintains semantic fidelity to the original prompt and can even enhance image coherence. The experiments show that DiSCO is robust to benign adversarial prompts and works effectively across different text-to-image architectures without modifications to the underlying models.
AI.conclusion: DiSCO provides an effective, scalable, and strictly black-box defense mechanism for improving safety in text-to-image generative models. By performing distribution-guided prompt suffix expansion with contrastive scoring over model-generated safe/unsafe image pools, it can mitigate NSFW and other harmful outputs, including those triggered by benign adversarial prompts, without modifying or accessing model internals. The method consistently reduces attack success rates while preserving or improving semantic alignment and coherence, and because it is architecture-agnostic and plug-and-play, it can be easily integrated into any existing text-to-image system.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Decision Making in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly answer questions whose correctness depends on visual, textual, temporal, acoustic, document, chart, or embodied evidence. Their failures are therefore not only linguistic. A fluent answer may conceal poor input quality, a perceptual error, weak grounding, conflict between modalities, unstable reasoning, distribution shift, or a question that is not answerable from the supplied evidence. This survey organizes the literature on uncertainty-aware MLLMs around a decision-centered framework: uncertainty sources give rise to observable signals, signals must be calibrated or controlled for risk, and calibrated uncertainty should determine the system action. We review work on token and logit uncertainty, semantic disagreement, perturbation instability, grounding and attribution scores, verbalized confidence, verifier and judge scores, conformal prediction, selective answering, abstention, clarification, retrieval, self-checking, and escalation. The central argument is that uncertainty should not be evaluated only as a confidence number; it should be evaluated by whether it improves behavior under insufficient, conflicting, shifted, or high-risk multimodal evidence. We position this survey against text-only uncertainty and abstention surveys, broad MLLM surveys, MLLM hallucination surveys, and safety-oriented reviews. We conclude with open problems in source-aware decomposition, action-aware benchmarks, calibration under shift, black-box uncertainty estimation, broader modality coverage, reproducible reporting, and human-centered uncertainty communication.

AI.tldr: Survey of uncertainty in multimodal LLMs and how it should drive system decisions, not just be a confidence number.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs rely on diverse evidence sources (images, audio, documents, etc.), so their mistakes stem from many non-linguistic factors such as bad inputs, perception errors, and modality conflicts. Existing work on uncertainty has focused mainly on text-only models and on scalar confidence, which is insufficient to manage the richer, riskier failure modes of MLLMs. There is a need to systematically organize how uncertainty arises in MLLMs, how it is measured and calibrated, and how it should guide system behavior, especially under insufficient, conflicting, or shifted evidence.
AI.method: The paper conducts a structured survey using a decision-centered framework. It decomposes the pipeline into: (1) sources of uncertainty in multimodal settings; (2) observable signals of uncertainty (e.g., token/logit-level metrics, semantic disagreement, perturbation-based instability, grounding/attribution scores, verbalized confidence, verifier/judge scores); (3) calibration and risk-control mechanisms (e.g., conformal prediction, black-box methods); and (4) downstream actions (selective answering, abstention, clarification, retrieval, self-checking, escalation). It compares and categorizes existing work across these stages and across modalities and tasks, and contrasts MLLM-specific uncertainty work with earlier text-only and safety/hallucination-focused surveys.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes and classifies a broad body of work on uncertainty-aware multimodal LLMs, mapping each method to its uncertainty source, signal type, calibration approach, and resulting action. It highlights techniques such as token/logit uncertainty, semantic and verifier-based disagreement, perturbation tests, grounding scores, and decision policies like abstention, selective answering, and escalation. It also delineates the gaps between current practice and the ideal of decision-relevant, source-aware uncertainty handling in MLLMs, especially under distribution shift and across diverse modalities.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that uncertainty in MLLMs must be judged by its effect on system behavior under challenging evidence conditions, not just by numerical confidence calibration. They emphasize source-aware decomposition of uncertainty, action-aware benchmarks that test whether uncertainty improves decisions, and robust calibration under distribution shifts. The survey identifies open challenges including black-box uncertainty estimation, covering more modalities and tasks, standardized and reproducible evaluation, and improving how uncertainty is communicated to humans, setting an agenda for future research on uncertainty-aware MLLMs.

title: KernelArc: A Multi-Agent Framework for GPU Kernel Optimization
summary: We present KernelArc, a multi-agent framework for autonomous GPU kernel optimization across heterogeneous workloads. Strategy-specialized agents run in parallel and coordinate through conclusions-only shared memory, a deterministic benchmark guard, and read-only cross-agent state with plateau-triggered drafting. We evaluate \kernelarc{} on NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs using category-representative SOL-ExecBench workloads. The resulting implementations span custom BF16 GEMM, static cuBLASLt Expert-API configuration tables, fused mixture-of-experts backward, shape-gated decoder-layer fusion, native NVFP4 grouped-query attention, and paged prefill attention. At the public SOL-ExecBench leaderboard snapshot recorded on July~30, 2026, these submissions ranked first on representative L1, L2, Quantization, and FlashInfer tasks. The trajectories support the paper's central motivation: shared multi-agent search can broaden exploration and reach stronger incumbents within a fixed candidate budget, while the value of individual coordination features depends on the kernel and optimization stage.

AI.tldr: KernelArc is a multi-agent system that automatically optimizes GPU kernels for diverse workloads, outperforming existing methods on several benchmark categories.
AI.motivation: Manual kernel optimization and single-strategy autotuners struggle to explore the large search space of GPU implementations across heterogeneous workloads within a limited candidate budget. The authors want a way to coordinate multiple specialized optimization strategies so that search coverage improves and better-performing kernels are found reliably under fixed evaluation constraints.
AI.method: They design KernelArc, a multi-agent framework where different strategy-specialized agents run in parallel. Agents coordinate indirectly via conclusions-only shared memory, a deterministic benchmarking guard, read-only access to each other’s states, and a plateau-triggered drafting mechanism that allows agents to build on others’ progress when improvements stall. The framework is evaluated on NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs using SOL-ExecBench workloads covering several kernel types and use cases.
AI.result: KernelArc generates high-performance implementations for multiple kernel families, including custom BF16 GEMM, cuBLASLt Expert-API configuration tables, fused MoE backward passes, shape-gated decoder-layer fusions, native NVFP4 grouped-query attention, and paged prefill attention. On the SOL-ExecBench public leaderboard as of July 30, 2026, these implementations achieve first place on representative L1, L2, Quantization, and FlashInfer tasks.
AI.conclusion: Shared multi-agent search can significantly improve GPU kernel optimization under a fixed candidate budget by broadening exploration and discovering stronger incumbent solutions. However, the effectiveness of specific coordination mechanisms (like shared memory, drafting, and benchmarking guards) is kernel- and stage-dependent, suggesting that coordination designs should be adaptive to the optimization context.

title: There is No Theoretical Curse of Multilinguality For Embedding Space Structure
summary: A central goal of multilingual NLP is to achieve high monolingual performance per language and cross-lingual alignment for large-scale language coverage with a multilingual model. The curse of multilinguality describes the phenomenon of degradation in multilingual model performance as we increase language coverage, posing a threat to the above goal. This paper asks whether multilingual embedding spaces are inherently incapable of achieving perfect multilinguality without a prohibitive increase in required capacity. We first formalize the goal of "perfect multilinguality", embodied in two multilinguality conditions. We then prove that the minimum dimensionality required for perfect multilinguality grows only logarithmically in the number of languages. That is, we show that there is no theoretical curse of multilinguality for embedding space structure. This suggests that the empirical curse of multilinguality is a result of real world data and training conditions. We back this understanding with a small-scale empirical study. Our paper provides the first theoretical and intrinsic perspective on the curse of multilinguality, with implications for the scientific understanding of this phenomenon.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that, in principle, multilingual embedding spaces can support many languages without a large increase in dimensionality, so the observed “curse of multilinguality” must come from practical data/training issues rather than fundamental geometric limits.
AI.motivation: Multilingual NLP models often perform worse on individual languages as the number of supported languages increases, a phenomenon called the curse of multilinguality. This raises a fundamental question: is there a theoretical limitation in shared embedding spaces that makes it impossible to maintain high monolingual performance and good cross-lingual alignment as we add languages, unless we blow up model size? The authors want to understand whether this performance degradation is inevitable from a representational standpoint or merely an artifact of how we currently train and use data.
AI.method: The authors first define what they call “perfect multilinguality” using two formal conditions that capture: (1) high-quality monolingual representations for each language and (2) consistent cross-lingual alignment across languages within a single embedding space. They then derive theoretical bounds on the minimum dimensionality required for an embedding space to satisfy these conditions as the number of languages grows. Specifically, they prove that the required dimensionality scales only logarithmically with the number of languages, implying that many languages can, in principle, be represented efficiently. To connect theory with practice, they also run a small empirical study, testing multilingual embeddings under controlled conditions to see how real models compare with the theoretical predictions.
AI.result: The main theoretical result is that the minimal embedding dimension needed for perfect multilinguality increases only logarithmically with the number of languages. This formally shows that, from a geometric/representational perspective, there is no inherent curse of multilinguality in embedding spaces themselves. The empirical study supports this theoretical view by indicating that observed performance degradation in multilingual models is not dictated by unavoidable dimensionality constraints but is more plausibly due to issues such as data imbalance, optimization, and model training regimes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that multilingual embedding spaces are, in theory, capable of supporting many languages with high-quality monolingual performance and good cross-lingual alignment without requiring a prohibitive increase in dimensionality. Thus, the commonly observed curse of multilinguality is not a fundamental property of representation spaces but instead arises from practical factors like data quality, distribution, and training procedures. This theoretical reframing provides a new basis for understanding and addressing multilingual performance degradation and suggests that future work should focus on improving data and training strategies rather than assuming hard representational limits.

title: A decodability criterion predicts when hidden-state selection beats majority voting in large language models
summary: Combining the answers a large language model (LLM) samples for a question into one decision is a test-time information fusion problem, usually solved by majority voting. Voting is unreliable on difficult questions, where the sampled answers share correlated errors, so the wrong answer can win and drawing more samples makes the decision worse. Selecting a candidate by reading a correctness signal from the model's hidden states is a promising alternative, but its accuracy varies across models and tasks, and no measure indicates when it can be trusted. In this paper, we propose CASE (Correctness-Axis SElection), a dynamic selection combiner that trains a linear gate on the answer-token hidden state and selects the highest-scoring candidate. Its main contribution is decodability, a leakage-free measure of how well the gate ranks a question's correct candidates above its incorrect ones, which predicts whether hidden-state selection will outperform voting. A conventional probe appears accurate only because of question-identity leakage, which vanishes under question-grouped evaluation. On held-out data, decodability predicts the accuracy gain of selection over voting with a Pearson correlation r=0.75 and a decision threshold near AUC=0.60. Across general and medical LLMs, CASE improves over voting by up to 19 points on medium-difficulty questions and 16.8 points on hard questions. Decodability depends on the aligned knowledge a model must recall, not on its scale, and its prediction transfers to an unseen scientific domain within 3.8 points. It thus provides a practical criterion, measurable in advance for a given model and task, for choosing between learned selection and majority voting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CASE, a method to better combine multiple LLM sampled answers at test time by using hidden-state-based selection instead of majority vote, and introduces a new reliability metric (decodability) that predicts when this selection will beat voting.
AI.motivation: Majority voting over multiple sampled LLM answers fails on hard questions because samples share correlated errors, so taking more samples can reinforce the wrong answer. Existing hidden-state correctness probes can sometimes outperform voting but are unreliable and lack a principled signal indicating when they can be trusted. There is a need for a robust, advance-measurable criterion to decide whether to use hidden-state selection or simple voting for a given model and task.
AI.method: They introduce CASE (Correctness-Axis Selection), which trains a linear gate on the hidden state of the answer token for each candidate answer. At inference, CASE scores each candidate and selects the highest-scoring one instead of using majority vote. The key methodological innovation is the concept of decodability: a leakage-free measure, based on how well the gate ranks correct over incorrect candidates, computed under question-grouped evaluation to avoid question-identity leakage. They compare CASE-based selection to majority voting across models, tasks, and domains, and correlate decodability (AUC) with the observed accuracy gain of selection over voting.
AI.result: Decodability correlates strongly with when hidden-state selection outperforms majority voting, with Pearson r=0.75 between decodability and the accuracy gain over voting, and a practical decision threshold around AUC=0.60. They show that conventional probing looks good mainly due to question-identity leakage, which disappears under group-wise evaluation. Across general and medical LLMs, CASE improves over majority vote by up to 19 percentage points on medium-difficulty and 16.8 points on hard questions. Decodability is tied to the aligned knowledge the model must recall rather than model scale, and predictions generalize to an unseen scientific domain within 3.8 percentage points of expected performance.
AI.conclusion: CASE offers a more reliable way to aggregate multiple LLM samples by using a trained linear gate on hidden states and, crucially, by providing decodability as an advance metric to decide whether to trust hidden-state selection over majority voting for a given model-task pair. Decodability is leakage-free, predictive of actual gains, relatively scale-invariant, and transferable across domains, giving practitioners a concrete, measurable criterion for choosing between learned selection methods and simple majority voting at test time.

title: A Glyph Is Not a Letter, a Token Is Not a Word, a Space Is Not a Space: What the Units of Voynichese Are Not
comment: 33 pages, 7 figures, 3 appendices. Analysis code and data are included as ancillary files and mirrored at https://github.com/lrozanova/voynich-units
summary: The Voynich manuscript (Beinecke MS 408) is usually analysed on three unstated assumptions: that its glyphs are letters, that the strings between blanks are words, and that every blank is a word space. We test all three against the Zandbergen-Landini transliteration with matched prose, cipher, and pseudo-text controls and quire-level resampling. None holds, and the failures share a shape: the order in Voynichese sits at the edges of tokens and at graded boundaries between them, not in the succession of tokens themselves. Glyph regularity is too strong for one-to-one substitution of any tested plaintext (conditional entropy 2.7 bits against about 3.5 for Latin, Italian, and English) and resolves instead onto a quire-stable scale of recurrent multi-symbol units. Tokens form a plausible vocabulary, yet the identity of one token predicts the next by under 1% of token entropy, below every matched control (2-10%), while the glyphs at token edges share 0.2 bits of mutual information, more than in any prose control. Blanks fall into two regimes: the separators transcribers marked uncertain behave like word-internal junctures, are physically narrower on the page (AUC 0.905 from independent image coordinates, with the same sign in a small blind ink audit), and are crossed by learned units even when every space is erased before learning. This profile is also what discriminates. A published Voynich-imitating cipher and a self-citation text generator both reproduce the low entropy, the unit scale, the weak token order, and the null result of a calibrated substitution attack; neither reproduces the edge-glyph coupling or the open, hapax-rich vocabulary (70% singleton types against 41% and 59-60%). Any account of the manuscript must therefore earn, rather than assume, the step from glyphs, tokens, and separators to letters, words, and word spaces, and these are the measurements on which to do so.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges three common but usually unstated assumptions about the Voynich manuscript: that its glyphs are letters, its tokens are words, and its blanks are word spaces, and shows statistically that these assumptions do not hold as normally conceived.
AI.motivation: Research on the Voynich manuscript usually presumes it encodes a natural language via a substitution cipher, where each glyph corresponds to a letter, tokens are words, and blanks separate words. These assumptions drive almost all linguistic and cryptanalytic work on the manuscript but are rarely tested directly. The authors aim to rigorously test these foundational assumptions using modern quantitative methods, in order to clarify what structural properties any viable theory of the manuscript must explain.
AI.method: Using the Zandbergen-Landini transliteration of the Voynich manuscript, the authors compare its structure to matched controls: genuine prose texts, ciphers, and pseudo-text generators. They perform quire-level resampling to avoid overfitting to specific sections. They compute conditional entropy of glyph sequences, mutual information at token edges, token-transition predictability, and the behavior of blanks as separators. They analyze the scaling of recurrent multi-symbol units, examine the physical widths of spaces on the manuscript pages, and test substitution attacks. They also analyze published Voynich-like ciphers and text generators to see which properties can and cannot be reproduced artificially.
AI.result: The authors find that: (1) Voynich glyph sequences have lower conditional entropy (2.7 bits) than typical natural-language plaintexts in Latin, Italian, and English (~3.5 bits), inconsistent with simple one-to-one substitution of letters. Instead, structure appears at the level of recurrent multi-symbol units that are stable by quire. (2) Tokens behave like a vocabulary but exhibit extremely weak sequential dependence: knowing one token predicts the next at under 1% of token entropy, far weaker than in matched prose and cipher controls (2–10%). (3) Glyphs at token boundaries show unusually strong mutual information (~0.2 bits), higher than in the prose controls, indicating that local edge structure is more regular than internal token structure. (4) Blanks separate into two types: uncertain separators behave like internal junctures within words, are measurably narrower in the manuscript images (AUC 0.905), and are traversed by the learned multi-glyph units even when spaces are removed before learning. (5) Existing Voynich-imitating ciphers and text generators can match global statistics like low entropy, unit scale, weak token order, and resistance to substitution decoding, but fail to reproduce specific features such as strong edge-glyph coupling and an unusually open, hapax-rich vocabulary (70% singleton types vs 41% and 59–60% in controls).
AI.conclusion: The manuscript’s structure cannot be straightforwardly modeled as ordinary text in an alphabetic substitution cipher where glyphs are letters, tokens are words, and blanks are word spaces. Order and regularity reside mainly at token boundaries and in recurrent multi-glyph units rather than in token sequences themselves. Blanks include both true separators and word-internal junctures, and the vocabulary is unusually open and hapax-rich. Any serious account of the Voynich manuscript must therefore justify, not assume, how glyphs, tokens, and blanks correspond to linguistic units, and must match the detailed statistical and physical measurements described in this study.

title: Toward Personal Intelligence Through Cooperative Observation
summary: A personal AI system needs a model of the user's goals, constraints, and ongoing commitments to plan and act on their behalf, and the quality of that model is bounded by what the system can observe. Broader observation does not by itself improve assistance because a bounded system must select and compress information for the task at hand. We argue that this observation bottleneck has a cooperative structure: the system builds a partial model of the user's changing life, the user evaluates its actions, and the user's consent and control shape what it can observe next. Useful and inspectable behavior can give users a reason to maintain or expand the observation channel, while failures can lead them to correct, narrow, revoke, or abandon it. We use the term cooperative observation for this feedback loop among usefulness, trust, and future access, and propose it as a framework for personal intelligence. We report a preliminary single-subject account from Organizm, a prototype used over six months, and outline evaluation directions for measuring how observation quality shapes personal AI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and motivates the concept of 'cooperative observation' as a framework for how personal AI systems model users through an ongoing feedback loop between observation, usefulness, and user control.
AI.motivation: Personal AI assistants must understand users’ goals, constraints, and commitments to act effectively on their behalf, but their models are limited by what they can observe. Simply increasing the breadth of observation does not automatically yield better assistance because systems are computationally bounded and must selectively compress information. There is a need for a principled framework that explains how user consent, trust, and system performance jointly determine what the AI can observe and how its user model evolves over time.
AI.method: The authors conceptually analyze the observation bottleneck in personal AI and propose the notion of 'cooperative observation'—a feedback loop where the system forms a partial model of the user, the user evaluates its actions, and this evaluation plus consent controls future observation. They then ground this framework in a preliminary, single-subject case study using Organizm, a prototype personal AI system deployed with one user over six months. They outline possible empirical evaluation directions rather than presenting large-scale experiments.
