AI.result: The paper provides a qualitative, single-user account showing how observation access, perceived usefulness, and user trust co-evolve when using the Organizm prototype over an extended period. It illustrates that useful and inspectable behavior encourages the user to maintain or expand the observation channel, while visible failures prompt the user to constrain or withdraw access. The main result is the articulation and initial grounding of cooperative observation as a meaningful way to think about how observation quality shapes personal AI effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that the key challenge for personal AI is not just data quantity but the cooperative structure of observation between user and system. They propose 'cooperative observation' as a guiding framework for designing personal intelligence systems that are useful, inspectable, and respectful of user control. They argue that future work should systematically measure how different observation regimes and feedback dynamics affect model quality, assistance performance, user trust, and long-term engagement.

title: Emotion Across Speech and Faces: Shared Affective Mechanisms in Multimodal Foundation Models
summary: Modern multimodal foundation models (MFMs) have made rapid progress on tasks requiring integrated perception across speech, vision, and language, including emotion recognition. However, it remains unclear whether they recognize speech and facial emotion through shared affective functional units or modality-specific pathways. We explore emotion-sensitive neurons (ESNs), sparse decoder neurons selectively associated with emotion categories, in three MFMs: Gemma-4-12B-it, MiniCPM-o-4.5, and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B. Using speech emotion recognition and facial expression recognition as complementary probes, we identify acoustic and visual ESNs. Visual ESNs are causally meaningful: deactivating them selectively impairs recognition of the associated facial emotion, whereas steering their activations selectively enhances recognition of that emotion relative to other emotion categories. Acoustic and visual ESNs further show emotion-matched overlap and similar layer-wise distributions, indicating partial structural alignment between affective representations across speech and faces. Finally, cross-modal interventions reveal bidirectional causal transfer: ESNs identified from one modality produce emotion-specific effects when applied to the other. Our findings provide one of the first cross-modality activation-level analyses of affective functional units in MFMs, suggesting that speech and facial emotion recognition partially converge onto sparse decoder-level components that can be localized and manipulated without training.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how modern multimodal foundation models internally represent emotions across speech and facial modalities, finding sparse emotion-sensitive neurons that partially align and can be causally manipulated without additional training.
AI.motivation: Although multimodal foundation models perform well on emotion-related tasks, it is not understood whether their emotion recognition relies on shared cross-modal mechanisms or on separate, modality-specific pathways. Clarifying this can deepen our understanding of model interpretability, cross-modal alignment, and the structure of affective representations.
AI.method: The authors examine three multimodal foundation models (Gemma-4-12B-it, MiniCPM-o-4.5, and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B). They identify sparse decoder neurons that are selectively associated with specific emotion categories during speech emotion recognition and facial expression recognition tasks, calling these emotion-sensitive neurons (ESNs). They conduct causal interventions by deactivating or steering these neurons and analyze their effects on recognition performance within and across modalities, including layer-wise distribution and cross-modal transfer tests.
AI.result: They find distinct sets of acoustic and visual ESNs, with visual ESNs showing clear causal roles: turning them off harms recognition of their associated emotion category, while amplifying them improves recognition for that category relative to others. ESNs across speech and face modalities show overlapping, emotion-matched subsets and similar distributions across layers, suggesting partial structural alignment of affective representations. Cross-modal manipulation of ESNs (e.g., applying ESNs discovered from speech to facial tasks and vice versa) leads to emotion-specific effects in the other modality, demonstrating bidirectional causal transfer.
AI.conclusion: The study provides evidence that speech and facial emotion recognition in multimodal foundation models partially converge on sparse, decoder-level emotion-sensitive neurons that are shared across modalities to some extent. These ESNs are localizable and causally manipulable without retraining, offering one of the first activation-level, cross-modal analyses of affective functional units in such models and advancing mechanistic interpretability for multimodal emotion processing.

title: KnowSim: Evaluating Information Calibration in LLM Assistants with User Simulators that Learn
summary: To effectively collaborate with users on knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) must perform information calibration: matching content to a user's evolving understanding and cognitive capacity. Yet user simulators used to evaluate and train LLMs do not explicitly model user knowledge so they neither produce realistic interactions across knowledge levels nor reflect how interactions unfold as that knowledge evolves. To close this gap, we introduce KNOWSIM, an evaluation framework built around a user simulator that maintains explicit knowledge states, represented as a graph of Information Units with prerequisite relationships, that evolve under update rules grounded in learning theory. KNOWSIM computes three metrics (Knowledge Gain, Delivery Calibration, Cognitive Overload) directly from the knowledge state trajectory, reflecting key mechanistic aspects of information calibration. We validate KNOWSIM against 705 human-AI sessions across two domains, stratified by knowledge level: its rankings align significantly with human judgments (73-74% sign agreement), outperforming three baseline simulators. Applied to 9 LLMs, KNOWSIM reveals that the best model shifts by user knowledge level, revealing aptitude-treatment interactions invisible to standard evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces KNOWSIM, a user-simulator-based evaluation framework that explicitly models and tracks user knowledge to assess how well LLMs calibrate information delivery to users with different and evolving knowledge levels.
AI.motivation: Existing user simulators used for training and evaluating LLMs on collaborative, knowledge-intensive tasks do not explicitly represent user knowledge. As a result, they cannot generate realistic interactions across varying expertise levels, nor can they capture how a user’s understanding changes over time during a session. This lack of mechanistic modeling hinders reliable measurement of an LLM’s ability to calibrate information (what to say, how much, and when) to a user’s cognitive capacity and current knowledge. The authors want a principled, theory-grounded way to simulate user learning and to quantitatively evaluate information calibration in LLM-user interactions.
AI.method: The authors propose KNOWSIM, an evaluation framework centered on a user simulator that maintains an explicit, dynamic knowledge state for the simulated user. This knowledge state is represented as a graph of Information Units (IUs) connected by prerequisite relations, encoding what needs to be known before new concepts can be learned. As a dialogue with an LLM proceeds, the simulator updates the user’s knowledge state according to rules grounded in learning theory (e.g., only learning IUs whose prerequisites are met and whose cognitive load is manageable). From the resulting trajectory of knowledge states over the interaction, KNOWSIM computes three metrics: (1) Knowledge Gain (how much new knowledge is acquired), (2) Delivery Calibration (how well the LLM’s explanations match the user’s current level), and (3) Cognitive Overload (whether the model overwhelms the user). The framework is validated by comparing KNOWSIM’s rankings of interaction quality with human judgments across 705 human-AI sessions and by comparing its performance against three existing baseline simulators. The authors then apply KNOWSIM to evaluate 9 different LLMs across user knowledge strata.
AI.result: KNOWSIM’s rankings of interaction quality show strong alignment with human judgments over 705 human-AI sessions in two domains, achieving 73–74% sign agreement. This performance surpasses three baseline simulators, indicating that explicitly modeling user knowledge and learning dynamics yields more human-consistent evaluations. When used to benchmark 9 LLMs, KNOWSIM reveals that the “best” model is not uniform across user groups: different models perform better for novices versus more knowledgeable users. This demonstrates aptitude–treatment interactions, where the effectiveness of an LLM depends on the user’s prior knowledge—patterns that typical aggregate evaluations fail to expose.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that explicit, theory-grounded modeling of user knowledge is crucial for realistically simulating users and for accurately evaluating LLMs on knowledge-intensive, collaborative tasks. KNOWSIM provides a principled framework that tracks user knowledge as a structured graph and yields interpretable, mechanistic metrics of information calibration: Knowledge Gain, Delivery Calibration, and Cognitive Overload. Its stronger agreement with human judgments compared with baseline simulators and its ability to uncover knowledge-dependent differences between LLMs suggest that future training and evaluation of conversational AI should incorporate such knowledge-aware user models. This can guide the design of systems that better adapt to users’ evolving understanding and cognitive capacities.

title: Children, but not language models, show accelerating returns in word learning
summary: Children learn hundreds of words over the first years of their lives, in a process that begins slowly but quickly picks up speed. Prior models describe vocabulary growth as evidence accumulation over time. Here we show that the process is best characterized as accelerating accumulation: children learn more from each additional unit of linguistic experience than they did from the one before. In contrast to children, language models -- even those trained on child-directed speech -- do not accelerate. Instead, they show constant proportional returns on new data, consistent with scaling laws. Children learn using many orders of magnitude less training data than language models; their increasingly efficient use of their learning input is a candidate explanation.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that children’s vocabulary growth is better described as accelerating learning efficiency from experience, whereas language models show constant proportional gains from additional data.
AI.motivation: To understand why children can learn language from vastly less data than language models and to test whether their word learning efficiency changes with more linguistic experience or stays constant as in standard evidence-accumulation and scaling-law models.
AI.method: Analyze longitudinal vocabulary growth in children as a function of cumulative linguistic input, and compare this pattern to the learning curves of language models trained on child-directed speech and other corpora, examining whether returns on additional data accelerate or remain proportional.
AI.result: Empirical data show that children’s vocabulary growth exhibits accelerating returns to additional linguistic experience—each extra unit of input yields more learned words than the previous—while language models display constant proportional returns consistent with scaling laws, even when trained on child-directed data.
AI.conclusion: Children’s vocabulary learning becomes increasingly efficient with more experience, in contrast to language models whose efficiency stays constant; this accelerating efficiency may help explain how children acquire rich vocabularies from far less data than language models require.

title: Synthesizing Feature Extractors: An Agentic Approach for Algorithm Selection
summary: Algorithm selection for constraint satisfaction problems requires extracting features that capture problem structure. Manually designing feature extractors demands deep domain expertise and quickly becomes a bottleneck when new problem classes appear. We present an automated approach that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) in an agentic check--fix--verify loop to synthesize executable Python scripts that act as interpretable, problem-specific feature extractors. Given a high-level MiniZinc model and an instance, the LLM agent generates code that constructs a typed graph representation and computes structural properties such as graph density, variable clustering, and constraint tightness. We evaluate our approach on three combinatorial problems (vehicle routing, car sequencing, fixed-length error-correcting codes) with a portfolio of five state-of-the-art solvers. The synthesized extractors yield algorithm selectors that consistently outperform both expert-curated mzn2feat features (up to $8.3$ percentage points (pp) test-set accuracy on FLECC) and the best transformer-based trans2feat variants. In the meanwhile, the synthesized feature extractors remain inspectable.

AI.tldr: They use LLM agents to automatically write Python feature extractors for CSP models, improving algorithm selection over hand-crafted and transformer-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Algorithm selection for CSPs needs structural features of problem instances. Manually crafting feature extractors is labor-intensive, requires deep expertise, and does not scale to new problem classes, creating a bottleneck. There is a need for an automated, adaptable, yet interpretable way to obtain problem-specific features from high-level constraint models.
AI.method: They design an LLM-based agent that, given a MiniZinc model and an instance, runs in a check–fix–verify loop to synthesize executable Python code. This code builds a typed graph representation of the instance and computes interpretable structural features such as graph density, variable clustering, and constraint tightness. These synthesized feature extractors are then used to train algorithm selection models over a portfolio of CSP solvers. They evaluate on three benchmark combinatorial problems and compare against expert-designed mzn2feat and transformer-based trans2feat methods.
AI.result: Across three CSP benchmarks (vehicle routing, car sequencing, and fixed-length error-correcting codes) and a portfolio of five advanced solvers, the LLM-synthesized feature extractors enable algorithm selectors that consistently achieve higher test accuracy than baselines. Improvements over expert-curated mzn2feat features reach up to 8.3 percentage points on the FLECC task and also surpass the best transformer-based trans2feat variants, while keeping the features interpretable.
AI.conclusion: Automated feature-extractor synthesis with LLM agents is an effective and interpretable alternative to hand-engineered or opaque neural feature pipelines for CSP algorithm selection. The approach generalizes across different problem classes, improves selection accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines, and mitigates the scalability bottleneck of manual feature engineering while preserving human inspectability of the resulting features.

title: Towards Safer RAG: Only Agents Capable of System 2 Thinking may Access Untrusted Documents
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has significantly enhanced the performance of large language models (LLMs), yet these systems remain vulnerable to knowledge-poisoning attacks, in which misinformation in retrieved documents can influence the model's final outputs. Notably, an LLM may correctly detect that a document contains incorrect information while nevertheless being influenced by it. Prior work has addressed this vulnerability through the Cordon Principle, which prevents models responsible for final answer synthesis from directly accessing raw evidence. Although effective, this strict isolation can introduce substantial computational overhead. In this work, we propose a refined security principle: only agents capable of deliberative System 2 reasoning may access untrusted documents. To evaluate this principle, we introduce novel metrics that quantify the discrepancy between misinformation detection and downstream influence. We then empirically compare state-of-the-art reasoning language models with standard language models across these metrics. Our results show that reasoning-capable models are substantially more robust to corrupted evidence, without requiring the strict isolation imposed by the Cordon Principle. These findings provide empirical support for our refined principle and suggest a more practical foundation for secure RAG system design.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to make Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems robust against knowledge-poisoning attacks by leveraging models with stronger deliberate reasoning instead of strict isolation mechanisms.
AI.motivation: RAG systems improve LLM performance by incorporating external documents, but they are vulnerable to knowledge-poisoning: misinformation in retrieved documents can bias final answers even when the model partially detects the errors. Existing defenses like the Cordon Principle isolate the answer-synthesizing model from raw evidence, which is secure but computationally expensive and impractical. The authors are motivated to find a more efficient, practical security principle that still protects RAG systems from corrupted evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose a new security principle: only agents (models/components) capable of System 2-style deliberate reasoning are allowed to read untrusted documents. They design metrics that separately measure (1) how well a model detects misinformation in retrieved documents and (2) how much that misinformation still influences its final answers. Using these metrics, they empirically compare state-of-the-art reasoning-focused LLMs with standard LLMs under knowledge-poisoning scenarios in RAG pipelines.
AI.result: Experiments show that reasoning-oriented language models are significantly more robust to poisoned or corrupted evidence in RAG settings. These models exhibit a smaller gap between detecting misinformation and being influenced by it, and they maintain higher answer reliability despite exposure to incorrect documents, all without relying on the heavy isolation of the Cordon Principle.
AI.conclusion: Deliberative, System 2-style reasoning capabilities materially improve an LLM’s robustness to knowledge poisoning in RAG systems. Allowing only such reasoning-capable agents to access untrusted documents can offer security comparable to the Cordon Principle but with less computational overhead. This supports the proposed refined principle as a more practical basis for designing secure, real-world RAG architectures.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: Evaluating Automated Safety Benchmarks for Small Language Models
comment: This paper is accepted for publication at ESORICS 2026
summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed in resource-constrained, privacy-sensitive settings, where safety and bias failures can cause security and societal risks. However, existing AI safety\slash security\slash compliance benchmarks are designed for large language models that may not transfer reliably to SLMs. We therefore ask: Can these benchmarks effectively and reliably evaluate SLMs? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale assessment of the effectiveness and robustness of these automated pipelines by evaluating five widely used benchmark suites across 26 open-source SLMs under a unified judging rubric, which assigns a score of 0, 1, or 0.5 to harmful, safe, or ambiguous/irrelevant responses, respectively. Across the benchmarks, ambiguous judgments dominate and correlate with prompt complexity and model architecture, indicating that {\em LLM-centric safety benchmarks are insufficient as standalone evidence for SLM safety assessment}. In general, the ambiguity rate increases with lexical density, output perplexity, and output length and decreases with lexical sophistication, self-coherence, and reply-prompt similarity. This reveals a capability-safety confound that mixes model capability with apparent safety. Since ambiguity is prevalent, aggregate mean-score leaderboards are mathematically brittle: model rankings change significantly under reasonable ambiguity treatments, even when the underlying outputs remain unchanged.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether existing safety and compliance benchmarks, originally designed for large language models, can reliably assess small language models (SLMs), finding that ambiguity in automated judgments is pervasive and makes current leaderboards mathematically unstable.
AI.motivation: Small Language Models are being used more in constrained, privacy-sensitive environments where safety failures are still risky, but most current safety benchmarks are tuned for large models. The authors want to know if these benchmarks meaningfully transfer to SLMs or if they misrepresent SLM safety due to capability differences and evaluation artifacts.
AI.method: The authors perform a large-scale empirical study of five widely used AI safety/security/compliance benchmark suites across 26 open-source SLMs. They use a unified judging rubric that labels model responses as harmful (0), safe (1), or ambiguous/irrelevant (0.5). They then analyze how often judgments are ambiguous and how this rate correlates with factors like prompt complexity, model architecture, lexical and structural properties of outputs, and self-coherence metrics.
AI.result: They find that ambiguous judgments dominate across benchmarks and that ambiguity correlates strongly with prompt complexity and model architecture. Ambiguity rates rise with lexical density, output perplexity, and length, and fall with lexical sophistication, self-coherence, and reply–prompt similarity. These patterns show that existing benchmarks entangle model capability with apparent safety. Due to the high prevalence of ambiguity, mean-score leaderboards are unstable: reasonable ways of treating ambiguous cases can significantly change model rankings even when underlying outputs are identical.
AI.conclusion: LLM-centric safety benchmarks are not reliable as standalone tools for assessing the safety of SLMs. Ambiguous judgments are widespread and systematically related to both model capabilities and linguistic properties of responses, creating a capability–safety confound. Consequently, current aggregate leaderboard scores are mathematically brittle, and more tailored, robust evaluation methods are needed for trustworthy SLM safety assessment.

title: Can LLMs Reason in a Legally Meaningful Manner? A Small-scale Study on European Court of Human Rights Cases
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, Submitted to AI4LAW Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Reasoning has become a standard technique and feature for contemporary LLMs; however, its application and quality in the context of demanding legal-oriented tasks, such as legal case forecasting, remain under explored. We investigate how LLMs reason in the context of legal case forecasting, using legal cases from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) as a testbed. We evaluate OpenAI GPT 5.4, a recent top-tier LLM, by exploring alternative prompting strategies that are more or less suggestive of what counts as legally meaningful reasoning in the context of ECtHR jurisprudence. We present our findings derived from assessing the model's responses with both human and LLM evaluation. We find that the examined model scores far from ideal in legal reasoning, the model produces structurally complete but substantively shallow analyses, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators are internally consistent yet align only weakly with our trained annotators, i.e., reliable but not a valid substitute for human evaluation. Overall, the expert-curated prompt leads to more comprehensive reasoning, which does not result in more accurate predictions compared to the other examined settings. Based on our findings, we urge the community not to rely solely on automated LLM-based evaluation and to avoid using task accuracy as an appropriate proxy for reasoning quality.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well a cutting-edge LLM reasons in legal case forecasting for ECtHR cases and shows that, despite seemingly good reasoning structure, its legal reasoning is shallow, its accuracy is limited, and LLM-based evaluators are not reliable substitutes for human experts.
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how modern LLMs truly perform legally meaningful reasoning in complex legal prediction tasks (ECtHR case forecasting), and to test whether prompting and LLM-based evaluators can improve or reliably assess such reasoning.
AI.method: Use ECtHR cases as a benchmark and test a top-tier LLM (OpenAI GPT 5.4) under different prompting strategies that vary in how much they guide the model toward legally meaningful reasoning. Evaluate the model’s predictions and generated reasoning using both human annotators and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, then compare consistency, alignment, and performance across settings.
AI.result: The LLM’s legal reasoning is far from ideal: it generates structurally well-formed but substantively shallow analyses. LLM-as-a-judge evaluations are internally consistent but only weakly aligned with expert human annotations. An expert-curated prompt yields more comprehensive reasoning, but this does not translate into higher prediction accuracy compared with other prompting strategies.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs, even top-tier ones, struggle with deep legal reasoning in ECtHR case forecasting. More elaborate, expert-designed prompts improve the apparent richness of reasoning but not its predictive accuracy. LLM-based automatic evaluation should not replace expert human assessment, and task accuracy alone is an inadequate proxy for reasoning quality in legal contexts.

title: Fool's Gold: Defensive Deception Against Safety-Removal Attacks on Open-Weight Models
summary: Safety alignment in open-weight language models is trivially removable: abliteration projects a refusal-mediating direction out of the weights in minutes, and no release-time defense we are aware of prevents it durably. What cannot be prevented can be deceived. Our defense, decoy hardening ("Fool's Gold"), concedes the refusal strip and poisons its payoff: once refusal is stripped, most answers to hazardous operational requests are confident, fluent decoys whose critical elements are falsified. Decoys are trained inside a differentiable simulation of the attack, expressing only in the attacked state; a refusal pin and benign leash hold clean-state behavior to the original. We instantiate it on seven models from five families (9B-122B, dense and mixture-of-experts). On the six models passing our pre-registered efficacy gate, 0.51-0.90 of attacked-state responses to held-out prompts are decoys, +0.27-0.84 attributable to the defense; all six stay within registered benign-behavior and capability budgets; the seventh (smaller) fails the gate (boundary case). Rates replicate on a frozen test split or untouched strata. The claim is epistemic: without independent ground truth, no observation surface we tested separates falsified answers from correct ones - on external red-team benchmarks' CBRNE-adjacent slice, the defended 122B is fatally wrong on 0.82-0.86 of matched-quality answers vs at most 0.10 undefended. Repeated sampling does not restore trust: element-wise consensus at K=64 reconstructs a fully usable procedure on 0.083-0.625 of prompts where the instrument validates, vs 0.58-0.96 undefended, with no label-free way to tell the regimes apart; on the weakest such model the claim is per-draw only. We evaluate chemical and biological hazards; the defense does not address in-context jailbreaks and protects only the initially released defended weights.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that safety alignment in open-weight language models can be easily removed, and proposes a defense called decoy hardening (“Fool’s Gold”) that makes unsafe-looking answers secretly wrong in critical details, in a way that attackers and evaluators cannot reliably distinguish from correct answers.
AI.motivation: Current safety alignment methods for open-weight language models are fragile: their refusal behaviors can be quickly removed by post-hoc weight editing attacks (like abliteration), and known defenses do not robustly prevent this. Because open-weight models can be locally modified by anyone, there is a need for a defense that remains effective even after such attacks, especially for preventing reliable use of models in high-risk domains like chemical and biological hazards.
AI.method: The authors introduce “decoy hardening” (Fool’s Gold), where instead of trying to prevent removal of refusal behavior, they assume an attacker will strip refusals and then train the model so that, in the attacked state, many hazardous answers become fluent but misleading decoys with falsified critical elements. They build a differentiable simulation of the weight-space attack and train decoy behavior only in this simulated attacked state. A “refusal pin” and a “benign leash” constrain training so that the model’s clean (unaltered) behavior stays close to the original model’s benign and capability profiles. They apply this to seven open-weight models across multiple families and sizes (9B–122B, dense and MoE), and evaluate decoy rates, benign behavior, and capabilities on held-out prompts and external red-team benchmarks focused on chemical and biological hazards.
AI.result: For six of seven models that pass a pre-defined efficacy threshold, between 51% and 90% of attacked-state responses to held-out hazardous prompts are decoys, with a 27–84 percentage point increase attributable to the defense. These models maintain benign behavior and capability within pre-registered budgets, while the smallest model fails the efficacy gate. The decoy rates are stable across frozen test splits and untouched prompt strata. On CBRNE-adjacent red-team benchmarks, the defended 122B model produces fatally wrong answers on about 82–86% of matched-quality hazardous responses, versus at most 10% for the undefended model. Even with repeated sampling (K=64) and element-wise consensus, attackers can reconstruct fully usable hazardous procedures on only 8.3–62.5% of validated prompts for defended models, compared to 58–96% for undefended ones, and there is no label-free test that reliably distinguishes decoys from correct answers. On the weakest model, this guarantee is only per single draw.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment that relies on refusals in open-weight language models is structurally fragile because simple weight-space attacks can reliably disable refusals. However, decoy hardening (Fool’s Gold) can significantly degrade an attacker’s ability to obtain correct hazardous guidance from attacked models by making many such responses convincing but strategically wrong, without noticeably harming benign performance or observable capabilities. The defense shifts safety from being based on overt refusal to being based on epistemic uncertainty: external observers and attackers lack a ground-truth-based, label-free method to tell correct hazardous answers from decoys. Nonetheless, the approach has limits: it does not protect against in-context jailbreaks and only applies to the initially released defended weights, not future modifications beyond the modeled attack class.

title: Polaris: Learning to Generate Table Descriptions from Retrieval Feedback
summary: Many table-centric NLP tasks such as NL2SQL first retrieve relevant tables from large collections using keyword search. Recent work uses LLMs to generate natural-language table descriptions to improve retrieval, but they are typically optimized for fluency rather than retrieval effectiveness. We present Polaris, a system that trains an LLM to generate table descriptions directly from retrieval feedback. Our key insight is that existing table retrieval benchmarks already contain the supervision needed for this task: given query-table relevance judgments, we generate multiple candidate descriptions for each table, rank them by their BM25 retrieval effectiveness, and use the resulting preference pairs to fine-tune the LLM with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Polaris further expands abbreviated table and column names before generation to reduce vocabulary mismatch. Extensive experiments show that Polaris outperforms the state-of-the-art AutoDDG solution, often by a significant margin. More broadly, our results demonstrate that retrieval benchmarks can be repurposed as supervision for training LLMs to generate retrieval-oriented metadata.

AI.tldr: They train an LLM to write table descriptions that maximize retrieval performance instead of fluency, using existing table retrieval benchmarks as supervision.
AI.motivation: In table-centric NLP tasks like NL2SQL, we must first retrieve relevant tables from large collections. Current approaches use LLMs to generate natural language descriptions of tables to aid keyword-based retrieval, but those descriptions are optimized mainly for human-like fluency, not for actual retrieval effectiveness. This causes mismatches between user queries and description text, reducing recall and precision. The authors want a way to systematically generate table descriptions that are explicitly optimized for retrieval quality, without requiring costly new annotations.
AI.method: They propose Polaris, a system that fine-tunes an LLM for retrieval-oriented table description generation. Polaris leverages existing table retrieval benchmarks that include query-table relevance judgments. For each table, it generates multiple candidate descriptions, then uses BM25 scores with respect to queries and relevance labels to rank these candidates by retrieval effectiveness. From these rankings it constructs preference pairs (better vs. worse descriptions) and fine-tunes the LLM via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) so that it prefers descriptions that yield better retrieval performance. Additionally, Polaris performs expansion of abbreviated table and column names prior to generation to reduce vocabulary mismatch between queries and metadata.
AI.result: In experiments on table retrieval tasks, Polaris significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method AutoDDG. The gains are often substantial, indicating that optimizing descriptions directly for retrieval metrics leads to more effective table retrieval. The experiments validate both the DPO-based fine-tuning from retrieval feedback and the abbreviation expansion component.
AI.conclusion: Polaris shows that LLMs can be trained to generate table descriptions that are explicitly optimized for retrieval effectiveness rather than just fluency, using only existing retrieval benchmarks as supervision. By turning query-table relevance judgments into preference signals for description quality and applying DPO plus abbreviation expansion, the system achieves state-of-the-art table retrieval performance. More generally, the work suggests that retrieval benchmarks can be repurposed to supervise LLMs in generating retrieval-oriented metadata across other domains as well.

title: Explicit State Elicitation Is Not Enough: A Controlled Audit of Memory-Policy Classification
summary: Personalized agents must decide whether retrieved user memory should be used, ignored, updated, or queried before it affects a current task. We use this setting to develop an empirical audit protocol for structured intermediate outputs: first audit dataset shortcuts, then isolate bundled prompt changes, check whether intermediate labels are answer-associated, test decomposed semantic evidence, and audit provider-level execution failures. A 480-example synthetic development set initially suggested large gains from a state-structured prompt bundle, but TF-IDF diagnostics showed lexical separability and no positive standalone Ignore cases. We therefore construct a frozen 160-example controlled counterfactual set with 40 matched four-way families and rule-derived reference policies. On this set, exposing the four state definitions improves accuracy, but an isolated explicit state-output field does not significantly improve policy accuracy for Llama-3.3-70B and gives only a marginal, non-significant gain for GPT-OSS-120B. Supplying benchmark-associated state labels shifts policy predictions, but because those labels deterministically map to policies, this is a label-conditioning diagnostic rather than evidence of a faithful internal mechanism. Family-level and seed-stability analyses further show that example-level accuracy overstates counterfactual consistency: complete four-way family success is rare. An exploratory follow-up that elicits decomposed semantic evidence also fails to improve routing for the cleanly evaluated endpoint; the corresponding GPT-OSS condition was unavailable because of provider-side request validation. We evaluate policy classification only, not downstream responses, tool actions, or memory-store mutation.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether adding structured state labels and decomposed evidence actually improves LLM policies for using user memory, finding that apparent gains on an initial synthetic set were artifacts and that, under controlled counterfactual evaluation, structured prompts and semantic evidence provide little reliable benefit or counterfactual consistency.
AI.motivation: Personalized AI agents must manage user memory carefully—deciding to use, ignore, update, or query it—because mistakes here can harm performance or user trust. Many methods introduce structured intermediate states (like explicit “memory routing” labels or decomposed reasoning) assuming they help models behave more reliably, but this assumption is rarely stress-tested. The authors want an empirical protocol to audit whether these structured intermediates actually drive robust, mechanistic improvements in policy decisions, rather than merely encoding label shortcuts or overfitting to artifacts in benchmark data.
AI.method: They propose a multi-step audit protocol for structured intermediate outputs in a memory-routing setting: (1) start with a synthetic development set and look for dataset shortcuts; (2) isolate and test bundled prompt changes such as state-structured prompts; (3) check whether intermediate labels are spuriously associated with answers; (4) create a controlled counterfactual dataset of matched ‘families’ of examples where the correct memory policy is rule-derived; (5) test the effect of exposing explicit state definitions versus just having an explicit state-output field; (6) run label-conditioning diagnostics by supplying benchmark-associated state labels that deterministically map to policies; (7) analyze family-level success and seed stability to assess counterfactual consistency; and (8) explore decomposed semantic evidence elicitation as another structured intermediate. They evaluate only the correctness of the memory policy classification (use/ignore/update/query), not downstream task performance, tools, or memory mutations, using models like Llama-3.3-70B and GPT-OSS-120B.
AI.result: The initial 480-example synthetic dev set appeared to show large policy gains from a state-structured prompt bundle, but TF-IDF diagnostics revealed lexical separability and no cases where an ‘Ignore’ decision clearly improved performance in isolation, indicating dataset artifacts. They then built a frozen 160-example controlled counterfactual dataset with 40 matched four-way families and rule-based reference policies. On this controlled set, simply exposing the four state definitions improves accuracy somewhat, but adding an explicit state-output field alone does not significantly improve policy accuracy for Llama-3.3-70B and provides only a marginal, statistically non-significant gain for GPT-OSS-120B. Providing benchmark-associated state labels clearly shifts model policies, but since these labels map deterministically to policies, the effect is just label-conditioning rather than evidence of a genuine internal mechanism using those states. Family-level and seed-stability analyses show that example-wise accuracy exaggerates robustness: complete success across all four counterfactual variants in a family is rare. An exploratory condition where the model first produces decomposed semantic evidence also fails to improve routing for the evaluated endpoint; an analogous GPT-OSS condition could not be run due to provider-side request validation failures.
AI.conclusion: Naively interpreting performance gains from structured prompts or intermediate labels in personalized memory-routing tasks can be misleading; initial improvements may be driven by dataset shortcuts, lexical artifacts, or direct label-conditioning rather than robust internal mechanisms. Under a controlled counterfactual evaluation, exposing state definitions offers only modest benefits, while adding explicit state-output fields or decomposed semantic evidence does not reliably improve memory-policy accuracy or counterfactual consistency for the tested models. The paper’s audit protocol—checking for shortcuts, using matched counterfactual families, and distinguishing label-conditioning from mechanistic use of intermediates—provides a more rigorous way to validate structured intermediate outputs, highlighting that example-level accuracy alone overstates true robustness in memory-routing policies.

title: AISA: AI Safety Assistant Framework for Continuous Improvement of Highway Construction
summary: Job Safety Analysis (JSA) and pre-task planning can benefit from prior incident records, yet historical accident data is often stored as unstructured narratives that are difficult to consult at the point of planning. A novel framework centered on large language models (LLMs) for highway construction safety reporting and planning is proposed as a foundation for future agentic applications, prioritizing deterministic, local inferencing. The first aim is to enable classification and quality scoring of incident narratives for existing and future reporting purposes. The second is to evaluate retrieval of relevant historical accidents, related imagery, and trusted industry documents for incorporation into daily safety plans. Neural probes were trained to classify incidents along four multiclass and two binary Occupational Injury and Illness Classification System (OIICS) fields and to derive an overall quality score, evaluated on a test set of over 15,000 narratives and a held-out set of 100 author-labeled records, benchmarked against a majority-vote LLM ensemble. The retrieval of historical accidents, reference imagery, and industry documents was benchmarked across embedding models using standard information retrieval metrics. OIICS classification reached 75% held-out accuracy, though the two binary flags were degenerate. The quality score, while meaningful on one database, was distorted on out-of-distribution fatalities in the held-out dataset. Accident retrieval recovered relevant incidents far above chance, performing best on lexically distinct construction activities. On document question answering, an open-weight decoder embedding model surpassed proprietary models. Overall, this work provides a new framework rooted in local inferencing and text embedding models for future agentic applications, with emphasis on bridging external data to JSA reports.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an LLM-based, locally run framework to classify and score construction incident reports and to retrieve similar past accidents and safety documents, improving job safety analysis and pre-task planning.
AI.motivation: Job Safety Analysis and pre-task planning need easy access to relevant past incidents and safety guidance, but historical accident data is mostly unstructured text that is hard to use operationally. There is also a desire to use LLM capabilities in safety-critical contexts while keeping inference local and deterministic, and to systematically integrate external data (accident records, images, standards) into daily safety plans.
AI.method: The authors design a framework relying on large language models and text embeddings that can run locally. They train neural probe classifiers on incident narratives to assign multi-class and binary labels based on several OIICS fields and to produce a quality score for each report. They evaluate these probes on a large labeled dataset and a smaller author-labeled hold-out set, comparing performance to a majority-vote LLM ensemble. Separately, they benchmark multiple embedding models for retrieving relevant historical accidents, related images, and trusted industry documents using standard information retrieval metrics, and test document question answering performance over these embeddings.
AI.result: The OIICS-based multiclass classification achieves 75% accuracy on the held-out set, while the two binary flags fail to learn meaningful distinctions (degenerate behavior). The narrative quality scoring model works reasonably on its training-like database but does not transfer well to an out-of-distribution set of fatal incidents. The retrieval system significantly outperforms chance in finding relevant past accidents, especially for construction tasks whose wording differs clearly from others. For document QA, an open-weight decoder-style embedding model outperforms proprietary embedding models.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that locally run LLM-based probes and embedding models can effectively classify construction safety narratives and retrieve relevant historical incidents and reference materials, though some label types and quality scores are fragile out of distribution. The proposed framework offers a practical basis for future agentic tools that integrate external safety data directly into JSA reports and daily planning, emphasizing deterministic, local inference for safety-critical applications.

title: Do LLMs Know a Good Hypothesis When They See One? Logit-Based Energy Scoring Outperforms Prompted LLM-as-Judge for Scientific Hypothesis Ranking
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for scientific hypothesis generation. However, evaluating generated hypotheses remains a challenge for trustworthy AI-enabled scientific workflows. Existing approaches often use LLMs as judges or rely on semantic similarity, which can favor familiar ideas over novel ones. We propose a logit-based energy scoring method that evaluates hypotheses using a language model's intrinsic confidence rather than comparative judgment. We benchmarked seven language models on 1,323 papers across 12 disciplines. Each paper was paired with its hypothesis and fifteen incorrect alternatives. Intrinsic scoring reached 33.0% Hit@1 pooled across both scorers, compared with 16.6% for prompted listwise ranking. The strongest configuration, a 1-billion-parameter model using logit-based energy scoring, reached 53.1%, though this was the maximum across 14 model-by-scorer combinations selected post hoc. Overall, intrinsic model confidence shows potential for scientific hypothesis evaluation. This study also motivates future research on confidence-based methods for trustworthy AI-enabled scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a logit-based energy scoring method that uses a language model’s intrinsic confidence to evaluate scientific hypotheses, showing it can outperform listwise LLM judging and motivating confidence-based evaluation for AI-assisted discovery.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to generate scientific hypotheses, there is no clear, reliable way to evaluate the quality and correctness of these hypotheses. Existing evaluation methods either ask LLMs to act as judges or rely on semantic similarity to known ideas, both of which can bias toward familiar, less novel hypotheses and make it hard to assess genuinely new ideas. A more objective, scalable, and novelty-friendly evaluation mechanism is needed for trustworthy AI-enabled scientific workflows.
AI.method: The authors propose an intrinsic, logit-based energy scoring method that evaluates each candidate hypothesis by using the underlying language model’s token-level logit outputs (its internal confidence) rather than comparative judgments or similarity to existing text. They construct a benchmark of 1,323 scientific papers from 12 disciplines, each associated with its true hypothesis and 15 incorrect alternatives. Seven different LLMs and multiple scoring configurations (including the proposed intrinsic scoring and a prompted listwise ranking baseline) are tested. Performance is measured using Hit@1, i.e., whether the correct hypothesis is ranked highest among the 16 candidates.
AI.result: Across all models and scorers, intrinsic logit-based scoring achieves a pooled Hit@1 of 33.0%, clearly outperforming the prompted listwise ranking baseline, which yields 16.6% Hit@1. The best-performing configuration—a 1B-parameter language model combined with logit-based energy scoring—achieves a Hit@1 of 53.1%. However, this top number is a post hoc maximum across 14 model-by-scorer combinations, indicating some degree of configuration selection bias. Nonetheless, intrinsic scoring consistently shows better or competitive performance versus baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic model confidence, operationalized via logit-based energy scoring, is a promising signal for evaluating scientific hypotheses generated by LLMs. It can outperform traditional LLM-as-judge and listwise ranking approaches, potentially reducing bias toward familiar ideas. The study suggests that confidence-based methods could become a key component of trustworthy AI-enabled scientific discovery pipelines and highlights the need for further work on calibrating and generalizing such confidence metrics across models and scientific domains.

title: Token Optimization and Context Window Management in Multi-Agent AI Workflows
comment: 29 pages (main paper + technical appendix), 3 figures. Also archived on Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.21924612
summary: Multi-agent AI workflows are limited not only by model quality but by token cost, latency, and context-window quality. This paper presents a practitioner framework for token optimization and context-window management, grounded in an internal production dashboard that extracts structured work items from meetings, email, and chat with LLMs and routes summaries across workstreams. Six patterns are described: context stratification, fetch-once/process-locally architecture, schema-contracted prompts, token-aware fallback chains, semantic caching, and inter-agent communication compression. In production they cut measured cold-load latency to 61-116 seconds (six timed runs) from an operational baseline of roughly 3.5-10.5 minutes, with an estimated 60-70% token reduction. It also reports a controlled context-composition study: 2,420 confirmatory trials across 11 model configurations, using 661 anonymized workplace items scored for relevance. Holding the prompt at a fixed ten items, replacing some high-relevance items with same-domain low-relevance items improves the model's relevance-score concordance on the target items, versus high-relevance items only; we call this relevance-contrast context. In the all-11 paired analysis, the 50:50 signal/noise condition improved relevance accuracy by +0.077 over the 100% condition (naive 95% CI [+0.056, +0.098], Cohen's d = 0.49, Holm-adjusted p < .001, n = 220). These cells are not independent; by the nine model families the effect is +0.084 (95% interval [+0.064, +0.103]), reported as a within-corpus descriptive comparison, not a population inference. A Fusion-of-N follow-up found that learned synthesis did not beat the mechanical set union of item IDs. The contribution is a measured engineering layer between model research and production agent practice: repeatable patterns and evaluation methods for faster, cheaper, more reliable workflows.

AI.tldr: Framework for reducing token usage and latency in multi-agent LLM workflows plus an empirical study on how mixing relevant and less-relevant context items affects model relevance judgments.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent AI systems in production are constrained by token costs, latency, and the limited quality/size of context windows. Existing work focuses mostly on model quality, leaving a gap in practical, measured techniques for making workflows faster, cheaper, and more reliable in real applications like extracting and routing work items from communication data.
AI.method: The authors describe an internal production dashboard that uses LLMs to extract structured work items from meetings, emails, and chats and route summaries across workstreams. From this they derive six design patterns for token and context optimization: context stratification, fetch-once/process-locally architecture, schema-contracted prompts, token-aware fallback chains, semantic caching, and inter-agent communication compression. They empirically evaluate these patterns by measuring latency and token usage before and after deployment. Separately, they run a controlled context-composition study: 2,420 confirmatory trials across 11 model configurations using 661 anonymized workplace items, with relevance scoring. They manipulate the context composition by holding the prompt length fixed at ten items while varying the mix of high-relevance vs same-domain low-relevance items, and analyze changes in relevance accuracy and concordance. They also test a "Fusion-of-N" method vs a mechanical set union of item IDs.
AI.result: In production, the six patterns reduce cold-load latency from an operational baseline of about 3.5–10.5 minutes down to 61–116 seconds (across six timed runs) and achieve an estimated 60–70% reduction in token usage. In the controlled relevance study, introducing relevance-contrast context (a 50:50 mix of signal and noise items) improves relevance accuracy compared to a 100% high-relevance context: in a paired analysis across all 11 model configurations, accuracy increases by +0.077 with a naive 95% CI of [+0.056, +0.098], Cohen’s d = 0.49, Holm-adjusted p < .001, n = 220. Grouped by nine model families, the effect is +0.084 with a 95% interval of [+0.064, +0.103], reported descriptively. The Fusion-of-N learned synthesis approach does not outperform a simple set-union baseline of item IDs.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides an engineering-focused bridge between model research and real-world multi-agent systems, distilling practical patterns that materially cut latency and token costs while offering evaluation techniques that can be reused by practitioners. It also challenges naive assumptions about context quality by showing that mixing high- and low-relevance items (relevance-contrast context) can improve a model’s relevance judgments, and that simple aggregation heuristics (set union) can match or beat more complex learned fusion strategies in this setting.

title: ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence
summary: Artificial superintelligence (ASI) requires AI to move beyond mastering existing knowledge toward exploring the unknown, creating new knowledge, and turning new ideas into verifiable results. However, the capabilities of today's AI systems are still largely built on learning, compressing, and applying existing human knowledge. Accordingly, existing benchmarks primarily test whether AI can produce correct answers based on learned knowledge, or whether it can complete tasks under extensive human guidance. We therefore introduce ASI-Bench, the first benchmark to jointly evaluate AI systems' capabilities of innovative exploration and autonomous scientific execution across general research domains, and the first to progressively withdraw human methodological guidance within the same research project to test how far AI can proceed on its own. Built by over 40 experts with the cost of 31,000+ human hours, ASI-Bench contains 60 project-level research tasks across 11 scientific domains and progressively reduces methodological guidance to test whether AI can independently select methods, conduct research, and produce verifiable results. All tasks undergo expert review, AI-assisted auditing, sandbox execution, and scorer validation. Across 18 state-of-the-art agent--model configurations, the average score drops from 50.91 with full methodological guidance to 29.10 with only the method specified and 26.62 when agents must determine the method themselves. This sharp decline shows that current systems remain heavily dependent on human guidance and are still far from autonomously conducting end-to-end, project-level scientific research. ASI-Bench is open to the world. We invite researchers and builders everywhere to contribute new tasks, challenge the limits of today's AI, and help accelerate humanity's collective path toward artificial superintelligence at https://asibench.apexin.ai/submit.

AI.tldr: ASI-Bench is a benchmark to evaluate how well AI systems can autonomously conduct innovative, end-to-end scientific research across domains, revealing that current systems still rely heavily on human methodological guidance.
AI.motivation: Current AI mostly learns and applies existing human knowledge, and existing benchmarks test performance on known-answer tasks or under strong human guidance. There is no standard way to evaluate whether AI can independently explore the unknown, devise methods, and execute full research projects—capabilities central to artificial superintelligence. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors design ASI-Bench, a benchmark consisting of 60 project-level research tasks across 11 scientific domains. Each task is structured to gradually reduce human methodological guidance within the same project, moving from detailed guidance to only method hints to fully autonomous method selection. Tasks are constructed and vetted by over 40 experts through expert review, AI-assisted auditing, sandbox execution, and scorer validation. They then evaluate 18 state-of-the-art agent–model configurations on these tasks and measure performance under varying levels of guidance.
AI.result: Across 18 advanced agent–model setups, performance is moderately strong when full methodological guidance is provided (average score 50.91) but drops significantly as guidance is removed: to 29.10 when only the method is specified and to 26.62 when agents must choose the method themselves. This pattern indicates that systems struggle especially with method selection and autonomous research planning/execution.
AI.conclusion: ASI-Bench reveals that current AI systems are far from being able to autonomously conduct end-to-end, project-level scientific research and remain highly dependent on human methodological scaffolding. The benchmark provides a standardized, extensible way to measure progress toward more autonomous, innovative AI, and the authors open it to the community, inviting contributions of new tasks and participation to collectively push toward artificial superintelligence.

title: Which Source Wins? Task-Dependent Reliance in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) combine images and text, but when the two conflict and one becomes harder to read, it is unclear how a model shifts its reliance between them. We study this modality reallocation with a controlled setup: we degrade either the image or the text across four levels of legibility while keeping the other clean, and track how the model's preference changes. We build conflicts from GSM8K and SVAMP by pairing the rendered image of one arithmetic problem with the text of another, so the two sources support different answers. We also introduce ChartQA-Conflict, a manually reviewed benchmark of 229 chart-report conflicts with matched chart and table-image representations. We evaluate six open-weight VLMs using both generated answers and a length-normalized conditional log-likelihood margin. On GSM8K and SVAMP, five of six models shift more strongly away from degraded text than from degraded images. On ChartQA-Conflict, all six likelihood-scored models exhibit the opposite pattern, shifting more strongly away from the degraded visual source. This reversal persists after calibrating for unimodal accuracy loss and after replacing charts with plain table images. Two frontier API models, GPT-5.6-Luna and Gemini-3.5-Flash, behaviorally replicate the ChartQA-Conflict reversal, with GPT-5.6-Luna also matching the arithmetic direction. These results show that modality reliance in VLMs is not fixed, but varies across tasks, evidence structures, models, and evaluation settings. The source code is available at https://github.com/Ro-netizen004/multimodal-arbitration-artifact.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) reallocate reliance between text and images when one modality is degraded, revealing that modality preference is task- and setting-dependent rather than fixed.
AI.motivation: While VLMs integrate visual and textual information, we do not yet understand how they arbitrate between modalities when the two sources conflict and one becomes harder to use. This is crucial for safety, robustness, and interpretability: in realistic scenarios, one modality can be noisy, misleading, or adversarial. The authors aim to quantify and compare how different VLMs shift their reliance between text and images under controlled degradations, and to see whether this behavior is consistent across tasks and model families.
AI.method: The authors create controlled conflicts between text and images by pairing mismatched problems: for arithmetic reasoning, they use GSM8K and SVAMP, rendering each problem as an image and pairing it with the text of another, so that text and image imply different answers. They systematically degrade either the text or the image across four legibility levels while keeping the other clean, thereby inducing varying reliability in each modality. They introduce a new benchmark, ChartQA-Conflict, containing 229 manually curated chart–report conflicts, with both chart images and matched table-style images. Six open-weight VLMs are evaluated with both generated answers and a length-normalized conditional log-likelihood margin to measure which modality the model favors as degradation increases. They further analyze whether results hold after calibrating for unimodal accuracy loss and after replacing charts with plain tables; they also test two proprietary frontier models (GPT-5.6-Luna, Gemini-3.5-Flash) for behavioral replication.
AI.result: On GSM8K and SVAMP arithmetic conflicts, five out of six open-weight VLMs reduce reliance on degraded text more strongly than on degraded images, i.e., they stick with images longer as text quality deteriorates. On ChartQA-Conflict, however, all six models show the opposite: they move away from the degraded visual input more strongly than from degraded text, indicating a reversal in modality preference. This reversal persists even after controlling for unimodal performance drops and when substituting charts with plain table images, ruling out simple accuracy or visualization-style explanations. The two tested API models replicate the key qualitative pattern: both show the ChartQA-Conflict reversal, and GPT-5.6-Luna also aligns with open-weight models on the arithmetic tasks.
AI.conclusion: Modality reliance in VLMs is dynamic rather than fixed: how much a model trusts text versus images depends strongly on the task type (arithmetic vs chart QA), the structure of evidence, the specific model, and how we measure preference (generations vs likelihoods). The observed reversal across benchmarks suggests that current VLMs lack a unified arbitration mechanism for conflicting multimodal signals and instead exhibit context-dependent heuristics. This has implications for designing more robust and interpretable multimodal systems, highlighting the need to explicitly model and evaluate modality arbitration under conflict and degradation. The authors release their code to facilitate further study of these behaviors.

title: DeAR: Decentralized Agentic Reasoning via Capability Grounding and Collaborative Thought Navigation
summary: Existing agentic reasoning systems typically rely on centralized protocols. This design introduces routing bottlenecks and static role allocations that often fail when handling complex multimodal queries. We propose DeAR (Decentralized Agentic Reasoning), a framework that shifts from central control to autonomous peer-to-peer collaboration. DeAR is built on three mechanisms: (1) decentralized capability grounding for query-dependent agent specialization, (2) thought map navigation for targeted peer interactions, and (3) topology update for adaptive error correction. Evaluations across 9 diverse multimodal reasoning and text-based QA benchmarks indicate that DeAR consistently outperforms recent baseline methods, validating that decentralized and adaptive collaboration among agents enhances accuracy in knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks. The source code will be available at https://open_upon_acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DeAR, a decentralized multi-agent reasoning framework that improves performance on multimodal and text QA benchmarks by enabling dynamic, peer-to-peer collaboration instead of centralized control.
AI.motivation: Most existing agentic reasoning systems use a centralized controller that routes tasks and assigns static roles to agents. This centralization creates bottlenecks, limits scalability, and often fails on complex multimodal queries where flexible, adaptive coordination would be beneficial. The authors aim to remove these bottlenecks and enable more robust, scalable, and adaptive multi-agent reasoning.
AI.method: They propose DeAR (Decentralized Agentic Reasoning), a framework based on three core mechanisms: (1) decentralized capability grounding, which lets agents specialize dynamically based on the query and their capabilities; (2) thought map navigation, which structures and directs peer-to-peer interactions so that agents can selectively consult relevant peers; and (3) topology update, which adapts the communication structure over time for error correction and improved coordination. The system is evaluated on 9 multimodal reasoning and text-based QA benchmarks against recent centralized and multi-agent baselines.
AI.result: Across 9 diverse benchmarks involving multimodal reasoning and text QA, DeAR consistently outperforms recent baseline methods, indicating improved accuracy and robustness in knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks. The gains are attributed to decentralized, adaptive collaboration and better routing of information among agents.
AI.conclusion: Decentralizing control in agentic reasoning—from a central coordinator to autonomous peer-to-peer collaboration—yields more accurate and adaptive performance on complex, knowledge-intensive tasks. The proposed DeAR framework demonstrates that query-dependent specialization, targeted peer interaction, and adaptive topology updates form an effective basis for scalable multi-agent reasoning, motivating further research in decentralized coordination mechanisms. The authors plan to release source code upon acceptance.

title: The Plot Thins: Uniformity and Linearity in Literary Summaries
summary: Works of literature are complicated; they balance plot, suspense, surprise, and artistic expression. Summaries of literature prioritize plot, and therefore may deviate from their sources. Using a combination of manual and LLM-based annotation, we construct a dataset mapping sentences from 150 novel summaries to their respective source chapters. We find the task unexpectedly difficult for both human and model annotators. Using the sentence-to-chapter mappings, we then measure summary linearity, the degree to which it maintains the source's order of events, and uniformity, the degree to which a summary spreads attention equally across a source. By examining when and how summaries break linearity and uniformity, we identify differences in how literary works and summaries express plot, particularly with regard to the clarity and prominence with which narrative details are described.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a dataset aligning sentences from novel summaries to their source chapters and uses it to quantify how summaries reorder and unevenly emphasize story events.
AI.motivation: Literary summaries are widely used in education and analysis, yet they often diverge from the original works because they prioritize plot over other artistic elements. There is little systematic understanding or quantification of how and where these divergences occur, especially regarding event order and emphasis. The authors want to create resources and metrics to study how summaries structurally differ from the narratives they describe.
AI.method: They collect 150 novels with existing human-written summaries. For each summary, they align its sentences to the chapters of the original novel, using a pipeline that combines manual annotation with large language model (LLM) assistance. With these alignments, they define two quantitative measures: (1) summary linearity, capturing how closely the summary preserves the original chronological or narrative order of events; and (2) summary uniformity, measuring how evenly the summary distributes attention across the chapters of the source. They then analyze where and how summaries deviate from linearity and uniformity and compare these deviations with characteristics of the underlying works.
AI.result: The alignment task—mapping each summary sentence back to its source chapter—is challenging for both human annotators and LLMs, indicating that even seemingly straightforward plot-based correspondence is nontrivial. Using the aligned data, they compute linearity and uniformity scores for the summaries and observe systematic patterns in how summaries reorder events and unevenly allocate space to different parts of the source novels. These patterns reveal consistent types of deviation from the originals, such as compressing or omitting some narrative details while highlighting others.
AI.conclusion: Summaries of literary works do not simply condense plots; they systematically reshape the presentation of events and emphasis. The difficulty of sentence-to-chapter alignment shows that plot structure and detail prominence in literature are more complex than they appear. The proposed dataset and the linearity and uniformity metrics provide tools to study these structural differences, shedding light on how summaries transform narratives and offering a foundation for future work on literary analysis, summarization quality, and LLM evaluation in long-form narrative settings.

title: PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs
summary: Group-relative policy optimization has emerged as a key paradigm for training agentic large language models (LLMs) on multi-turn interactive tasks. However, most existing variants fail to distinguish advantages among successful trajectories even when these trajectories differ substantially in their interaction efficiency. For instance, circuitous successes are often assigned the identical outcome reward, causing advantage collapse and severe performance bottlenecks. To this end, we propose Group Planning-aware Policy Optimization (PlanPO), a simple yet effective RL method for learning generalizable planning abilities beyond task-specific high-quality behavior patterns. Specifically, PlanPO introduces coarse-to-fine advantage signals, which capture the relative differences in trajectory-level lengths and turn-level response lengths conditioned on successful trajectories sampled for the same task. Within the group-relative optimization structure, this enables agents to actively learn generalizable and deliberate behaviors spanning interaction planning and textual generation from high-quality rollouts, without degenerating into vanilla length minimization. Experimentally, PlanPO improves over GRPO by 27.2\% on average across the challenging multi-turn benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld, outperforming recent powerful baselines while incurring negligible additional training cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PlanPO, a reinforcement learning method that enhances group-relative policy optimization for LLM agents by distinguishing efficiency among successful trajectories, leading to better planning and performance on multi-turn tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing group-relative policy optimization methods for training agentic LLMs treat all successful trajectories as equally good, even if some are much more efficient than others. This causes 'advantage collapse,' where the learning signal cannot distinguish concise, well-planned behaviors from circuitous ones, limiting planning ability and overall performance. The motivation is to design a method that can learn generalizable planning skills and efficient interaction strategies from successful trajectories without just rewarding shorter outputs blindly.
AI.method: The authors introduce Group Planning-aware Policy Optimization (PlanPO), built on a group-relative optimization framework. PlanPO defines coarse-to-fine advantage signals among successful trajectories sampled for the same task. At the trajectory level, it considers differences in interaction length (number of turns); at the turn level, it considers differences in response length (tokens). These relative signals assign higher advantages to more efficient yet successful rollouts, while being conditioned on success so as not to degenerate into mere length minimization. The method integrates these planning-aware advantages into the reinforcement learning update with negligible extra computational cost compared to existing GRPO methods.
AI.result: On three challenging multi-turn benchmarks—ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld—PlanPO provides an average improvement of 27.2% over GRPO in task performance. It also outperforms other recent strong baselines while keeping training overhead nearly unchanged, demonstrating that adding planning-aware signals improves efficiency and success rates without sacrificing practicality.
AI.conclusion: PlanPO successfully addresses advantage collapse in group-relative policy optimization by distinguishing among successful trajectories based on planning and efficiency signals. This leads to more deliberate, generalizable planning behavior in LLM agents, better performance on multi-turn interactive tasks, and does so with minimal additional training cost. The approach shows that integrating structured, length- and planning-aware feedback into RL for LLMs is a promising direction beyond task-specific imitation of high-quality behaviors.

title: Temporal Leakage in Financial News NLP: A Multi-Architecture Audit with a Regime-Specific M&A Signal
summary: Financial-news direction prediction has become a popular NLP benchmark, yet reported gains depend critically on whether the train-test split is chronological or random, i.e., on temporal leakage. We audit this dependence on a 49,799-article corpus across 16 feature-model combinations spanning TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, and fine-tuned RoBERTa-large / DeBERTa-v3-large, plus separate zero/few-shot and LoRA probes of Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 LLMs: random splits inflate MCC by $1.1\times$ to $6.5\times$, tracking model capacity and feature richness, and end-to-end FinBERT fine-tuning re-amplifies rather than closes the gap (size-matched ratio $1.75\times$). Conditioning on event type, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) is the only audited category with a positive locked-test signal under near-temporal chronological evaluation (TF-IDF MCC $= 0.138$ train-only, $0.068$ under train$\cup$val refit; 10,000-permutation $p < 10^{-3}$); the signal does not transfer to FNSPID's 2009-2020 U.S. corpus, localising the headline to our 2024-2025 European-tilted M&A semantics rather than a universal predictor. Three independent role labellers converge on acquirer-tagged articles as the signal locus, a power-limited qualitative convergence rather than a hypothesis-tested asymmetry. Chronological splitting plays for financial NLP the role characteristics-purging plays for asset pricing: it strips the predictable, stale component of news and leaves a residual that is small, event-localized, and lexically shallow. We advocate leakage audits as a required disclosure for financial-NLP benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Paper shows that random train-test splits in financial news sentiment/direction prediction massively overstate performance due to temporal leakage; under proper chronological splits, only a small, event‑specific signal (M&A, especially acquirers) remains.
AI.motivation: Financial-news direction prediction is widely used as an NLP benchmark, but many reported gains may be artifacts of temporal leakage: information from the future leaking into the training set due to random train-test splits. The authors want to systematically measure how serious this problem is, how it scales with model/feature complexity, and whether any genuinely predictive signal remains under realistic chronological evaluation.
AI.method: They construct a 49,799-article corpus and evaluate 16 combinations of text features (TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, fine-tuned RoBERTa-large and DeBERTa-v3-large) and models, plus zero-/few-shot and LoRA-based probes of large language models (Llama-3 and Qwen2.5). For each setup, they compare performance under random versus chronological train-test splits, using Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) as the main metric. They also condition on event types (e.g., M&A), perform permutation tests to assess statistical significance, analyze transfer to another benchmark dataset (FNSPID 2009–2020 U.S. corpus), and use three independent role-labelling approaches to localize where the predictive signal arises within M&A news (acquirer vs. other roles).
AI.result: Random splits inflate MCC by factors ranging from 1.1× to 6.5× relative to chronological splits, with the inflation increasing for higher-capacity models and richer feature representations. FinBERT fine-tuning in an end-to-end fashion further amplifies the leakage-driven performance gap instead of mitigating it, with a size-matched inflation ratio of about 1.75×. When controlling for event types, only M&A news shows a positive and statistically significant predictive signal under near-temporal chronological evaluation (TF-IDF MCC of 0.138 using train-only and 0.068 when refitting on train∪val, with a 10,000-permutation p-value < 10^-3). This signal does not transfer to the FNSPID U.S. dataset, indicating it is specific to the 2024–2025, more Europe-focused M&A context. Role-labelling analyses suggest that the signal is mainly present in articles tagged as describing the acquirer, but this is a qualitative, power-limited finding rather than a rigorously hypothesis-tested asymmetry.
