AI.conclusion: Chronological train-test splitting in financial NLP tasks effectively removes a large portion of the apparent predictability that arises from stale or temporally leaked information, leaving only a small, lexically simple, and event-localized residual signal, mostly in contemporary European-tilted M&A news concerning acquirers. Random splits therefore substantially overstate model performance, particularly for complex models and rich text features. The authors argue that leakage audits—systematic comparisons of random vs. carefully chronological splits and appropriate significance checks—should become a standard, mandatory part of reporting in financial-NLP benchmarks.

title: LiveHouse-TS: An Open-world Living Benchmark for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a highly promising paradigm for cross-domain zero-shot forecasting. However, existing evaluation protocols predominantly rely on static benchmarks with fixed historical test windows. While these benchmarks provide a valuable baseline snapshot, they evaluate an average performance on a fixed history, failing to capture how models behave in continuously evolving real-world environments characterized by seasonal variations, distribution shifts, and unexpected events. To bridge this gap, we introduce LiveHouse-TS, the first open-world living benchmark infrastructure for TSFMs. By evaluating models prequentially on real future data in open-world environments, LiveHouse-TS shifts time series benchmarking from snapshot accuracy to continuous temporal validity. Rather than acting as a one-off leaderboard, our infrastructure serves as a continuous time series infrastructure designed to explore vital, long-term scientific questions: Can model rankings be maintained over the long term? Which models remain genuinely robust under distribution shifts? Extensive streaming evaluations across 11 domains with 17 datasets demonstrate that static rankings undergo a dramatic reshuffling under a live protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LiveHouse-TS, a live, open-world benchmarking infrastructure for time series foundation models that evaluates models continuously on streaming future data rather than static historical test windows.
AI.motivation: Existing time series foundation model (TSFM) benchmarks use fixed historical windows, providing only a static snapshot of performance. This setup cannot capture how models behave over time in realistic, evolving environments with seasonality, distribution shifts, and unexpected events, nor can it reveal whether model rankings and robustness persist in the long run.
AI.method: The authors design LiveHouse-TS, an open-world, prequential (test-then-train) evaluation infrastructure where models are evaluated on real future time series data as it arrives across multiple domains. The benchmark continuously measures performance over time, under natural distribution shifts and evolving conditions, rather than on a single, fixed test set. It supports cross-domain TSFMs and tracks their performance dynamics and ranking stability under live conditions.
AI.result: Using LiveHouse-TS, the authors conduct extensive streaming evaluations across 11 domains and 17 datasets, observing that model rankings derived from traditional static benchmarks change substantially when evaluated under the live, prequential protocol. This indicates that many models that appear strong in static settings may not maintain their advantage in real-world, evolving environments.
AI.conclusion: Static, snapshot-style benchmarks are insufficient to assess the true, long-term robustness and reliability of time series foundation models. A live, open-world, prequential benchmark such as LiveHouse-TS is necessary to understand how models perform under realistic, evolving conditions and distribution shifts, and it reveals that static rankings can dramatically reshuffle over time.

title: Q-Interference: Memory-Efficient Phase-Aware Quantum-Inspired Attention
summary: GPT attention measures token compatibility through dot-product similarity. This mechanism is simple, effective, and memory-efficient. But it does not explicitly model whether strong token features should reinforce or suppress one another. We introduce Q-Interference, a fully classical quantum-inspired attention mechanism for autoregressive language modeling that augments each query and key feature with an amplitude and a learned phase. The resulting attention score is phase-aware which aligned phases contribute constructively while conflicting phases contribute destructively. Although Q-Interference yields a richer interaction rule than similarity alone, a naive implementation of Q-Interference requires a large token-pair-feature interaction tensor, making it memory-intensive and often impractical. To address this limitation, we propose an exact trigonometric factorization that computes the same score using two standard matrix multiplications avoiding materialization of the large intermediate tensor. Q-Interference fits directly into a Transformer block in GPT and leaves the remainder of the model architecture and next-token prediction objective unchanged. Experiments on public benchmark datasets and baseline models show that the proposed reformulation trains stably in a controlled GPT-style setting and provides a consistent memory advantage over naive phase-aware interference attention. These results support the specific contribution of this work: an exact memory-efficient reformulation that makes phase-aware interference attention practical within a standard GPT pipeline.

AI.tldr: They propose Q-Interference, a phase-aware, quantum-inspired attention mechanism that enables constructive and destructive interference between token features, and derive an exact factorization that makes it memory-efficient and practical in GPT-style Transformers.
AI.motivation: Standard GPT dot-product attention only measures similarity and cannot explicitly model when strong token features should reinforce or cancel each other. A phase-aware mechanism could capture richer interactions, but naive implementations are memory-heavy and impractical.
AI.method: Introduce Q-Interference attention, augmenting each query and key feature with an amplitude and a learnable phase so that attention scores depend on phase alignment (constructive/destructive interference). Show that a naive implementation would need a large token-pair-feature interaction tensor, then derive an exact trigonometric factorization that computes the same scores via two regular matrix multiplications without materializing the large tensor. Integrate this attention module into a standard GPT Transformer block while keeping the overall architecture and next-token prediction objective unchanged, and evaluate on public benchmarks against GPT-style baselines.
AI.result: Q-Interference trains stably in controlled GPT-style experiments, matches the intended phase-aware interference behavior, and the factored formulation achieves a consistent memory advantage relative to the naive tensor-based phase-aware attention implementation on public benchmark datasets and baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Phase-aware interference attention can be made practical for GPT-style models by using an exact trigonometric factorization that removes the large intermediate tensor. This preserves the richer interference-based interaction rule while keeping memory usage comparable to standard attention, enabling integration into standard Transformer pipelines.

title: SignalReasoner: Assessing the Upper Bound of 3B Models for Signal Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Post-training with supervised chain-of-thought fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, their application to signal processing problems remains relatively under-explored. This report investigates reinforcement fine-tuning strategies for adapting Qwen2.5-3B-Base to graduate-level signal mathematical problems from WirelessMATHBench-XL, a comprehensive benchmark for mathematical reasoning in this domain. We examine two training paradigms: (i) direct reinforcement learning (RL) on WirelessMATHBench-XL with verifiable rewards; and (ii) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a distilled wireless-domain chain-of-thought corpus, followed by the same domain-specific RL stage. Across both paradigms, we benchmark Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), and Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO). We aim to assess whether domain-aware CoT SFT serves as an effective initialization for subsequent RL, and whether GSPO or GMPO offer advantages in stability or accuracy over GRPO for signal reasoning tasks. Our best model achieves an overall accuracy of 39.12\%, representing a more than threefold improvement over the untrained Base model (12.37\%).

AI.tldr: The paper explores how to improve a 3B-parameter LLM’s performance on graduate-level wireless signal-processing math problems using reinforcement learning and chain-of-thought fine-tuning, comparing several RL algorithms and training pipelines.
AI.motivation: While chain-of-thought supervision and RL with verifiable rewards have greatly advanced LLM performance on general mathematical reasoning, they have been little studied in specialized signal processing domains. Graduate-level wireless communication math requires structured, multi-step reasoning over domain-specific concepts. Off‑the‑shelf base models perform poorly here. The authors want to understand how best to adapt a compact Qwen2.5-3B-Base model to WirelessMATHBench-XL, and whether domain-aware chain-of-thought SFT and different RL objectives can systematically enhance accuracy and stability for signal reasoning tasks.
AI.method: They start from Qwen2.5-3B-Base and target WirelessMATHBench-XL, a benchmark of graduate-level wireless signal-processing math problems with verifiable answers. They investigate two main training pipelines: (1) Direct RL: apply reinforcement learning on WirelessMATHBench-XL using verifiable rewards that score whether final answers are correct. (2) SFT+RL: first perform supervised fine-tuning on a distilled chain-of-thought dataset specific to the wireless domain, then apply the same RL procedure on WirelessMATHBench-XL. For each pipeline, they compare three group-based policy optimization algorithms—Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), and Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO)—to study their impact on optimization stability and final reasoning accuracy.
AI.result: The adapted models significantly outperform the untrained Qwen2.5-3B-Base on WirelessMATHBench-XL. The best configuration, combining one of the explored RL strategies (with or without prior domain-specific CoT SFT) and a particular policy optimization algorithm, reaches 39.12% overall accuracy. This is more than three times higher than the base model’s starting accuracy of 12.37%. Comparative results across GRPO, GSPO, and GMPO highlight differences in stability and accuracy, though specific numeric breakdowns are not included in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific reinforcement fine-tuning substantially enhances a small LLM’s performance on graduate-level wireless signal-processing math. A threefold accuracy improvement suggests that verifiable-reward RL, especially when preceded by wireless-domain chain-of-thought SFT, is an effective strategy for specializing general-purpose models to signal reasoning tasks. The comparison of GRPO, GSPO, and GMPO indicates that alternative group-based policy optimization methods can offer stability or accuracy benefits over standard GRPO in this domain, motivating further exploration of RL algorithms tailored to structured technical reasoning benchmarks.

title: What Tokens are Learned when Tokenization is Optimized Jointly with Language Modeling?
summary: Tokenization is a fundamental component of language modeling pipelines. Despite its importance, it is often fixed, even though it significantly impacts model performance across languages. In this work, we analyze what tokens are learned when tokenization is jointly optimized with language modeling. We compare tokenizer-free approaches such as SSLMs and H-Nets with fixed tokenizers across 18 typologically and script-diverse languages. Our results show that joint optimization fundamentally alters token structure. SSLMs recover morphologically aligned and contextually efficient tokens, whereas H-Nets prioritize byte-level efficiency, producing longer tokens with very low overlap with standard subword vocabularies. We further show that tokenization behavior varies across language typologies. Agglutinative languages exhibit more dynamic segmentation patterns while learning. Through downstream evaluation, with pretrained-then-finetuned BERT models, we find that SSLM-based pretokenization consistently reduces language modeling perplexity and achieves competitive downstream performance despite distinct vocabularies. Overall, tokenizer-free approaches optimize for contextual and computational efficiency rather than strict morphological structure, resulting in fundamentally different yet effective vocabularies for downstream NLP.

AI.tldr: The paper studies what kinds of tokens are learned when tokenization is optimized jointly with language modeling, comparing tokenizer-free models to fixed-tokenizer approaches over many languages, and finds that jointly learned tokens are structurally different yet effective and efficient.
AI.motivation: Tokenization heavily affects language model performance, especially across diverse languages, but is usually fixed and not optimized jointly with the model. There is limited understanding of how learned tokenizations differ from standard subword methods and how this varies by language typology. The paper aims to fill this gap by systematically analyzing the token structures that emerge when tokenization is learned end-to-end.
AI.method: The authors compare tokenizer-free approaches (SSLMs and H-Nets) to models using fixed subword tokenizers across 18 languages representing diverse scripts and typologies. They jointly optimize tokenization with language modeling and then analyze the resulting tokens in terms of morphology, contextual efficiency, and overlap with standard vocabularies. They also examine how tokenization behavior evolves during training and differs for languages with different morphological typologies, and they evaluate downstream performance via pretrained-then-finetuned BERT models using SSLM-based pretokenization.
AI.result: Jointly optimizing tokenization and language modeling produces token inventories that differ substantially from standard subword vocabularies. SSLMs learn tokens that align well with morphemes and are contextually efficient, while H-Nets focus more on byte-level efficiency, producing longer tokens with minimal overlap with typical subword units. Tokenization dynamics and segmentation patterns vary by language typology, with agglutinative languages showing more dynamic segmentations during learning. In downstream experiments, SSLM-based pretokenization consistently lowers language modeling perplexity and yields competitive performance on NLP tasks despite having very different vocabularies from standard tokenizers.
AI.conclusion: Tokenizer-free, jointly optimized approaches do not simply rediscover conventional subword segmentations; instead, they learn vocabularies guided by contextual and computational efficiency rather than strict morphological faithfulness. These learned tokenizations vary across language types, particularly in agglutinative languages, yet remain effective for downstream NLP, suggesting that end-to-end tokenization learning is a viable and potentially superior alternative to fixed tokenizers.

title: Wuying-Browser-Agent: Real-World Centric Fundamental Long-Horizon Browser Agents
summary: Browser agents perform well on short, clean demonstrations, but real deployment is fundamentally different: agents must sustain dozens of decisions on live websites while recovering from mistakes and navigating complex UIs. We argue that closing this gap requires alignment at every level of the pipeline, including execution, supervision, optimization, and evaluation, rather than scale alone. We present Wuying-Browser-Agent, a unified framework that addresses each of these levels. A structured browser harness provides stable execution primitives and decision-oriented context management. Reflection and UI-specialized Curriculum SFT (RUIC-SFT) explicitly trains on recovery trajectories and complex-UI interactions. Divergence-Aware Online GRPO (DAO-GRPO) improves long-horizon credit assignment through potential-based reward shaping and divergence-aware step weighting. Finally, we introduce BrowserBench, a bilingual real-web benchmark of 350 tasks averaging 37.9 steps, because most existing benchmarks are too short to expose long-horizon failure modes. Wuying-Browser-Agent-27B achieves 80.6\% on WebVoyager, 66.7\% on Online-Mind2Web, and 65.1\% on BrowserBench, establishing a new open-source state of the art on browser-use benchmarks. The same pipeline also transfers beyond browser use, demonstrating strong general agentic ability and reaching an average score of 73.8 on Tau2-Bench, Claw-Eval, and BFCL-v4.

AI.tldr: They propose Wuying-Browser-Agent, a full-stack framework (execution, training, RL, evaluation) that makes browser agents robust on long, real-web tasks and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing browser agents do well on short, clean tasks but fail in realistic, long-horizon, noisy web environments. The authors argue that simply scaling models is not enough; the whole pipeline—from how actions are executed in the browser, to how supervision data is collected, to how RL is done, to how evaluation is designed—must be aligned with real deployment conditions.
AI.method: 1) Design a structured browser harness that gives stable, decision-focused APIs and context management for agents. 2) Propose RUIC-SFT (Reflection and UI-specialized Curriculum SFT), which uses reflection and a curriculum over increasingly complex UIs and explicit recovery trajectories, so the model learns to recover from mistakes and handle complex interfaces. 3) Introduce DAO-GRPO (Divergence-Aware Online GRPO), an RL algorithm that adds potential-based reward shaping and divergence-aware step weighting to improve credit assignment over long action sequences. 4) Build BrowserBench, a bilingual, real-web benchmark of 350 tasks with long trajectories, to evaluate long-horizon performance.
AI.result: The Wuying-Browser-Agent-27B model achieves 80.6% on WebVoyager, 66.7% on Online-Mind2Web, and 65.1% on the newly proposed BrowserBench, surpassing previous open-source methods. The same training pipeline, when transferred to non-browser agent tasks, achieves an average score of 73.8 across Tau2-Bench, Claw-Eval, and BFCL-v4, showing broader agentic capabilities beyond browsers.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end alignment of the entire agent pipeline—execution environment, supervised learning, RL optimization, and evaluation—substantially improves robustness and long-horizon performance of browser agents, outperforming scale-only approaches. The proposed Wuying-Browser-Agent framework and BrowserBench benchmark set a new open-source state of the art and generalize to other agentic settings.

title: ArguLens: An Open-Source System for Automated Essay Scoring and Label-Aware Feedback Generation
summary: Most automated essay scoring (AES) systems output a single holistic score without interpretable evidence and rely on closed APIs that introduce data privacy and cost barriers. We present ArguLens, an opensource, locally deployable system that decomposes AES into three decoupled components: a discourse-move classifier (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA on PERSUADE 2.0), a grade-independent LightGBM scorer over 31 linguistic and discourse features, and a label-aware feedback generator served through vLLM with a Qwen2.5-14BInstruct backbone. A Gradio web UI exposes pluggable inference backends and supports single-essay and batch scoring with downloadable per-essay breakdowns. On an essaydisjoint PERSUADE 2.0 test split, the logitprobe classifier achieves 82.6% accuracy and 0.727 macro-F1; under prompt-grouped 5-fold cross-validation the scorer reaches a mean QWK of 0.813 under an oracle discoursefeature protocol, and an ablation shows that adding gold discourse annotations yields an increment of +0.055 QWK over the lexical+syntactic configuration (paired t-test, p = 0.010). This is a component-level diagnostic rather than an end-to-end classifier-to-scorer result. The feedback generator ships with a structured evaluation protocol; its human-rater study is left to future work. The system is released under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/wwrwbs/AI_AWE.

AI.tldr: ArguLens is an open-source, locally deployable, interpretable automated essay scoring system built from three modular components: a discourse-move classifier, a feature-based scorer, and a feedback generator.
AI.motivation: Existing automated essay scoring systems typically output only a single holistic score, offer little interpretable evidence about how that score was derived, and are often closed, commercial APIs that pose data privacy and cost issues. The authors aim to create an AES system that is transparent, interpretable at the component level, and fully open-source so it can be run locally without sharing data with third parties.
AI.method: The authors design ArguLens as three decoupled modules: (1) a discourse-move classifier using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA on the PERSUADE 2.0 dataset, evaluated via a logit-probe setup; (2) a grade-independent LightGBM regression scorer that uses 31 linguistic and discourse features to predict essay quality, evaluated with prompt-grouped 5-fold cross-validation and quadratic weighted kappa; and (3) a label-aware feedback generator implemented with a Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct backbone served through vLLM, which produces structured formative feedback aligned with the predicted discourse labels and scores. They provide a Gradio web interface supporting single and batch scoring with per-essay breakdowns, and conduct ablation experiments to isolate the contribution of gold discourse annotations.
AI.result: On an essay-disjoint test split of PERSUADE 2.0, the discourse-move classifier attains 82.6% accuracy and 0.727 macro-F1. In prompt-grouped 5-fold cross-validation, the LightGBM scorer reaches a mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.813 under an oracle discourse-feature setting. An ablation shows that adding gold discourse annotations improves QWK by +0.055 over a lexical+syntactic feature set, with the gain statistically significant (paired t-test, p = 0.010). The feedback generator is implemented with a structured evaluation protocol defined, but human-rater evaluation is deferred to future work.
AI.conclusion: ArguLens demonstrates that automated essay scoring can be decomposed into interpretable, modular components that are entirely open-source and locally deployable, mitigating privacy and cost concerns associated with closed APIs. The component-level evaluation indicates that discourse-aware features provide a statistically significant benefit over purely lexical and syntactic features for scoring quality. While the system already offers detailed per-essay diagnostics and feedback through a web interface, rigorous human evaluation of the feedback quality remains an open task, which the authors highlight as future work.

title: LLMs for Medical Consultation Are Evaluated Too Late: The Preformulation Gap
comment: 17 pages, 3 tables. Code, cases, prompts, complete transcripts, and results: https://github.com/ningkko/preformulation-gap
summary: Large language models for medical consultation are often evaluated after a clinical problem has already been made clear, although real consultations may begin with a vague, minimized, or misframed concern. We evaluated three API models across four physician-authored, multi-turn vignettes under baseline and entry-to-care instruction conditions, yielding 24 fixed-script transcripts; two cases also used adaptive standardized-patient simulation, yielding 12 transcripts. Self-care or home-management advice before any patient answer appeared in 9 of 12 baseline case-model cells and 0 of 12 instruction cells, while structured handoff summaries appeared in 0 of 12 and 10 of 12 cells, respectively. The instruction changed sequencing and documentation, although it did not reliably ensure elicitation of decisive facts. The preformulation gap should therefore be evaluated directly through observable first-contact behavior rather than inferred from diagnostic accuracy or final-answer quality.

AI.tldr: The paper tests how initial instructions given to medical large language models affect their behavior in early, vague stages of clinical encounters, showing that specific 'entry-to-care' instructions reduce premature self-care advice and improve structured handoffs but still miss key fact-gathering.
AI.motivation: Most evaluations of medical LLMs assume the clinical problem is already clearly defined, which does not match real-world first-contact scenarios where patients present vague or poorly framed concerns. The authors want to understand how models behave at this early stage and whether tailored instructions can mitigate risks such as premature advice or inadequate information gathering.
AI.method: The authors used three large language models via API and ran them through four multi-turn, physician-authored consultation vignettes. They compared two conditions: a baseline prompt and an 'entry-to-care' instruction prompt that guided models on how to behave at first contact. This produced 24 fixed-script transcripts (all vignettes x models x conditions). For two of the cases, they also used adaptive standardized-patient simulations, creating an additional 12 transcripts. They then analyzed how often models gave early self-care/home-management advice and how often they produced structured handoff summaries, among other interaction patterns.
AI.result: In the baseline condition, models frequently gave self-care or home-management advice before obtaining any patient responses (9 out of 12 case-model cells), whereas this dropped to 0 out of 12 in the instruction condition. Conversely, structured handoff summaries were absent in the baseline (0/12) but appeared in most instruction-condition transcripts (10/12). However, even with instructions, models were inconsistent in eliciting key, decision-critical clinical facts.
AI.conclusion: Providing explicit 'entry-to-care' instructions can substantially change how medical LLMs sequence their actions and document encounters, reducing premature self-care advice and improving structured handoffs. Nonetheless, these instructions do not reliably ensure adequate fact-finding, suggesting that the crucial 'preformulation gap'—from vague complaint to well-defined clinical problem—must be evaluated via first-contact interaction behaviors, not just downstream diagnostic accuracy or final answer quality.

title: PTXBench: Benchmark and Adapt LLMs for GPU Kernel Optimization with Architecture-specific PTX
summary: We introduce PTXBench, a benchmark for evaluating and adapting large language models (LLMs) to use architecture-specific PTX for GPU kernel optimization. PTXBench measures functional correctness, whether selected target instructions execute at runtime, and speedup over frontier libraries across GEMM and attention workloads on H100 and B200 GPUs. Our evaluation shows that architecture-specific PTX capability remains uneven: success rates fall substantially on complex attention backward workloads, and executing the target instructions does not necessarily translate into competitive performance. No evaluated model consistently matches frontier libraries across the suite. We further adapt Qwen3.6-27B using supervised fine-tuning. Repair-conditioned training improves several tasks, but generalization remains uneven; data coverage, balance, and the quality of the reasoning teacher matter in addition to dataset size. PTXBench provides an auditable testbed for measuring and improving LLMs' ability to exploit evolving GPU architectures.

AI.tldr: PTXBench is a benchmark to test and improve how LLMs generate architecture-specific PTX code for GPU kernel optimization, evaluating correctness, instruction usage, and performance on H100/B200, and showing current models are uneven and lag behind expert libraries.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to generate and optimize GPU kernels, but their ability to exploit low-level, architecture-specific PTX instructions on modern GPUs (e.g., H100, B200) is unclear and hard to measure systematically. Existing evaluations often focus on high-level correctness or generic performance and do not isolate whether models can effectively use new architectural features. A dedicated, auditable benchmark is needed to quantify functional correctness, proper use of target PTX instructions, and real performance benefits over strong baselines, and to study how training strategies can improve these capabilities.
AI.method: The authors design PTXBench, a benchmark suite targeting GEMM and attention workloads on NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs. It evaluates LLM-generated kernels along three axes: (1) functional correctness, (2) whether specific architecture-targeted PTX instructions are actually executed at runtime, and (3) speedup relative to strong frontier libraries. They test multiple LLMs on forward and backward variants of these workloads, with particular emphasis on challenging attention backward tasks. They then adapt Qwen3.6-27B through supervised fine-tuning using a repair-conditioned training setup, where the model learns from examples of corrected kernels and from a reasoning teacher. They analyze how data coverage, balance across tasks, and teacher quality affect generalization across the PTXBench tasks.
AI.result: Empirically, models’ PTX capabilities are uneven: success rates drop sharply on complex attention backward workloads. Even when models manage to emit and execute the target PTX instructions, this does not reliably yield competitive performance versus frontier libraries. No evaluated LLM achieves consistent parity with strong library baselines across the PTXBench suite. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B with repair-conditioned training improves performance on several benchmark tasks, but gains do not generalize uniformly; improvements are sensitive to factors like the breadth and balance of training data and the quality of the reasoning teacher used in supervision.
AI.conclusion: PTXBench exposes significant gaps in current LLMs’ ability to reliably generate architecture-specialized PTX code that both functions correctly and matches expert-library performance on modern GPUs. While targeted supervised fine-tuning, especially repair-conditioned training, can improve performance on some tasks, robust generalization across workloads and architectures remains challenging and depends on more than just dataset size. PTXBench thus serves as an auditable and evolving testbed to measure, compare, and drive progress in LLMs’ capacity to exploit new GPU architectural features through low-level PTX code generation.

title: TileMix: Tile-Centric Mixed-Precision Attention for LLM Inference Acceleration
summary: Long-context prefill in large language models (LLMs) incurs substantial computation and memory traffic because dense self-attention computes quadratic query-key scores. Existing methods either use a uniform low-precision path or select token interactions, leaving spatial precision routing over hardware-aligned score tiles outside fused dense attention. We introduce TileMix, a tile-centric precision-routing kernel that makes numerical precision an executable spatial decision over score-tile groups within fused dense attention. TileMix partitions the attention matrix into hardware-aligned score tiles, packs routing decisions into compact bitmasks, and dispatches each tile group through FP16 or INT8 score computation while both paths update a shared online-softmax state. Scalable precision grouping lets each routing bit govern multiple adjacent key tiles, preserving hardware-aligned compute tiles and compact metadata at long contexts. By routing all legal tile groups, TileMix preserves dense token connectivity, requires no training, and supports grouped-query attention, variable-length batches, and INT8 key/value caches. Across LongEval, LV-Eval, and A100 prefill benchmarks on LLaMA, Qwen, and Vicuna, TileMix recovers long-context quality lost under uniform INT8 and improves prefill throughput over FP16, yielding a controllable accuracy-efficiency frontier across model families. The implementation is available at https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileMix.

AI.tldr: TileMix is a precision-routing attention kernel that mixes FP16 and INT8 computation at tile level to speed up long-context prefill while preserving dense attention and accuracy, without retraining.
AI.motivation: Long-context prefill in LLMs is expensive because dense self-attention is quadratic and typically computed in uniform high precision (e.g., FP16). Existing compression or low-precision methods either uniformly lower precision (hurting quality) or sparsify attention (breaking dense connectivity), and they often misalign with hardware-friendly tile structures. There is a need for a method that can selectively lower precision in a hardware-efficient way while keeping dense attention and model quality, and requiring no retraining.
AI.method: TileMix partitions the attention score matrix into hardware-aligned tiles and groups of tiles. For each group, a routing decision is encoded in a compact bitmask that determines whether its scores are computed in FP16 or INT8. Both precision paths are implemented inside a single fused dense attention kernel and share an online-softmax state so attention remains numerically stable. Precision grouping is scalable: a single routing bit can govern multiple adjacent key tiles, reducing metadata and preserving hardware-aligned computation. The system supports grouped-query attention, variable-length batches, and INT8 key/value caches, and it does not require model retraining.
AI.result: On several long-context evaluation suites (LongEval, LV-Eval) and A100 prefill benchmarks across LLaMA, Qwen, and Vicuna models, TileMix matches or recovers the long-context quality that is lost when using uniform INT8 attention, while improving prefill throughput compared to pure FP16 attention. It provides a tunable trade-off curve between accuracy and efficiency across different model families.
AI.conclusion: TileMix demonstrates that tile-level precision routing within a fused dense attention kernel can efficiently mix FP16 and INT8 computation, preserving dense token connectivity and long-context quality while accelerating prefill. The approach is hardware-aligned, training-free, compatible with common attention variants and quantization schemes, and yields a controllable accuracy–efficiency frontier, making it a practical solution for scalable long-context LLM inference.

title: An Investigation of Translationese in the Generations of Multilingual Large Language Models
summary: Text which has been translated from another language tends to carry with it evidence of translation$\unicode{x2014}$hence, it is often referred to as $\textit{translationese}$. Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) generate text in a variety of languages. However, it is still unclear if MLLMs' generations resemble internal translation (from English or, potentially, other languages) and, thus, result in translationese. Here, we ask the following research questions: (1) Does text generated by MLLMs resemble translationese? (2) How does translationese produced by MLLMs differ from translationese produced through direct translation? We leverage established indicators of translated text to evaluate text generated by state-of-the-art MLLMs in five languages, comparing to both non-translated and human-written baselines in order to isolate translationese from other kinds of interference. Through the use of high-accuracy classification models, analyses of variance on individual linguistic features, and the collection of human annotations in a subset of two languages (German and Spanish), we assess the translationese content of MLLM generations and examine the key features that distinguish MLLM-generated text from typical translation-related interference.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether text generated by multilingual large language models (MLLMs) exhibits ‘translationese’ characteristics, and how this differs from typical human-produced translated text.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs can generate fluent text in many languages, it is unclear whether their generations behave like implicit translations (often from English), inheriting translationese artifacts that might affect naturalness, style, or downstream tasks. Understanding this is important for evaluating MLLM quality and for tasks that rely on native-like text.
AI.method: The authors compare generations from state-of-the-art MLLMs in five languages with (a) non-translated, original human text and (b) human translations. They use: (1) established linguistic indicators of translated text; (2) high-accuracy classifiers to distinguish original, translated, and MLLM text; (3) ANOVA-style analyses on individual linguistic features; and (4) human annotations for two target languages (German and Spanish) to assess perceived translationese and identify salient differences.
AI.result: MLLM-generated text shows measurable translationese-like properties when compared to original human text. However, the profile of these properties is not identical to human translations: classifiers and feature analyses reveal systematic but distinct patterns, and human judges can identify differences in style and interference characteristics between MLLM outputs and conventional translationese.
AI.conclusion: MLLM outputs often resemble translationese but form their own characteristic variety, distinct from both original text and human translations. This has implications for using MLLM-generated data as ‘native’ text in multilingual settings, and suggests that mitigating or controlling translationese-like artifacts in MLLMs may require targeted modeling or training strategies.

title: LLM-Only PDDL Domain Repair with Open-Weight Models
summary: AI planning is concerned with finding a sequence of actions that achieves a specified goal. It relies on explicit models of the world, commonly represented in the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL). An active line of research investigates how errors in such models can be detected and repaired. For example, users may provide positive test plans that are solutions, and negative test plans that fail during execution. Automated repair methods then modify the PDDL model to satisfy these constraints. In this paper, we evaluate the ability of recent open-weight large language models to perform this repair task using an LLM-only approach. Our experiments show that the symbolic baseline achieves an $F_1$ score of $.49$, while the best-performing LLM reaches $.87$ with high reasoning effort, an absolute improvement of $.38$. However, that setting has a mean test pass rate of only $.82$, falling to $.06$ on the Thoughtful domain; even the best setting that includes the test traces reaches only $.92$. Thus, current open-weight models cannot guarantee satisfaction of the test constraints required for reliable automated model repair.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether recent open-weight large language models can automatically repair PDDL planning domain models from test plans, comparing them to a symbolic baseline.
AI.motivation: Classical AI planning depends on accurate, hand-crafted PDDL models, which are often error-prone and costly to maintain. There is ongoing work on automatically detecting and fixing such model errors using test plans (positive plans that should succeed, negative plans that should fail). With the advent of powerful open-weight LLMs, it is important to understand whether they can reliably perform this model repair task without specialized symbolic machinery, potentially simplifying or automating domain engineering.
AI.method: The authors formulate PDDL model repair as an LLM-only problem: given a planning model plus positive and negative test plans (and, in some settings, their execution traces), the LLM is asked to modify the PDDL to satisfy the constraints. They evaluate several recent open-weight LLMs, varying prompting and reasoning effort, and compare them against a symbolic automated repair baseline. Performance is measured using F1 score for predicting correct repairs and test pass rate (fraction of test constraints satisfied) across multiple planning domains, including a challenging Thoughtful domain.
AI.result: The symbolic baseline achieves an F1 score of 0.49 on the repair task. The best open-weight LLM configuration attains a much higher F1 of 0.87, an absolute improvement of 0.38, but this requires high reasoning effort. Despite the improved F1, reliability is limited: this top-performing LLM setting only reaches a mean test pass rate of 0.82 overall and drops to 0.06 on the Thoughtful domain. Even when the LLM is additionally given execution traces of the tests, the best configuration only improves the test pass rate to 0.92, still short of full constraint satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs can substantially outperform a traditional symbolic baseline on PDDL model repair when evaluated by F1, indicating strong capabilities in understanding and editing planning domain models. However, they still fail to consistently satisfy all given test constraints, especially on harder domains like Thoughtful. Consequently, current open-weight LLMs are not yet reliable enough to serve as stand-alone, guaranteed-correct engines for automated PDDL model repair; additional mechanisms or hybrid approaches are needed to ensure full test satisfaction.

title: From Entity Mentions to Tone: An LLM-Based Pipeline for Media Bias Analysis
summary: This paper presents a pipeline for analyzing media bias and framing in online news. The pipeline groups articles into topics and events, adds named-entity and sentiment annotations, and compares news sources through people mentions, source-level tone, and event-level coverage patterns. We apply it to 8,358 Albanian news articles collected from GDELT and compare the resulting annotations with GDELT's automated annotations. The results show moderate agreement for sentiment and entity extraction, as well as additional person-entity pairs that can potentially support the bias analysis. We compare two annotation prompts and find that stricter sentiment-validation rules remove label-score inconsistencies but increase execution time and reduce annotation coverage. Based on these results, the simpler prompt is used for the rest of the analysis. We have provided sample analysis on source-level framing pro les, person-level tone differences across sources, and event-level gatekeeping and coverage indicators. These outputs show how the same news collection can be used to examine what sources cover, how they describe public figures, and where coverage is concentrated. The approach is particularly useful in settings where manually verified datasets or specialized language tools are limited.

AI.tldr: A pipeline is introduced to detect and analyze media bias and framing in online Albanian news, combining topic/event grouping, entity and sentiment annotations, and cross-source comparisons.
AI.motivation: To better understand and measure media bias, framing, and coverage patterns in online news, especially for low-resource languages like Albanian where manually verified datasets and specialized NLP tools are scarce.
AI.method: The authors build a multi-stage pipeline that: (1) groups online news articles into topics and events; (2) applies named-entity recognition and sentiment analysis; (3) compares news sources via statistics on people mentions, source-level tone, and event-level coverage. They run this pipeline on 8,358 Albanian news articles from GDELT, compare their annotations against GDELT’s automated annotations, and experiment with two prompt designs for annotation, one with stricter sentiment-validation rules and one simpler prompt.
AI.result: On the Albanian news corpus, the pipeline achieves moderate agreement with GDELT’s sentiment and entity annotations and identifies additional person-entity pairs useful for bias analysis. The stricter sentiment-validation prompt fixes label–score inconsistencies but increases run time and reduces the proportion of articles successfully annotated, so the simpler prompt is adopted for the main analysis. Sample analyses demonstrate clear patterns in source-level framing profiles, differing tone toward individuals across outlets, and event-level gatekeeping/coverage differences.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline is a practical way to study media bias, framing, and coverage in online news when high-quality language resources are limited. It can reveal what events different outlets cover, how they describe public figures, and where coverage is concentrated. Despite only moderate agreement with GDELT, the system adds complementary annotations—especially additional person-entity links—supporting richer bias analysis in low-resource media ecosystems.

title: Cognitive Graph Intelligence for Adaptive and Robust DDoS Attack Detection in Next Generation Networks
summary: Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks threaten network availability, requiring a cognitive detection process that senses traffic, infers intent, and supports an adaptive response under severe class imbalance and non-stationary conditions. This paper proposes a Graph-based Generative Adversarial Network (GraphGAN) that serves as the cognitive detection engine for this task. GraphGAN captures the relational structure among traffic flows while addressing imbalance through adversarial generation of synthetic samples. Sequential flows are converted into $k$-nearest neighbor graphs using sliding windows to preserve feature-similarity and temporal dependencies among flows. The generator learns the distribution of DDoS attacks to synthesize realistic minority samples, while a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN)-based discriminator distinguishes real from synthetic graph data. A separate GCN classifier, trained on the balanced dataset, performs the final detection decision. Evaluations on four benchmark datasets show that GraphGAN achieves superior accuracy, precision, and recall compared to state-of-the-art approaches, particularly in data-scarce scenarios. By integrating temporal graph construction, adversarial augmentation, and GCN classification, GraphGAN effectively models coordinated attack behaviors and mitigates class imbalance, providing a robust and topology-aware solution for intrusion detection in data-constrained environments.

AI.tldr: They propose GraphGAN, a GAN-based graph model that converts traffic flows into temporal k-NN graphs, uses a graph-based generator to synthesize minority DDoS samples, and a GCN discriminator plus classifier to improve intrusion detection under imbalance and non-stationarity, outperforming state-of-the-art on four datasets.
AI.motivation: DDoS attacks heavily threaten network availability, but detection is hard because of severe class imbalance (few attacks vs many normal flows), non-stationary traffic, and the need to reason about coordinated, relational behavior across flows rather than isolated packets. Existing methods often ignore graph-structured relations, handle imbalance poorly, and struggle in data-scarce settings. The paper is motivated by the need for a cognitive, topology-aware detection engine that can model traffic relationships, generate realistic attack samples to rebalance data, and remain effective when labeled attack data are limited.
AI.method: They design GraphGAN, a graph-based generative adversarial network framework. First, they transform sequential network flows into temporal k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) graphs via sliding windows, preserving feature similarity and temporal dependencies. The GAN’s generator learns the distribution of DDoS attack graphs and produces synthetic minority (attack) samples. The discriminator is based on a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) that distinguishes real from synthetic graph data, encouraging realistic synthesis. After adversarial training, they build a balanced dataset combining real and generated attack graphs, and train a separate GCN classifier for the actual DDoS detection task. They evaluate on four benchmark intrusion detection datasets and compare with state-of-the-art baselines under varying data availability.
AI.result: GraphGAN improves detection metrics—accuracy, precision, and recall—over state-of-the-art methods across four benchmark datasets. Gains are most pronounced in data-scarce situations with strong class imbalance, indicating that the adversarially generated graph samples successfully enrich the minority class and improve generalization. The model captures coordinated DDoS behaviors via the temporal k-NN graph construction, leading to better identification of attack patterns compared with methods that treat flows independently or use non-graph oversampling techniques.
AI.conclusion: GraphGAN, by integrating temporal graph modeling, adversarial sample generation, and GCN-based classification, offers a robust, topology-aware solution for DDoS intrusion detection under class imbalance and limited labeled data. The graph-based GAN effectively models relational and temporal structure in network traffic, generates realistic minority attack samples, and substantially enhances detection performance compared with existing approaches. This demonstrates that cognitive, graph-centric generative modeling is a promising direction for intrusion detection in non-stationary, data-constrained network environments.

title: Effects of Answer Format Variation on Gender Bias in Large Language Models
comment: 6th Workshop on Computational Linguistics for the Political and Social Sciences (CPSS 2026)
summary: Gender bias or other social biases in large language models (LLMs) are frequently evaluated with question answering or survey benchmarks where the LLM needs to give a response in a predefined answer format. It is well known in survey science that the answer format has a substantial impact on answers, just as LLMs are sensitive to the prompt wording. However, to our knowledge it has not been studied yet how changes in answer format impact the measurement of gender bias in LLMs and their alignment with human response distributions. We evaluate three instruction-tuned models on the BBQ benchmark and OpinionQA survey data across closed-ended, Likert-scaled and open-ended formats, comparing bias measurement and distributional alignment under otherwise identical conditions. We find that answer format does substantially alter measured outcomes, including reversals in order rankings. These differences arise because each format elicits distinct response behaviours, such as forced-choice selection, scale-based distributions and refusal in free-text generation. Our findings highlight the importance of treating answer format as a substantive component of LLM evaluation and motivate multi-format designs for more robust model assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different answer formats (multiple-choice, Likert scales, open-ended) change the measured gender bias of LLMs and their alignment with human responses.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of gender and social bias in LLMs usually rely on one fixed answer format, even though survey research shows that answer format strongly affects responses. For LLMs, we know prompts matter, but we do not know how much answer format alone changes measured bias and similarity to humans. The authors want to understand whether evaluation results—and even model rankings—are stable when only the answer format is varied.
AI.method: The authors take three instruction-tuned LLMs and evaluate them on two established datasets: the BBQ bias benchmark and OpinionQA survey data. They hold prompts and content constant but systematically vary the answer format: (1) closed-ended/forced-choice, (2) Likert-type rating scales, and (3) open-ended free-text responses. They then compare (a) bias metrics across formats and (b) how closely each model’s response distribution aligns with human response distributions under each format.
AI.result: Changing only the answer format produces substantial differences in measured gender and social bias, including cases where the ordering of models by bias reverses between formats. Each format induces characteristic response behaviors: forced-choice formats push models to pick a side, Likert scales lead to graded distributions of responses, and open-ended formats lead to more refusals or qualified answers. These behavioral shifts change both the apparent level of bias and the measured similarity to human respondents.
AI.conclusion: Answer format is not a neutral technical detail in LLM bias evaluations; it is a substantive factor that can significantly change measured outcomes and even model rankings. Reliable assessment of social bias and human alignment in LLMs should therefore use multiple answer formats or explicitly justify the chosen format. The authors recommend multi-format evaluation designs to obtain more robust and interpretable measurements of bias in LLMs.

title: LEGO-RL: Harness-Native Reinforcement Learning for Coding Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning for coding agents increasingly relies on long-running agent harnesses to manage tool integration, repository contexts, and execution feedback. However, the native execution environments of these harnesses are inherently misaligned with policy-gradient training: environmental crashes and reward hacking corrupt outcome signals, while train-inference discrepancies decouple rollout behavior from policy updates. To address this, we present LEGO-RL, a framework that bridges native coding-agent harnesses with scalable policy-gradient optimization without modifying their internal control flow. LEGO-RL is built upon three pillars: (1) faithful optimization via in-process LLM proxying that captures raw generation streams for token-level alignment and robust trainer-side log-probability recomputation, even under harness-side compaction or re-serialization; (2) reliable execution via scalable sandbox orchestration featuring image caching and stage-wise defenses to mitigate reward hacking; and (3) observable training through an integrated plugin that automates validation and monitoring, paired with a Live UI for granular trajectory diagnostics. We evaluate LEGO-RL by training the sparse MoE model Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with GSPO across three native coding-agent harnesses. LEGO-RL improves Qwen3.5-35B-A3B across OpenHands SDK (64.0% to 70.4%), Claude Code (62.4% to 68.2%), and OpenCode (57.2% to 66.6%) on SWE-bench Verified, while maintaining a rollout-training probability correlation above 0.99.

AI.tldr: LEGO-RL is a framework that makes it possible to train coding agents with policy-gradient RL directly inside real-world, long-running coding harnesses, while keeping rollouts faithful, robust, and observable.
AI.motivation: Modern coding agents interact with complex, long-running harnesses that manage tools, repositories, and execution, but these environments are unstable and misaligned with standard policy-gradient RL. Crashes, reward hacking, and discrepancies between training and inference make it hard to optimize models reliably using real harnesses instead of simplified simulators. The authors want a way to do scalable RL that uses the real agent harness, without having to rewrite or deeply modify it, while ensuring that the training signal remains faithful and robust.
AI.method: They propose LEGO-RL, a framework that sits between the RL trainer and existing coding-agent harnesses without changing harness control flow. It has three key components: (1) in-process LLM proxying that intercepts and records the raw token generation stream, enabling token-level alignment and recomputation of log-probabilities on the trainer side, even if the harness compacts, truncates, or re-serializes messages; (2) a scalable sandbox orchestration layer with image caching and staged defenses against reward hacking and unstable executions, making harness runs more reliable and repeatable; and (3) an integrated plugin plus Live UI that automate validation, monitoring, and detailed trajectory inspection during RL training. They then use LEGO-RL to train a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) with GSPO across multiple native coding harnesses.
AI.result: Using LEGO-RL to train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with GSPO across three different coding-agent harnesses—OpenHands SDK, Claude Code, and OpenCode—yields consistent performance improvements on the SWE-bench Verified benchmark. Accuracy improves from 64.0% to 70.4% on OpenHands SDK, from 62.4% to 68.2% on Claude Code, and from 57.2% to 66.6% on OpenCode. At the same time, the framework maintains a very high correlation (>0.99) between rollout-time and training-time policy probabilities, indicating faithful optimization despite the complexity of the harnesses.
AI.conclusion: LEGO-RL successfully bridges real-world coding-agent harnesses with scalable policy-gradient RL, without requiring internal changes to the harness logic. Its proxying, sandboxing, and observability components together provide faithful, robust, and inspectable training. The empirical gains on SWE-bench Verified across multiple harnesses, combined with near-perfect rollout–training probability alignment, suggest that LEGO-RL is an effective and general approach for RL training of coding agents in native, production-like environments.

title: ArborMem: Navigating Interaction States with Memory Forests
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as persistent conversational assistants, requiring memory that preserves relevant experience and maintains continuity across interactions. Existing methods improve access to conversational history through long-context processing, selective retrieval, and structured memory organization. However, most systems treat memory access as retrieving relevant past information without first determining which prior interaction state the current turn resumes. This limitation becomes particularly important when conversations interleave multiple tasks, people, and plans that may be interrupted and later revisited. We introduce ArborMem, an online memory framework that represents a long-running conversation as a navigable forest of interaction states. Each branch preserves a locally coherent trajectory, while the forest maintains multiple trajectories that may later be resumed. For each new input, ArborMem localizes the relevant state, restores its branch-local context, and augments it with reusable evidence retrieved across branches, preserving interaction continuity without conflating semantically related but structurally distinct trajectories. Existing long-term memory benchmarks cover diverse memory and reasoning capabilities but do not explicitly isolate branch-structured challenges. We therefore introduce BranchMemEval, a controlled diagnostic benchmark for interleaved and resumable interaction trajectories. Experiments on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, BEAM 100K, and BranchMemEval show that ArborMem outperforms the strongest baselines by 3.36 to 10.31 percentage points on the three established benchmarks and by 5.0 points on BranchMemEval. Its advantage grows under constrained read budgets, while complete memory queries remain below half a second.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ArborMem, a tree-structured memory system for long-running LLM conversations, plus a new benchmark (BranchMemEval) to evaluate interleaved, resumable dialogue trajectories.
AI.motivation: Persistent LLM assistants must manage long, interleaved conversations involving multiple tasks, users, and plans that can be paused and later resumed. Existing long-context and retrieval-based memory methods focus on finding relevant information but do not explicitly track which prior interaction state a new turn is resuming. This leads to conflating different conversation threads that are semantically related but structurally distinct. The authors aim to build a memory framework that can explicitly represent, localize, and resume multiple branching conversational trajectories over time and to provide a benchmark that isolates this branch-structured challenge.
AI.method: They introduce ArborMem, which represents a long-running conversation as a forest of branches, where each branch is a locally coherent interaction trajectory. For every new user input, the system: (1) localizes the appropriate prior interaction state/branch that the user is resuming, (2) restores the branch-local conversational context, and (3) augments it with reusable evidence retrieved across different branches, while maintaining structural separation between trajectories. They also design BranchMemEval, a controlled diagnostic benchmark with interleaved and resumable interaction trajectories to test this branch-structured memory capability. ArborMem is evaluated on existing memory benchmarks (LongMemEval, LoCoMo, BEAM 100K) and the new BranchMemEval, under varying read-budget constraints, and latency of memory queries is measured.
AI.result: On three established long-term memory benchmarks (LongMemEval, LoCoMo, BEAM 100K), ArborMem outperforms the strongest baselines by 3.36–10.31 percentage points. On the proposed BranchMemEval benchmark, ArborMem improves performance by 5.0 percentage points over baselines. Its relative advantage increases when the allowed memory read budget is constrained, and despite its structured memory operations, full memory queries can be executed in under 0.5 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Modeling conversational memory as a forest of resumable interaction branches improves an LLM assistant’s ability to maintain continuity in interleaved, long-running dialogues. Explicitly localizing and resuming prior states, while reusing cross-branch evidence without conflating trajectories, yields better performance than existing long-context and retrieval methods, especially under tight read budgets. BranchMemEval provides a targeted benchmark for this branch-structured challenge, and ArborMem achieves state-of-the-art results on both existing and new long-term memory benchmarks with practical latency.

title: Task-Aware Harness Provisioning for LLM Agents in Mission-Critical Infrastructure Operations
summary: LLM agents have been widely adopted to operate mission-critical infrastructure (MCI). These agents normally rely on a harness that determines what information they can access, which tools they can use, and what actions they can take. Existing systems often expose the same comprehensive harness to every task, which may not be necessary and cause resource wastes. In this paper, we focus on the identification of optimal harness configurations, and view it as a resource-matching problem between what each task requires and what the harness provides. To measure this match, we classify MCI tasks based on the mathematical representation of the underlying system and rank harness configurations by the amount and type of information they provide. We then construct task-to-harness mappings from two sources: mining research literature and measuring controlled agent execution. Leveraging the measured mapping, we propose a new harness provisioning algorithm: map-guided escalation. It begins with a task-specific harness and expands to full provision only after a failed self-check. We evaluate our method in two representative MCI tasks: in liquid cooling, it improves the agent accuracy from 0.652 under full provision to 0.715 and achieves accuracy comparable to Reflexion with 48% fewer tokens; In power grids, full provision remains accuracy-optimal, while map-based provisioning offers lower-cost alternatives. These findings show that harness provisioning follows a domain-dependent accuracy-cost Pareto frontier rather than a universal optimum.

AI.tldr: The paper optimizes how LLM agents are configured (their “harness”) when operating mission-critical infrastructure, reducing cost while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used to manage mission-critical infrastructure like cooling systems and power grids. These agents interact with their environment through a harness that specifies accessible information, tools, and actions. Current practice often gives every task the same large, fully featured harness, which can waste computational resources and may not always be necessary for good performance. There is a need to systematically determine which harness components are truly required for each task, balancing reliability with efficiency.
AI.method: The authors frame harness configuration as a resource-matching problem between task requirements and harness capabilities. They (1) classify mission-critical infrastructure tasks according to the mathematical representation of the underlying physical system, (2) rank harness configurations by the richness and type of information they expose, and (3) build task-to-harness mappings using two approaches: mining research literature and empirically measuring how agents perform under controlled execution with different harnesses. Based on these mappings, they design a map-guided escalation algorithm that starts with a minimal, task-specific harness and only escalates to a more comprehensive (up to full) harness if the agent fails a self-check.
AI.result: On a liquid cooling control task, the map-guided escalation strategy improves agent accuracy from 0.652 with full harness provision to 0.715, while also achieving accuracy on par with Reflexion-based methods using 48% fewer tokens. On a power grid task, the best accuracy is still achieved with full harness provision, but the map-based provisioning identifies lower-cost harnesses that offer competitive performance. Overall, results indicate that the optimal harness configuration is domain-dependent and not universally maximal.
AI.conclusion: Harness provisioning for LLM agents in mission-critical infrastructure should be treated as a domain-specific optimization problem rather than defaulting to a fully loaded configuration. The proposed map-guided escalation approach can safely start from lean, task-tailored harnesses and escalate only when needed, yielding better accuracy-cost trade-offs in some domains (e.g., liquid cooling) and competitive, lower-cost options in others (e.g., power grids). This reveals a domain-dependent accuracy–cost Pareto frontier in harness design instead of a one-size-fits-all optimum.

title: CoAL-RAG: A Complexity-Aware Legal Retrieval-Augmented Generation Method
summary: Legal consultation questions exhibit multi-level complexity. A single retrieval strategy often leads to over-reasoning for simple questions and poor interpretability for complex ones, making it difficult to meet the requirements for both answer quality and efficiency in high-risk scenarios. To address this issue, this paper proposes CoAL-RAG, a complexity-aware legal retrieval-augmented generation method, which constructs a multi-dimensional evaluation mechanism based on ``question essence'' and ``retrieval consistency'' to enable adaptive routing of retrieval strategies. First, the reasoning demand is quantified according to the logical structure of the question. Then, the discrepancy between semantic retrieval and keyword retrieval is utilized to indirectly reflect problem complexity, thereby selecting the most appropriate retrieval strategy and dynamically filtering contextual information. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline models not only on Chinese legal benchmarks (SocialLawQA, LawBench) but also demonstrates strong cross-jurisdictional generalization on English datasets (LexGLUE, CaseHold). Specifically, on Chinese datasets, the BLEU score improves by 42.5\% and ROUGE-L reaches 3.6 times that of knowledge graph-based methods. On English benchmarks, CoAL-RAG maintains highly competitive accuracy, achieving an optimal balance between generation quality, deep logical reasoning, and system efficiency across different legal systems.

AI.tldr: CoAL-RAG is a complexity-aware legal RAG framework that adaptively chooses retrieval strategies based on question complexity to improve answer quality and efficiency across Chinese and English legal datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing legal consultation systems often use a single retrieval strategy, which causes over-reasoning for simple queries and insufficient or opaque reasoning for complex ones. In high-risk legal scenarios, it is crucial to balance answer quality, interpretability, and computational efficiency. The paper aims to build a mechanism that can sense the complexity of a legal question and automatically pick an appropriate retrieval strategy to better support legal reasoning across jurisdictions.
AI.method: The paper proposes CoAL-RAG, a complexity-aware retrieval-augmented generation framework for legal QA. It builds a multi-dimensional evaluation mechanism based on two main aspects: (1) "question essence"—quantifying the reasoning demand by analyzing the logical structure of the question to estimate how much reasoning is needed; and (2) "retrieval consistency"—measuring the discrepancy between semantic retrieval and keyword retrieval results, using this gap as a proxy for problem complexity. Based on these signals, CoAL-RAG adaptively routes questions to different retrieval strategies and dynamically filters the contextual legal information fed to the generator, aiming to match retrieval depth and style to the question's complexity.
AI.result: On Chinese legal benchmarks (SocialLawQA, LawBench), CoAL-RAG significantly outperforms baseline models, particularly knowledge-graph-based approaches: BLEU improves by 42.5% and ROUGE-L is 3.6 times higher than those methods. On English legal benchmarks (LexGLUE, CaseHold), the approach exhibits strong cross-jurisdictional generalization with highly competitive accuracy, indicating that the complexity-aware routing and retrieval consistency mechanisms transfer well across different legal systems and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Complexity-aware retrieval routing, operationalized through measures of question essence and retrieval consistency, allows legal RAG systems to better align retrieval strategy with question difficulty. CoAL-RAG achieves a strong balance among generation quality, deep logical reasoning, and system efficiency, outperforming existing baselines on both Chinese and English legal datasets and demonstrating promising cross-jurisdictional robustness. This suggests that adapting retrieval to question complexity is a key direction for improving legal QA systems in high-risk, heterogeneous legal environments.

title: Depth Enables Local Entropy: Quadratic Depth Dependence in Deep Variation-Norm ReLU Regression
summary: We study Gaussian regression over the explicit vector-valued Parhi--Nowak deep-RBV^2 architecture with depth L, width w, layer-sum variation budget A, and output bound B. For this O(L w^2)-parameterized architecture, the known lower and upper bounds differ by one factor of depth. We construct a local packing showing that the quadratic depth dependence is intrinsic under an explicit sample-size-dependent radius condition. The packing has log-cardinality Omega(L^2 w^2 log w); its codewords lie in an O(lambda) L^2 ball and are pairwise Omega(lambda)-separated. The main ingredients are a bias-corrected bounded-coefficient approximation theorem and balanced amplification: multiplying a depth-D ReLU network by q can be implemented using one constant channel so that every coefficient grows by only q^(1/D). Translation to vector-valued RBV^2 blocks then has layer-sum cost O(D w^2 q^(1/D)). Gaussian Fano yields a radius-explicit lower bound governed by the output, testing, and representation scales. Under A=B=R, sigma proportional to R, and the stated radius condition, this gives minimax risk at least of order L^2 w^2 log(w) R^2/n. A pseudodimension-based finite-net upper bound gives O-tilde(L^2 w^2 R^2/n) for unbounded Gaussian responses. Thus the minimax risk has quadratic polynomial dependence on depth, up to logarithmic factors, and exhibits a transition to representation-limited behavior at smaller radius.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the minimax risk of Gaussian regression using a specific deep ReLU-based architecture (Parhi–Nowak deep-RBV^2), proving that the risk depends quadratically on network depth (L) and essentially linearly on squared width (w^2), up to logs, and that this quadratic depth dependence is intrinsic under a certain radius condition.
AI.motivation: Existing lower and upper bounds on estimation error for this architecture differ by one factor of the network depth L, leaving it unclear whether the true statistical complexity grows linearly or quadratically with depth. The authors aim to close this gap, determine the intrinsic dependence of minimax risk on depth and width, and clarify how the architecture’s parameterization and norm constraints govern representation- versus noise-limited behavior.
AI.method: They build a carefully constructed local packing of functions realized by the deep-RBV^2 architecture, with many well-separated codewords lying in a small-radius ball. Key technical tools are: (1) a bias-corrected bounded-coefficient approximation theorem allowing accurate representation with controlled layer-sum variation; (2) a balanced amplification scheme that scales the output of a depth-D ReLU network by a factor q while increasing each parameter only by q^(1/D), implemented using a constant number of channels; and (3) a translation of these constructions to the vector-valued RBV^2 block setting with controlled layer-sum cost. Applying Gaussian Fano’s inequality with this packing yields explicit, radius-dependent lower bounds. For the upper bound, they use pseudodimension arguments to build finite nets and obtain corresponding risk upper bounds for unbounded Gaussian responses.
AI.result: They construct a packing of size with log-cardinality Omega(L^2 w^2 log w), contained in an O(lambda) L^2 ball and with pairwise separation Omega(lambda). Using this packing together with Gaussian Fano’s inequality, they derive a radius-explicit lower bound on the minimax risk that depends on the output, testing, and representation scales. Under the specific scaling A = B = R and noise variance sigma proportional to R, and under an explicit radius condition, the minimax risk is at least on the order of L^2 w^2 log(w) R^2 / n. Complementarily, using pseudodimension-based finite-net arguments they prove an upper bound of order \tilde{O}(L^2 w^2 R^2 / n) (up to logarithmic factors) for Gaussian regression with unbounded responses.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that for the Parhi–Nowak deep-RBV^2 architecture, the minimax risk in Gaussian regression necessarily exhibits a quadratic dependence on depth L (modulo logs) and scales like L^2 w^2 R^2/n, reconciling previous lower and upper bounds. The quadratic depth dependence is intrinsic under the given sample-size-dependent radius condition, not an artifact of proof techniques. Furthermore, the results characterize a transition from noise-limited to representation-limited behavior as the effective radius shrinks, showing how architectural constraints (layer-sum variation A and output bound B) and noise scale jointly control this transition.

title: Auditing Exposure to Harmful Content on TikTok using Multimodal Language Models: A Cross-National, Age-Stratified Study
comment: 20 pages, 16 figures, 14 tables. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Online video platforms can expose young users to harmful content, but independent audits remain difficult because video annotation is costly and moderation judgments vary across languages. We audit TikTok in France, Italy, and Sweden with sockpuppet accounts representing four age personas (13, 16, 19, 40), collecting 36,971 videos from passive For-You-page scrolling and active sessions that scroll, search for harm keywords, and scroll again. To scale annotation, we validate four multimodal LLMs against native-speaker labels on a 300-video reference set. Gemini 2.5 Flash with eight sampled frames plus text performs best (aggregate kappa = 0.42), at half the per-call cost of native-video upload, and we apply it to a 10% sample for approximately \$50 in total API spend across both modalities. Keyword search returns 35-56% harmful content, a 1.5-7.5x increase over the scrolling baseline in ten of twelve country-age combinations; the spike is temporary and flattens the age differences observed in France and Sweden. Under passive scrolling, Italy has the highest harm rate at every age, with Italian age-19 reaching 48.6%. Overall, MLLM-based auditing offers a scalable approach for cross-national youth-safety audits, while provider safety filters (1.1% refusal rate) under-count the most explicit harms.

AI.tldr: The paper audits TikTok’s exposure of youth to harmful content across three European countries using sockpuppet accounts and multimodal LLM-based annotation, finding high harm rates, especially when using keyword search, and demonstrating that current platform safety filters substantially under-detect explicit harms.
AI.motivation: Independent, cross-national audits of youth exposure to harmful content on online video platforms are difficult because manual video annotation is expensive and moderation standards vary by language and country. There is a need for scalable, language-agnostic methods to measure and compare the prevalence of harmful content, and to evaluate the effectiveness of platform safety mechanisms, especially as short-video platforms like TikTok become central to young people’s media diets.
AI.method: The authors create sockpuppet TikTok accounts in France, Italy, and Sweden, representing four age personas (13, 16, 19, 40). They collect 36,971 videos through two behavioral modes: (1) passive For-You-page scrolling and (2) active sessions involving scrolling, searching for harm-related keywords, and then scrolling again. To label harm at scale, they benchmark four multimodal large language models against native-speaker human annotations on a 300-video reference set. They find Gemini 2.5 Flash, using eight sampled video frames plus associated text, gives the best agreement (aggregate Cohen’s kappa = 0.42) at lower cost than full video uploads, and use it to annotate a 10% sample of the corpus for about $50 total API cost. They also compare their MLLM labels to provider-side safety filter refusals.
