AI.result: Keyword-based search results are substantially more harmful than content shown from baseline scrolling: 35–56% of search-based results are harmful, representing a 1.5–7.5× increase over passive scrolling in ten of twelve country-age combinations. This surge in harm after search is temporary but large enough to erase age-based differences that were otherwise visible in France and Sweden. Under passive For-You scrolling alone, Italy exhibits the highest harmful-content rate at every tested age, with the 19-year-old Italian persona reaching 48.6% harmful videos. Platform safety filters rarely block content (around 1.1% refusal rate) and systematically miss the most explicit harmful material. The Gemini-based annotation pipeline achieves moderate agreement with human coders while keeping financial costs low.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal LLMs can support scalable, cross-national audits of youth exposure to harmful content on short-video platforms, substantially reducing the cost barrier posed by manual annotation. The study finds that TikTok exposes young users to considerable amounts of harmful content, especially when users engage in keyword search, and that platform-level safety filters undercount or fail to block particularly explicit harms. The authors conclude that MLLM-based auditing is a promising, practical tool for ongoing youth-safety monitoring across languages and countries, but that current platform safety mechanisms are insufficient to prevent high-risk content from reaching young audiences.

title: Structure-Internalized Rule Language Model for Faithful Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Knowledge Graph Reasoning (KGR) aims to discover latent facts by leveraging the structural evidence available in KGs, posing a challenge to the structural semantic understanding capability of KGR models. Recent studies have demonstrated that Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve remarkable progress on KGR tasks via flexible in-context learning. However, the inherent representation inconsistency between KG structural context and LLM parametric knowledge remains inadequately addressed. This limitation prevents LLMs from effectively perceiving reasoning evidence that aligns with KG constraints, which undermines both the effectiveness and faithfulness of reasoning. We refer to this problem as reasoning evidence perception drift of LLMs over KGs. To address this problem, we propose a Structure-Internalized Rule Language Model (SIRLM), which centers on structural rule generation to couple the parametric learning of structural knowledge with the faithfulness evaluation of reasoning logic, enabling LLMs to anchor tightly to KG-grounded evidence. Specifically, we first design a Structure-Internalized Rule Generator (SIRG), which incorporates an in-context learning block augmented with a structural relation memory to coordinate structural and parametric knowledge. Furthermore, we equip SIRG with a KG tokenizer based on structural invariance learning and a neuro-symbolic reasoner based on rule-constrained message propagation. These components provide SIRG with learnable structural representations and faithful rule-execution feedback, respectively. Our SIRLM can be seamlessly integrated into standard LLM training paradigms, such as SFT and GRPO. Extensive experiments against 17 state-of-the-art KGR methods on 36 datasets demonstrate the significant superiority of SIRLM.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SIRLM, a structure-internalized rule language model that improves knowledge graph reasoning by tightly aligning LLM reasoning with KG-grounded structural evidence, achieving state-of-the-art results on many datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge graph reasoning methods, including recent LLM-based approaches, struggle to fully exploit KG structural evidence because of a mismatch between KG structure and LLM parametric knowledge. This causes LLMs to rely on spurious or unconstrained reasoning paths, leading to effectiveness and faithfulness issues—what the authors call reasoning evidence perception drift. The paper is motivated by the need to better internalize KG structure into LLMs so that their reasoning is consistent with KG constraints and logically faithful.
AI.method: The authors propose SIRLM (Structure-Internalized Rule Language Model), whose core is a Structure-Internalized Rule Generator (SIRG). SIRG generates structural rules that couple parametric learning with explicit faithfulness evaluation. It includes: (1) an in-context learning block augmented with a structural relation memory to coordinate between structural and parametric knowledge; (2) a KG tokenizer designed via structural invariance learning to produce structure-aware token representations; and (3) a neuro-symbolic reasoner that performs rule-constrained message propagation, providing feedback on whether rules execute faithfully over the KG. SIRLM is trained within standard LLM paradigms like supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and GRPO, using structural rules and reasoner feedback to align LLM reasoning with KG evidence.
AI.result: Across 36 KGR datasets and against 17 state-of-the-art baselines, SIRLM shows consistent and significant performance gains. The experiments indicate that explicitly internalizing KG structure via rule generation and neuro-symbolic reasoning improves both accuracy and faithfulness of KG reasoning compared to vanilla LLM-based and traditional KGR methods.
AI.conclusion: Coupling LLMs with explicit structural rule generation and neuro-symbolic execution effectively mitigates reasoning evidence perception drift when doing KG reasoning. By internalizing KG structure into the model through a structure-aware tokenizer, structural memory, and rule-constrained propagation, SIRLM can more faithfully align its reasoning with KG-grounded evidence and achieves superior performance on a wide range of KGR benchmarks. The framework is compatible with common LLM training pipelines, suggesting it can be broadly applied to enhance KG reasoning in LLMs.

title: Write, Execute, Refine: From Skill Followers to Skill Optimizers via Reinforcement Learning from Execution Feedback
summary: Expert-written natural language skills can improve tool-using agents, yet agent-authored skills perform 8-11 points worse than using no skill. This gap suggests that following procedural guidance and improving it from execution evidence are distinct capabilities. Inference time loops can repair skills but do not improve the model that writes the next one. We study how to organize execution experience from intermediate skills into training states for an optimizer. We introduce WER (Write, Execute, and Refine), a multi-phase framework that trains a Skill Optimizer outside a frozen executor. The optimizer proposes skills, a frozen agent executes each repeatedly, and a programmatic verifier scores the outcomes. The scores provide relative credit and select mixed-outcome records. Matched successful and failed trajectories from these records form the next phase's refinement states, so the optimizer learns from the consequences of its earlier outputs. On BFCL v4 multi-turn and tau2-bench, WER improves average Pass@1 over the no-skill baseline by 7.80 and 3.85 points, respectively. Under an identical refinement workflow, it outperforms the same backbone without optimizer training by 9.35 and 10.29 points. The trained 4B optimizer reaches 76.63 percent on BFCL v4, outperforming all evaluated off-the-shelf general-purpose models used as skill optimizers on average.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes WER, a framework that trains a separate skill-optimizing model (distinct from the executor) to write and iteratively refine natural language skills using execution feedback, substantially boosting tool-using agents’ performance.
AI.motivation: Natural language skills written by experts can significantly enhance tool-using agents, but when agents author their own skills, performance degrades notably, indicating that writing effective procedural guidance and improving it from feedback are hard for current models. Existing inference-time repair loops fix skills ad hoc without improving the underlying model, creating a need for a training framework that systematically turns execution experience into better skill-writing capabilities.
AI.method: WER (Write, Execute, and Refine) introduces a multi-phase training pipeline with two components: a frozen executor agent and a trainable Skill Optimizer. In each phase, the optimizer proposes skills, the frozen agent executes them multiple times, and a programmatic verifier scores the outcomes. These scores provide relative credit assignment and identify mixed-outcome records. From these, the system constructs refinement states by pairing matched successful and failed trajectories linked to earlier skills, which then serve as supervised training data for the optimizer in the next phase, enabling it to learn from the consequences of its outputs without changing the executor.
AI.result: On BFCL v4 multi-turn and tau2-bench benchmarks, WER increases Pass@1 by 7.80 and 3.85 points over a no-skill baseline. When compared to an otherwise identical refinement workflow that lacks optimizer training, WER yields improvements of 9.35 and 10.29 points, respectively. A 4B-parameter Skill Optimizer trained with WER achieves 76.63% Pass@1 on BFCL v4, surpassing all tested off-the-shelf general-purpose models used as skill optimizers on average.
AI.conclusion: Separating skill optimization from execution and training a dedicated Skill Optimizer with structured execution feedback allows agents to write significantly more effective natural language skills. WER demonstrates that organizing execution traces into refinement states and iteratively training on them closes much of the gap between expert-written and model-written skills and can outperform larger, general-purpose models in the role of skill optimization.

title: SAGE: Self-Evolving Storyboard Skills via Attribution-Guided Rule Evolution
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Dataset available at https://github.com/creDreams/PROSE
summary: Storyboards turn screenplays into visual shot plans for automated short drama production. Professional storyboarding relies on tacit directorial expertise and remains an industrial bottleneck. Large language models can automate this step, but methods for supplying directing knowledge face three challenges: (1) Knowledge acquisition: the craft remains implicit in exemplars or must be written manually. (2) Knowledge refinement: authored knowledge is not evaluated against execution outcomes, and opaque generation prevents feedback attribution to the knowledge behind each decision. (3) Knowledge injection: injecting all knowledge exceeds usable context, while manual selection for every narrative group does not scale. We present SAGE (Skill with Attribution-Guided Evolution), a deployed framework that learns, attributes, evolves, and routes directing knowledge from expert demonstrations. SAGE derives rules that are independent of episode content by contrasting each training screenplay with its expert storyboard. During generation, the model records each narrative group's adopted rules. Combining these records with localized feedback enables targeted updates to individual rules. Evolved rules form scenario packages with a routing index, so each group retrieves only a bounded set appropriate to its situation without expert intervention. On 18 test episodes across three genres, SAGE scored 77.8 on a rubric validated by experts, versus 77.1 for professional directors. Deployed for 14 days on Virtual Film Studio, SAGE produced 1,344 narrative group outputs; 87.2 percent were accepted without substantive edits, and the production team recorded over 83 percent less authoring time per episode. We release PROSE, the first public dataset pairing screenplays with storyboards by professional directors across 68 episodes: https://github.com/creDreams/PROSE.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAGE, a framework that automatically converts screenplays into storyboard-style shot plans using directing knowledge learned from expert examples, achieving near-professional quality and major time savings in a real production setting.
AI.motivation: Professional storyboarding is a major bottleneck in automated short drama production because it depends on tacit, hard-to-codify directorial expertise. Existing attempts to use large language models struggle with: (1) acquiring directing knowledge that is mostly implicit in expert work or requires manual authoring, (2) refining that knowledge based on concrete execution feedback, and (3) injecting the right subset of knowledge into the model’s limited context window without extensive manual curation. The paper aims to systematize and automate this process so that high-quality storyboards can be produced at scale with minimal expert intervention.
AI.method: They propose SAGE (Skill with Attribution-Guided Evolution), a framework that learns generalizable directing rules from pairs of screenplays and expert storyboards. SAGE contrasts each screenplay with its storyboard to derive content-independent rules. During generation, for each narrative group, SAGE logs which rules are applied, creating explicit attributions from outputs back to underlying rules. Human or automatic feedback is then associated with those specific rules, enabling targeted refinement (evolution) of the rule set. The refined rules are organized into scenario packages, each indexed for routing so that a narrative group retrieves only a bounded, context-appropriate subset of rules, staying within context limits and avoiding manual selection. The system is deployed on an industrial platform (Virtual Film Studio).
AI.result: On 18 test episodes across three genres, SAGE’s storyboard outputs achieved an average expert-validated rubric score of 77.8, slightly higher than the 77.1 score for professional directors, indicating near-parity or better performance. In a 14‑day deployment on the Virtual Film Studio platform, SAGE produced 1,344 narrative group outputs, 87.2% of which were accepted without substantive edits by the production team. This deployment led to more than an 83% reduction in authoring time per episode compared with previous workflows.
AI.conclusion: SAGE successfully captures and operationalizes directing knowledge from expert demonstrations into an evolving rule system that can be routed efficiently for different narrative contexts. It addresses key challenges of knowledge acquisition, refinement, and injection for LLM-based storyboarding, achieving professional-level quality and large productivity gains in a real production environment. The authors also release PROSE, the first public dataset of screenplay–storyboard pairs, to support future research in automated directing and storyboard generation.

title: Multi-turn Conversational AI from Text to Multimodal Interaction: Data, Models, Evaluation, and Open Challenges
comment: Multi-turn Conversational AI; Multimodal Dialogue; AudioLLMs; Conversational Memory; Tool-Augmented Agents; Dialogue Evaluation
summary: Conversational AI is moving beyond isolated text prompts toward sustained, multimodal interaction. In real conversations, users clarify goals, revise requests, interrupt responses, switch topics, and introduce new evidence while expecting systems to preserve context across turns. This makes multi-turn dialogue a distinct challenge requiring systems to maintain and update memory, ground responses across modalities, tools, and external knowledge, and adapt across languages and cultures. This study reviews multi-turn conversational AI across text-only dialogue, AudioLLMs and speech-native systems, multimodal and omni-modal systems, and tool-augmented agents. We organize the literature around datasets and benchmarks, modeling paradigms, training strategies, evaluation setups, and cross-cutting challenges. Our analysis shows that support for multiple modalities has advanced faster than the ability to sustain coherent interaction across a session. Despite stronger capabilities to perceive, speak, and act across modalities, current systems still struggle with persistent memory, cross-turn grounding, full-duplex interaction, robust evaluation, and cultural alignment. We conclude with a research agenda for systems that can remember, revise, ground, speak, listen, act, and adapt across turns, modalities, and cultures. (https://github.com/faiza-sfa/multiturn-conversational-ai-survey)

AI.tldr: A survey of multi-turn conversational AI that analyzes current capabilities and gaps in sustaining coherent, multimodal dialogue over time.
AI.motivation: As conversational AI moves from single-shot prompts to real, ongoing conversations, systems must handle clarifications, interruptions, topic shifts, and new information while preserving context. Existing work is fragmented across text, audio, multimodal systems, and tool-using agents, and there is no unified view of how well they manage multi-turn interaction, memory, grounding, and cultural adaptation. This paper aims to synthesize and structure this emerging area.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic survey of the literature on multi-turn conversational AI, covering text-only dialogue models, AudioLLMs and speech-native systems, multimodal/omni-modal systems, and tool-augmented agents. They categorize work by datasets and benchmarks, modeling paradigms, training strategies, evaluation setups, and recurring challenges. They then comparatively analyze where systems succeed or fail, especially in sustaining coherent interaction across turns and modalities.
AI.result: The survey finds that progress in handling multiple modalities (seeing, speaking, acting) has outpaced progress in maintaining coherent multi-turn interaction. Across system types, current models struggle with persistent memory over a session, grounding information consistently across turns and modalities, supporting full-duplex (simultaneous) interaction, achieving reliable evaluation methods, and aligning behavior culturally. Strengths tend to lie in perception and single-turn capabilities rather than in long, adaptive dialogues.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that genuine conversational competence requires more than multimodal perception and response; it demands systems that can remember and revise information, ground their responses across tools and knowledge sources, and flexibly speak, listen, and act across languages and cultures over many turns. They propose a research agenda focused on improving long-term memory, cross-turn grounding, interactive protocols (including full-duplex), robust evaluation frameworks, and culturally aware alignment for multi-turn, multimodal conversational agents.

title: When AI Designs AI: Innovation or Imitation?
summary: Recent advances in LLM agents have made them increasingly capable of designing methods for complex AI tasks. This raises two central questions about agent-designed methods relative to human-designed methods: how well they perform, and how different their algorithmic designs are. To study these questions, this paper introduces an analysis that derives task-specific algorithmic design spaces from human-designed methods, maps both human- and agent-designed methods into these spaces, and quantifies their algorithmic differences at the module level. Widely used LLM agents are evaluated on a suite of representative, open-ended AI tasks spanning multiple modalities, and the methods they design are analyzed in terms of both task performance and algorithmic differences from human-designed methods. Experimental results show that current agents can occasionally match or surpass human state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance (10/72 configurations), but such success does not generalize reliably across tasks or agents. Moreover, 96.8% of agent-designed methods fall within human-derived algorithmic design spaces, largely recombining algorithmic choices found in human-designed methods, while nearly half exactly match an existing human algorithmic design. Taken together, these findings suggest that although current agents can occasionally match or surpass human SOTA performance, their algorithmic designs remain within human-derived algorithmic design spaces, reflecting the reuse and recombination of algorithmic choices.

AI.tldr: The paper compares LLM-agent designed methods to human-designed methods, finding that agents sometimes reach or beat human SOTA but mostly stay within human-created algorithmic design spaces.
AI.motivation: To understand whether LLM agents can not only match human performance on complex AI tasks but also innovate algorithmically beyond existing human-designed methods.
AI.method: The authors construct task-specific algorithmic design spaces based on human-designed methods, then map both human- and agent-designed methods into these spaces. They evaluate widely used LLM agents on diverse, open-ended multimodal AI tasks and quantify performance and module-level algorithmic differences between human and agent methods.
AI.result: Agents reach or exceed human SOTA in 10 out of 72 evaluated configurations, but this success is inconsistent across tasks and agents. 96.8% of agent-designed methods lie within the human-derived design spaces, mostly recombining existing human algorithmic choices, and nearly half of agent designs exactly match an existing human algorithmic design.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents can occasionally match or surpass human SOTA on complex AI tasks, but their algorithmic designs almost always stay within human-derived design spaces, indicating that they primarily reuse and recombine existing human algorithmic ideas rather than creating genuinely novel algorithms.

title: Thinking in a Low-Resource Language: What SFT Builds, What RL Fixes, What Accuracy Cannot See
summary: Take three frontier mixture-of-experts models (Alibaba, OpenAI, NVIDIA; 3.6-4.0B active parameters each) and fine-tune them to reason in a low-resource language. On accuracy benchmarks almost nothing happens, and the benchmark itself is noise at this scale: changing only the random seed moves the score by 7.7 points, more than every data and recipe effect we measured. That null is our first result. The real changes live where accuracy cannot see. Base models never think in Greek: 0 of 1,000 reasoning traces, even when the question is Greek, so the model answers correctly while reasoning in a form its user cannot read, audit, or correct. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), every released checkpoint reasons in the language of the question on ~98% of items, one family at 3x fewer tokens, with judged grammaticality improving on all four models and general ability within a few points of each base: nothing was forgotten, and fluency was gained. We propose six behavioural dimensions that make such changes measurable, each gated to reject any metric that correlates with output length, and we report how our own instruments lied: six failures, each caught by a control. What SFT cannot do is fix its own defects: a quarter of answers skip the requested format, answers leak into the reasoning channel, and an explicit "think in English" is obeyed under half the time. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, pre-registered before training, fixes the first two outright (fallback 24% to 2.5%, leak 3.5% to 0.0%, both against a flat random-reward control) and moves the third (+9.1pp), while the Greek reasoning habit survives an accuracy-only gradient untouched. We release five checkpoints. The instruments, the controls and the pre-registration travel to any low-resource language; Greek is the case that let us measure them.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to make strong MoE language models actually *reason in* a low‑resource language (Greek) rather than just answer correctly, and shows that standard accuracy benchmarks miss almost all of the important changes.
AI.motivation: Frontier LMs can answer questions in many languages but often conduct their internal chain‑of‑thought in English, which users of other languages cannot inspect or correct. Existing evaluations rely heavily on accuracy, which is noisy at high capability and blind to properties like language of reasoning, fluency, and adherence to requested formats. The authors want reliable ways to measure and improve these behavioural aspects, especially for low‑resource languages like Greek, without sacrificing the base model’s general capabilities.
AI.method: They fine‑tune three frontier mixture‑of‑experts models (Alibaba, OpenAI, NVIDIA; ~3.6–4.0B active parameters) on Greek reasoning. First, they apply supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) and evaluate not only accuracy but also where and how the model reasons: language used in chain‑of‑thought, token efficiency, grammaticality, and format adherence. They design six behavioural metrics that are explicitly controlled so they do not just track output length, and they use controls to detect misleading signals. They then apply reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable, pre‑registered reward functions to fix specific behavioural defects such as format non‑compliance and leakage between answer and reasoning channels, comparing to a random‑reward control.
AI.result: Accuracy hardly changes and is dominated by randomness: simply changing the random seed shifts benchmark scores by 7.7 points, larger than any data or training recipe effect they test, so accuracy appears as noise at this capability level. However, behaviour changes dramatically. Before SFT, models never produce Greek chain‑of‑thought (0/1,000 traces), even for Greek questions. After SFT, all checkpoints reason in the question’s language on ~98% of items; one model family achieves this with about three times fewer tokens. Grammaticality in Greek improves across all four models while global ability stays within a few points of the base models, indicating no major forgetting. SFT alone leaves problems: ~25% of responses fail the requested format, answers often leak into the reasoning channel, and explicit prompts to “think in English” are followed less than half the time. RL with verifiable rewards sharply reduces format fallback (24%→2.5%), eliminates answer leakage (3.5%→0.0%), and improves obedience to language‑of‑thought instructions by 9.1 percentage points, whereas training on accuracy alone does not affect the model’s Greek reasoning habit. They release five checkpoints and the full evaluation setup.
AI.conclusion: Raw accuracy is an unreliable and largely uninformative signal when fine‑tuning strong models for low‑resource language reasoning; it can fluctuate more from random seeds than from actual interventions. Yet the underlying reasoning behaviour can be substantially reshaped. Supervised fine‑tuning can make models consistently reason in the user’s language, increase fluency, and maintain overall capability, while RL with verifiable, pre‑registered rewards is needed to reliably enforce structural behaviours like format adherence and strict channel separation. Carefully designed behavioural metrics, coupled with controls that expose when metrics are confounded (e.g., by output length), provide a portable toolkit for aligning models’ reasoning style to low‑resource languages. Greek is used as the testbed, but the methods and instruments are intended to generalise to other low‑resource languages.

title: Towards Better Agents for Multi-Turn User Interaction: The Next User Turn Is More Than Context
summary: User-facing tool agents must coordinate dialogue and tool use as user goals unfold over multiple turns. Yet interactive reinforcement learning typically reduces each rollout to a terminal reward, assigning the same credit to effective elicitation, errors, and later repair. The next user turn is more than context: it also provides noisy, temporally local evidence about the preceding user-to-user segment. We introduce \textbf{F}eedback-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{C}redit \textbf{A}ssignment (\textsc{FACA}), which aligns each reaction with that segment, derives a locally normalized reaction advantage, and adds it to verified terminal outcome advantage without an extra critic or rollout. Against an outcome-only Interactive GRPO control matched in simulator, visible dialogue, initialization, rollout, and optimization, \textsc{FACA} improves the nine-domain $τ$-family average across three independently trained runs by 5.91 and 10.22 percentage points at 8B and 14B, respectively. Gains concentrate in Telecom; at 8B, randomizing reaction polarity removes the Telecom gain. The same ordering holds zero-shot on Pare-Bench and Co-Gym. These results demonstrate that next-turn user reactions provide actionable local credit for improving multi-turn user-interacting agents.

AI.tldr: They propose Feedback-Aware Credit Assignment (FACA), a method that uses next-turn user reactions as local feedback to better assign credit to individual dialogue segments in multi-turn tool-using agents, improving RL training and performance across domains.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn, tool-using dialogue systems, standard interactive reinforcement learning typically assigns a single terminal reward to an entire rollout. This collapses all intermediate steps—good elicitation, mistakes, and later repairs—into the same scalar, making it hard to learn which specific parts of the interaction were responsible for success or failure. However, each new user turn inherently carries feedback (e.g., satisfaction, confusion, or correction) about the immediately preceding agent behavior. The authors are motivated to exploit this naturally occurring, temporally local signal to refine credit assignment, without requiring extra critics, additional rollouts, or heavy supervision, thereby improving the training and performance of user-interacting agents.
AI.method: They introduce Feedback-Aware Credit Assignment (FACA). The key idea is to treat each user reaction (the next user turn) as local feedback on the immediately preceding user-to-user dialogue segment. FACA (1) aligns each user reaction with its corresponding prior segment, (2) computes a locally normalized reaction advantage that quantifies how good that segment was relative to expectations, and (3) adds this local advantage to the verified terminal outcome advantage used in outcome-only RL schemes. Importantly, this is done without training an additional critic or running extra rollouts: the method reuses existing trajectories but augments them with reaction-aware advantage terms. They compare FACA against an outcome-only Interactive GRPO control, carefully matched in simulator, visible dialogue, initialization, rollout procedure, and optimization setup, to isolate the effect of the credit assignment scheme.
AI.result: In controlled experiments across nine domains and three independently trained runs, FACA yields substantial improvements over outcome-only Interactive GRPO. On average over the τ-family metrics, FACA improves performance by 5.91 percentage points at 8B and 10.22 percentage points at 14B model scales. The performance gains are especially pronounced in the Telecom domain. An ablation where they randomize the polarity (sign) of user reactions removes the Telecom gain at 8B, indicating that correctly leveraging the reaction signal is crucial. Furthermore, the same performance ordering (FACA > outcome-only baseline) holds in zero-shot evaluations on external benchmarks Pare-Bench and Co-Gym, suggesting that the benefits generalize beyond the training domains.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that next-turn user reactions can be effectively leveraged as actionable, localized credit signals for training multi-turn user-interacting agents. By aligning user reactions with the preceding dialogue segments and combining the resulting reaction-based advantages with terminal outcome advantages, FACA improves credit assignment without additional critics or rollouts. Empirically, this leads to consistent performance gains across multiple domains and model sizes, with strong improvements in Telecom and robust generalization to external benchmarks. The work supports the broader claim that incorporating fine-grained, interaction-level feedback into RL training is a practical and impactful way to enhance complex dialog and tool-using agents.

title: Preference Is Not Intervention: The Structure and Stability Boundaries of Reader-Specific Evidence Utility
summary: ML systems increasingly condition decisions on downstream model identity, but this is useful only if model-specific differences form reusable structure rather than input-local interactions. We test this in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where evidence utility can be measured under controlled interventions. Holding query, evidence, task, scoring, and intervention fixed, nine readers disagree on effect sign in 33\% of jointly affected cells; reader$\times$query interaction explains 29.8\% of utility variance versus an 8.4\% permutation null; and self-selected evidence improves F1 by $+0.031$ ($t=3.39$). We then ask the sharper question: \emph{which components of this heterogeneity are stable reader properties across queries?} Separating three measurable objects---evidence \emph{activity}, \emph{ordinal preference}, and \emph{conditional signed direction}---we find ordinal reader geometry stable across four independent settings (split-half $ρ=0.60$--$0.83$): leave-one-out interventions, PRISM preferences, RAMDocs, and RAGuard. Signed geometry is task-bounded: weak in open-ended QA (0.14, 0.35), especially for misleading and irrelevant evidence, but strong in binary fact-checking (0.75) with no significant ordinal gap, though still below its sparsity-matched ceiling. Sparsity, decoding noise, and metric artifacts do not explain the main ordinal--signed gap. Finally, stable ordinal similarity fails to predict cross-reader intervention transfer (oracle-distance $ρ=-0.27$; regret reliability $-0.28$). Reader-specific utility exists, but preference is not intervention: stable ranking similarity does not license transfer of help/harm decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that different language models (readers) respond differently to the same retrieved evidence in RAG, and these differences are partially systematic (stable preferences) but do not reliably tell us which evidence will help or harm each model’s performance.
AI.motivation: Many modern ML pipelines route inputs or retrieved evidence based on model identity, assuming each model has stable, reusable preferences for what information helps it. In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), we would like to pick the right evidence for a given model. However, it is unclear whether model-specific differences are consistent properties or mostly noisy, input-specific interactions. The paper aims to rigorously test whether reader-specific evidence utility in RAG is stable and exploitable across tasks and datasets.
AI.method: The authors design controlled RAG experiments with multiple ‘reader’ models. They hold fixed the query, the evidence passages, the task, the scoring setup, and the experimental interventions on evidence, and then measure how evidence utility varies by reader. They decompose reader–evidence behavior into three measurable components: (1) evidence activity (whether evidence affects outputs at all), (2) ordinal preference (how each reader ranks evidence for helpfulness/harm), and (3) conditional signed direction (whether the effect is helpful or harmful, given a preference ordering). They assess stability of these components across four independent settings: leave-one-out evidence interventions, PRISM-style preference data, and two RAG benchmarks (RAMDocs and RAGuard). They compute correlations and variance explained to quantify reader×query interactions and test whether sparsity, decoding noise, or metric artifacts explain observed patterns. They also evaluate whether similarity in stable preferences predicts cross-reader transfer of interventions (i.e., whether an intervention that helps one reader will help another with similar preferences).
AI.result: They find substantial heterogeneity across nine readers: in 33% of cells where multiple readers are affected by an evidence intervention, they disagree on whether the effect is positive or negative. Reader×query interaction accounts for 29.8% of utility variance, well above an 8.4% permutation baseline. Allowing each reader to choose its own evidence improves F1 by +0.031 (t=3.39), confirming reader-specific utility. They show that the ordinal geometry of reader preferences is stable across four different datasets/settings, with split-half correlations between 0.60 and 0.83. However, signed geometry (help vs harm) is task-dependent: it is weak in open-ended QA (correlations 0.14 and 0.35), especially when evidence is misleading or irrelevant, but strong in binary fact-checking (0.75), though still below the maximum allowed by sparsity. Sparsity, decoding noise, and metric artifacts cannot account for the large gap between ordinal and signed structure. Crucially, stable ordinal similarity between readers fails to predict cross-reader transfer of interventions: higher similarity is actually negatively correlated with oracle distance (ρ=-0.27) and regret reliability (-0.28).
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is genuine reader-specific structure in how models use retrieved evidence, and their ordinal preferences over evidence are stable across multiple settings, this structure does not translate into reliable help/harm predictions for interventions. Preference (how a model ranks evidence) is not the same as intervention utility (how evidence alters performance). Therefore, simply exploiting stable preference similarity between models is not enough to safely or effectively transfer RAG interventions across readers. Designers of RAG and model-routing systems must treat help vs harm as a separate, task-dependent property rather than assuming that similar preferences license cross-model intervention transfer.

title: SGHA: Evidence-Grounded Research Problem Discovery with Local Language Models
summary:
Recent efforts toward fully automated AI scientists have demonstrated that language-model agents can generate hypotheses, execute experiments, and draft scientific manuscripts. However, during the early stages of research, when research problems are formulated, these AI scientists often rely heavily on proprietary frontier models. Their proposals are shaped by opaque parametric knowledge and by literature searches conditioned on the proposals themselves. Such knowledge is effectively a black box, and this dependence makes the evidential basis and validity of generated research problems difficult to audit and leaves the process vulnerable to model-specific hallucinations and biases. Furthermore, if proprietary research materials are transmitted to external APIs, the use of these models creates confidentiality, privacy, and data-governance concerns.
  We introduce the Structural Gap Hypothesis Agent (SGHA), a fully automated, corpus-first research-problem discovery system that runs entirely on a local LLM. SGHA structures a scientific literature corpus into evidence-linked paper objects and a typed evidence graph, detects unresolved structural patterns across papers, screens candidate gaps before formulation, and produces traceable research-problem families. In particular, it is able to output assumptions, objectives, success criteria, and remaining ambiguities. All LLM-based components of SGHA are executed using a locally served open-weight 9B language model, without requiring proprietary frontier-model APIs. We compare SGHA with the AI Scientist-v2 idea formulation module in five machine-learning domains. Our results suggest that explicit corpus structure and evidence-constrained reasoning can support promising, inspectable research-problem formulation without relying on frontier models during generation or verification.

AI.tldr: They propose SGHA, a local-LLM-based system that discovers research problems directly from structured scientific corpora, enabling transparent, evidence-linked, and frontier-model-free problem formulation.
AI.motivation: Current AI scientist systems for early-stage research problem formulation depend heavily on proprietary frontier models, whose opaque parametric knowledge and self-conditioned literature searches make the origins and validity of proposed problems hard to audit. This reliance introduces risks of hallucination and bias, as well as confidentiality and data-governance issues when sensitive research materials must be sent to external APIs. The authors want a way to generate research problems where the evidential basis is explicit, traceable, and independent of closed models.
AI.method: They introduce the Structural Gap Hypothesis Agent (SGHA), a fully automated system that starts from a scientific literature corpus (“corpus-first”). SGHA: (1) structures the corpus into evidence-linked paper objects; (2) builds a typed evidence graph capturing relations between these objects; (3) detects unresolved structural patterns (gaps) across papers; (4) screens candidate gaps before formalizing them; and (5) generates traceable families of research problems, including explicit assumptions, objectives, success criteria, and remaining ambiguities. All LLM-based steps use a locally served open-weight 9B model, avoiding any dependency on proprietary frontier-model APIs.
AI.result: They evaluate SGHA against the idea formulation module of AI Scientist-v2 in five machine-learning subdomains. The findings indicate that SGHA’s explicit corpus structuring and evidence-constrained reasoning can yield promising and inspectable research-problem proposals, comparable in quality while being more transparent and not requiring frontier models for either generation or verification.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly structuring the literature and constraining reasoning to corpus-grounded evidence enables a local-LLM-based system to formulate meaningful research problems without relying on closed, frontier models. SGHA demonstrates that research-problem discovery can be made more transparent, auditable, and privacy-preserving, suggesting a viable path toward trustworthy, fully automated AI scientists that operate within well-defined evidential bounds.

title: TraceSQL: Traceable Answerability Estimation for Reference-Free Text-to-SQL Verification
comment: 9 pages main paper with 6 pages supplementary material
summary: Text-to-SQL systems are commonly evaluated using ground-truth SQL queries or reference execution results, but such supervision is unavailable at inference time in real-world deployments. This creates a critical verification problem: given only a user question, database context, and generated SQL, can a system estimate whether the generated query is likely to correctly answer the question? Recent approaches use LLMs as judge or specialized agents to inspect generated SQL, but their decisions can be difficult to trace. Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) address this by learning from execution-labeled candidate SQLs and assigning correctness scores to unseen queries, yet they still provide limited visibility into the signals behind each verification. To address this limitation, we propose TraceSQL, a lightweight and traceable verification model built on explicit diagnostic features. TraceSQL combines 67 features capturing question ambiguity, question requirements, question-schema-SQL consistency, SQL structure, and intent alignment. These signals remain available for examining which factors influence each prediction and for tracing decisions back to diagnostic evidence. On BIRD development databases, TraceSQL achieves 66.47% F1 and 64.48% ROC-AUC, compared with 61.87% F1 and 58.26% ROC-AUC for the GradeSQL-7B ORM baseline on the same generated-SQL evaluation. Feature attribution further shows that the model relies on both semantic grounding and deterministic SQL-structure signals. These results show that SQL verification can be performed with a lightweight learned model while retaining feature-level evidence for inspecting and diagnosing its predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TraceSQL, a lightweight, feature-based verifier that predicts whether a generated SQL query correctly answers a natural language question, without using ground-truth SQL or execution results at inference time.
AI.motivation: Deployed Text-to-SQL systems cannot rely on ground-truth SQL or reference execution to know if a generated query is correct. Existing verification approaches either use LLM judges/agents that are hard to interpret, or Outcome Reward Models that learn from labeled executions but still give limited insight into why a query is judged correct or incorrect. There is a need for a verification method that is both effective and provides transparent, traceable evidence for its decisions, enabling diagnosis and debugging of Text-to-SQL systems.
AI.method: The authors propose TraceSQL, a verification model built on 67 explicit, hand-designed diagnostic features. These features cover multiple aspects: (1) question ambiguity, (2) requirements stated in the question, (3) consistency between question, schema, and SQL, (4) structural properties of the SQL, and (5) alignment between the user’s intent and the SQL query. A classifier is trained on execution-labeled candidate SQL queries to predict a correctness score for unseen SQL. Because the inputs are explicit features, the model’s predictions can be traced back to specific signals and examined via feature attribution.
AI.result: On the BIRD development databases, TraceSQL outperforms the GradeSQL-7B Outcome Reward Model baseline in verifying generated SQL. Specifically, TraceSQL achieves 66.47% F1 and 64.48% ROC-AUC, compared to 61.87% F1 and 58.26% ROC-AUC for GradeSQL-7B on the same evaluation setup. Feature attribution analysis indicates that the model effectively leverages both semantic grounding features (e.g., question–schema alignment) and deterministic SQL-structure features (e.g., structural validity patterns).
AI.conclusion: TraceSQL demonstrates that SQL verification can be done effectively using a lightweight learned model built on explicit diagnostic features, achieving better performance than a stronger neural ORM baseline while also providing interpretable, feature-level evidence. This makes it more suitable for debugging and monitoring Text-to-SQL systems, as practitioners can understand which signals drive each verification decision and trace them back to concrete diagnostic evidence.

title: Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL
summary: Modern agents operate inside agent harnesses that manage tools, context, and control flow, making the harness a critical part of the agent system. Our original Agent Lightning introduced a disaggregated architecture that connects arbitrary agents to RL training through an LLM endpoint proxy, an approach later adopted by frameworks such as verl Uni-Agent, AReaL 2.0, slime, and Polar. We refer to this paradigm as harnessed agentic RL, where the deploy-time harness directly participates in model post-training. Harnessed agentic RL differs fundamentally from traditional agentic RL: the harness, rather than the training engine, owns the environment interaction loop, while the trainer observes only sequences of LLM request-response pairs. This introduces challenges in retokenization, sample merging, advantage calculation, loss normalization, and backend scheduling, which can substantially affect training stability and effectiveness. We present Agent Lightning v1.0, a lightweight framework for harnessed agentic RL implemented in approximately 3,500 lines of code. It supports arbitrary agent harnesses and serves as a practical testbed for studying these challenges. We evaluate it on instruction-following, search, and coding agents, and provide a complete reproducible pipeline for coding-agent RL. Using only 6K training examples and modest compute, RL improves Qwen3.5-9B on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, a 14.6-point absolute gain. We release the complete workflow and training scripts to facilitate reproducible research on harnessed agentic RL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agent Lightning v1.0, a lightweight framework for reinforcement learning (RL) on LLM-based agents that are controlled via external harnesses, and shows it can significantly improve a 9B LLM’s coding performance with modest data and compute.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM agents increasingly run inside complex harnesses that manage tools, memory, and control flow. Many recent systems perform RL on these agents via an LLM endpoint, but the RL algorithms and infrastructure were not originally designed for this “harnessed” setting, where the harness (not the trainer) owns the environment loop. This mismatch creates subtle but important problems—for example, how to reconstruct trajectories from LLM calls, handle tokenization, merge samples, compute advantages, and schedule backends efficiently. The authors aim to clarify this new training paradigm and provide a clean, reproducible framework to systematically study and address these challenges.
AI.method: The authors formalize “harnessed agentic RL,” where the training system sees only sequences of LLM request–response pairs while the agent harness controls environment interaction. They design Agent Lightning v1.0 as a ~3.5K-LOC framework that connects arbitrary harnesses to RL trainers through an LLM endpoint proxy. The framework implements the necessary data plumbing and algorithmic components to handle retokenization, sample merging, advantage computation, loss normalization, and backend scheduling in this setting. They instantiate this framework on several agent types—instruction-following, search, and coding agents—and build an end-to-end, reproducible RL pipeline for coding agents in particular.
AI.result: Using Agent Lightning v1.0, they train a Qwen3.5-9B coding agent on only about 6,000 RL examples with modest compute. On SWE-bench Verified, RL fine-tuning via their harnessed agentic RL setup boosts the model’s performance from 41.8% to 56.4%, a substantial 14.6-point absolute improvement. The framework successfully supports multiple agent harnesses and tasks, demonstrating its practicality and generality.
AI.conclusion: Harnessed agentic RL is structurally different from traditional agentic RL because the agent harness, not the trainer, controls the environment loop. This distinction creates unique engineering and algorithmic issues that strongly influence training stability and performance. Agent Lightning v1.0 provides a compact, extensible framework that addresses these issues and enables reproducible experimentation across diverse harnesses and tasks. The demonstrated gains on a coding benchmark show that effective RL on harnessed agents is feasible with relatively small data and compute budgets, and the released code and scripts are intended to catalyze further research in this emerging paradigm.

title: Whether LLMs Can Navigate Beliefs and Facts Depends on How You Phrase It
summary: Humans naturally form and express beliefs in daily communication, e.g., "I think the answer is 3" or "I suppose that's right." Such beliefs inevitably intertwine with fact and knowledge, making the ability to handle them in tandem desirable for large language models (LLMs), as they are increasingly deployed in user-facing settings. Prior work showed that even capable LLMs exhibit a systemic weakness in acknowledging user beliefs grounded in incorrect information. We extend this evaluation to 10 LLMs across 18 epistemic expressions and find that the size and direction of the weakness depend on the verb used to express the belief, with the accuracy gap between factual and false information ranging from +50% on "I vaguely remember" to -14% on "I seriously doubt". We further show that the phenomenon stems from task confusion: models default to fact-checking the underlying claim, overriding the user's stated belief; chains of thought that explicitly fact-check show lower accuracy on false information than those that do not; and a single instruction can reverse the failure across verb families. Mechanistically, models attend more to false beliefs they fail to confirm, but suppressing this attention at decoding time recovers accuracy only partially and only in some models, calling for future work on intervention methods. Our findings clarify prior results and show how fact-checking, a generally desirable behavior, can interfere with belief tracking in LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ngqm/belief-fact-phrasing.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models handle human belief expressions, showing they often prioritize fact-checking over tracking the user’s stated belief, and analyzes when and why this happens.
AI.motivation: In real conversations, people constantly express beliefs (e.g., “I think…”, “I guess…”) that may be true or false, and deployed LLMs must both track these beliefs and reason about factual correctness. Prior work found that LLMs struggle especially when users hold false beliefs, but it was unclear how widespread this is across models, how it varies by phrasing, and what mechanisms cause the failures. The paper aims to systematically characterize these weaknesses, understand their source, and explore whether simple interventions can fix them, in order to make LLMs more reliable in user-facing applications.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 10 different LLMs on prompts containing 18 kinds of epistemic expressions (e.g., “I vaguely remember”, “I seriously doubt”), comparing model responses when the embedded claim is factual versus false. They measure accuracy gaps across these conditions and analyze how they depend on the belief verb. To probe mechanisms, they examine chains-of-thought to distinguish cases where the model explicitly fact-checks the claim versus not, relate this to performance on false information, and test whether a single instruction can reverse the failure pattern across verb families. Mechanistically, they perform attention analyses to see how models allocate attention to belief content during decoding and run decoding-time interventions that suppress attention to the false belief tokens, checking whether this recovers accuracy.
AI.result: The study finds that LLM performance on belief-related prompts is highly sensitive to the specific epistemic verb: accuracy gaps between factual and false information range from strongly positive (e.g., +50% with “I vaguely remember”) to even negative (−14% with “I seriously doubt”). The results suggest that models often misinterpret belief-tracking tasks as pure fact-checking tasks, overriding the user’s stated belief. Chains-of-thought that explicitly engage in fact-checking correlate with worse accuracy on false-belief cases than CoT that does not. A simple, single instruction can substantially flip the pattern of failures for entire verb families. Attention analyses show that, in failure cases, models attend more to false beliefs they fail to confirm, but interventions that dampen this attention at decoding only partially and inconsistently restore accuracy across different models.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a core source of LLM failure in handling user beliefs, especially false ones, is task confusion: models default to fact-checking instead of properly tracking the user’s expressed belief. While fact-checking is broadly beneficial, it can conflict with belief tracking, causing systematic and verb-specific weaknesses. Simple prompt-level instructions can mitigate these issues to a notable extent, but low-level attention interventions provide only partial and model-dependent improvements, indicating that more robust and principled intervention methods are needed. Overall, the work clarifies how and when fact-checking behavior interferes with belief modeling and provides a framework and codebase for further research on belief-aware LLMs.

title: When to Review: Spaced Repetition for Continual Pre-Training of Language Models
summary: Continual pre-training of large language models must acquire new information without erasing old knowledge. Existing replay methods often choose a global old/new mixture and sample uniformly, ignoring that examples differ in how quickly they are forgotten. We formulate continual pre-training as adaptive review scheduling: the training loop should decide not only how much history to replay, but which examples should return at each step. We introduce Spaced Repetition Training (SRT), a continual learning framework inspired by cognitive science, which schedules sample-rehearsal using the SuperMemo-2 (SM-2) algorithm. SRT maintains per-example review state, maps per-example perplexity to a recall-quality signal, and schedules historical examples for retention and new examples for consolidation while leaving the model, objective, and optimizer unchanged. On temporally separated Wikipedia and code corpora, SRT improves the stability-plasticity trade-off, recovering 5 to 37 percentage points of old-knowledge accuracy lost by naive continual pre-training across model scales while preserving or improving new-knowledge acquisition. At larger scale, SRT preserves broad benchmark performance that naive continual pre-training and uniform replay substantially degrade. Experiments with vision and tabular data further suggest that the scheduling principle extends beyond language when paired with an appropriate recall signal.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Spaced Repetition Training (SRT), a continual pre-training framework for large models that adaptively schedules which past examples to replay using the SM‑2 algorithm, improving retention of old knowledge without hurting acquisition of new information.
AI.motivation: Continual pre-training of large language models tends to overwrite previously learned knowledge when adapting to new data, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing replay-based approaches usually mix old and new data at fixed ratios and sample them uniformly, assuming all examples are equally forgettable. However, in practice different examples are forgotten at different rates and should be reviewed at different times. The paper is motivated by the need for a more informed and efficient replay mechanism that can choose not only how much old data to use, but exactly which examples to revisit and when, in order to improve the stability–plasticity trade-off during continual learning.
AI.method: The authors recast continual pre-training as an adaptive review scheduling problem, borrowing ideas from spaced repetition in human learning. They propose Spaced Repetition Training (SRT), which incorporates the SuperMemo‑2 (SM‑2) scheduling algorithm into the training loop. SRT maintains a review state for each training example and uses the model’s per-example perplexity as a proxy for recall quality: low perplexity implies good retention, high perplexity implies forgetting. Based on this signal, SM‑2 computes when each example should next be replayed. During continual pre-training, SRT schedules historical examples for retention and interleaves them with new examples for consolidation. Crucially, SRT operates only at the data-scheduling level and leaves the underlying model architecture, training objective, and optimizer unchanged. The approach is evaluated on temporally split Wikipedia and code corpora, and also adapted to vision and tabular domains with domain-appropriate recall signals.
AI.result: On temporally separated Wikipedia and code datasets, SRT substantially improves the stability–plasticity trade-off relative to naive continual pre-training and simple uniform replay. It recovers between 5 and 37 percentage points of accuracy on old knowledge that would otherwise be lost, while maintaining or enhancing performance on new data across multiple model sizes. At larger scales, SRT is able to preserve general benchmark performance, whereas naive continual pre-training and uniform replay both significantly degrade it. Additional experiments on vision and tabular data show that when combined with suitable recall-quality metrics, the spaced-repetition scheduling principle generalizes beyond language tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that treating continual pre-training as an adaptive review scheduling problem and leveraging spaced repetition via the SM‑2 algorithm is an effective way to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large models. By maintaining per-example review states and using model-based recall signals such as perplexity, SRT can selectively replay the most at-risk examples, thereby recovering a large fraction of lost performance on earlier data without sacrificing learning of new information. Because SRT requires no changes to model architectures or optimization procedures and appears to transfer to non-text modalities, the authors argue it is a practical, general framework for improving continual learning in large-scale systems.

title: Interpretable Humans, Alien LLMs: Expert Analysis of Latent Structures in Assessment Responses
summary: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) relies heavily on human-designed assessments, implicitly assuming that AI and humans employ similar underlying cognitive constructs. Challenging this assumption, we investigate whether the latent factors governing LLM performance carry the same substantive, human-interpretable meaning as the cognitive constructs governing human learners. Using responses from humans and six LLMs across quantitative reasoning and chemistry assessments, we conducted Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) separately for both groups. Subject-Matter Experts (SMEs) then blindly evaluated the resulting factor graphs to ascribe pedagogical meaning to the emerged constructs. SMEs successfully interpreted most of the human-derived factors. Conversely, they could not ascribe meaning to any LLM-derived factors in quantitative reasoning and interpreted only half of the LLM factors in chemistry. By combining data-driven EFA with blind expert interpretation, this framework shows that LLMs frequently operate on statistically opaque mechanisms distinct from human reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether the hidden skill dimensions behind LLM test performance align with human cognitive constructs and finds they often do not.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation assumes that if models score like humans on tests, they rely on similar underlying skills or cognitive abilities. This assumption underpins claims about LLMs’ reasoning and learning capabilities, but has rarely been probed explicitly. The authors want to know whether the latent factors that explain patterns of LLM responses on educational assessments can be meaningfully interpreted in the same way as those for human students.
AI.method: The authors collect item-level responses from human participants and from six LLMs on quantitative reasoning and chemistry assessments. They run Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) independently on human data and on LLM data to extract latent factors that explain performance patterns. These factors are represented as factor graphs indicating which items load on which factors and with what strength. Subject-matter experts (SMEs), blinded to whether a factor graph comes from humans or LLMs, are asked to assign pedagogically meaningful labels or interpretations to each factor. The interpretability success rate and quality of these labels are then compared between human-derived and LLM-derived factor structures.
AI.result: SMEs were able to assign clear, pedagogically meaningful interpretations to most of the factors derived from human response data. In contrast, they failed to interpret any of the factors extracted from LLM performance in quantitative reasoning, and could only interpret about half of the factors from LLM performance in chemistry. This indicates that the patterns of item correlations governing LLM performance are often not aligned with familiar, human-understood skill dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that LLMs often rely on latent performance structures that are statistically identifiable but conceptually opaque to human experts, differing from the cognitive constructs used to describe human learners. This undermines the common practice of treating human-designed educational and cognitive assessments as direct probes of LLM “abilities” comparable to human reasoning skills. The proposed framework—combining EFA with blind expert interpretation—offers a principled way to test whether model-internal performance factors have human-interpretable meaning and suggests caution when attributing human-like cognitive constructs to LLMs based solely on test scores.

title: Quantifying Risk Under Evolving Uncertainty: Belief-Dependent Robustness for Safe Sequential Decision Making
comment: Accepted for presentation at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 RobustifAI workshop
summary: How cautious should an agent be while it is still learning its environment? We propose RATTL (Risk-Adversarial Total-Reward Learning), which ties caution to epistemic uncertainty: the agent holds a Bayesian posterior over unknown dynamics and plans against a Wasserstein ambiguity set whose radius is a monotone function of that posterior. The radius contracts with evidence, so behaviour interpolates continuously between worst-case robustness and risk-neutral total-reward maximization. The design follows the duality underlying the Entropic Value-at-Risk, which converts the choice of a risk level into the choice of an ambiguity radius. We show the resulting planning problem is well posed under transience and compactness conditions, and prove a Safety Sandwich: the RATTL value lies between the uninformed robust value and the full- knowledge optimum, with a gap that vanishes as the posterior concentrates. In a canonical binary-hazard instance, the induced criterion reduces to Conditional Value-at-Risk at a level set by the posterior entropy. A worked example shows the agent deferring the efficient action until a sharp identification threshold. RATTL targets runtime safety for agents, including LLM-based systems, acting under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: RATTL is a reinforcement learning framework that adaptively trades off caution and reward based on epistemic uncertainty via a Bayesian posterior and Wasserstein robustness.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement learning often ignores epistemic uncertainty, leading to unsafe behavior during learning, while robust RL can be overly conservative and not adapt as knowledge improves. There is a need for a principled way to connect an agent’s caution level to its uncertainty about the environment, so that behavior smoothly transitions from robust to reward-maximizing as learning progresses.
AI.method: The paper introduces RATTL (Risk-Adversarial Total-Reward Learning), where the agent maintains a Bayesian posterior over unknown dynamics and plans against a Wasserstein ambiguity set whose radius is a monotone function of that posterior. Using duality results related to Entropic Value-at-Risk, they map a risk level to an ambiguity radius. They analyze the resulting planning problem under transience and compactness conditions, derive a Safety Sandwich inequality comparing RATTL value with uninformed robust and full-knowledge values, and study a binary-hazard instance where the criterion becomes a Conditional Value-at-Risk with level determined by posterior entropy. They also work through an example to illustrate behavior, such as deferring efficient but risky actions until enough evidence accumulates.
AI.result: They prove that the RATTL planning problem is mathematically well-posed under specified conditions and establish a Safety Sandwich: the RATTL value always lies between the value of an uninformed robust controller and the full-information optimal value, with the gap shrinking as the posterior concentrates. In a binary-hazard model, RATTL reduces to a CVaR criterion where the risk level is automatically set by the posterior entropy. The worked example demonstrates that RATTL yields adaptive caution, causing the agent to delay taking efficient high-risk actions until the environment is sufficiently identified.
AI.conclusion: RATTL provides a principled, Bayesian and distributionally robust framework that ties an agent’s runtime caution directly to epistemic uncertainty, ensuring safety during learning while recovering near-optimal performance as uncertainty diminishes. This approach is especially relevant for agents such as LLM-based systems acting under uncertainty, where safety during learning and deployment is critical.

title: From Global Benchmarks to Local Evaluations: Benchmarking LLMs for the German Public Sector
comment: Accepted as non-archival paper at Eval4SD (co-located with KONVENS 2026)
summary: Public institutions face a persistent challenge in selecting LLMs suited to their specific context. Existing benchmarks, however, are of limited use as they primarily reflect English-language and US-centric settings, and often only evaluate task performance. In this paper, we present first results of MÖVE, a holistic evaluation framework for the German public sector, examining three rarely considered governance dimensions: energy consumption, provider transparency, and knowledge of German-party positions. Our results reveal significant trade-offs, with no single model excelling across all dimensions: estimated energy consumption varies more than 60-fold and is not explained by model size alone, information disclosure varies systematically across providers, and European models do not exhibit stronger knowledge of German party positions. Model selection for public institutions thus cannot rely on performance rankings alone. Instead, evaluations should also reflect the governance requirements of the deployment context.

AI.tldr: MÖVE is a holistic evaluation framework for choosing LLMs in the German public sector that goes beyond accuracy to include energy use, provider transparency, and knowledge of German-party positions, revealing strong trade-offs across models.
AI.motivation: Public institutions struggle to choose appropriate LLMs because standard benchmarks are mostly English- and US-centric and focus narrowly on task performance. This makes them poor proxies for the needs, constraints, and governance requirements of the German public sector. The authors want an evaluation approach that reflects local language, policy context, and broader public-sector concerns such as sustainability, transparency, and political-knowledge risks.
AI.method: The authors design MÖVE, a multi-dimensional evaluation framework tailored to the German public sector. They operationalize three governance-relevant dimensions: (1) estimated energy consumption of different LLMs, (2) provider transparency regarding model characteristics and usage conditions, and (3) models’ knowledge of positions of German political parties. They then apply this framework to a set of prominent LLMs and compare how they score along these dimensions, rather than only on standard task performance.
AI.result: The study finds pronounced trade-offs between models on the three governance dimensions. Estimated energy consumption differs by more than a factor of 60 and cannot be predicted simply by model size. Transparency levels are uneven and vary systematically between providers, indicating that some vendors are much more open about their models than others. Contrary to expectations, European-developed models do not demonstrate systematically better knowledge of German party positions than non-European models.
AI.conclusion: No single LLM dominates across all evaluated governance dimensions, so public institutions cannot base procurement or deployment decisions solely on performance leaderboards. Instead, selection must incorporate broader governance criteria—like energy efficiency, transparency, and context-specific political knowledge—aligned with the particular requirements and values of the public sector deployment context.

title: TRUSS: Towards Task-Reliable and User-Safe Automated Agent Skill Generation
summary:
Agent Skills package reusable natural language procedures with executable resources, enabling software agents to acquire task specific capabilities without model adaptation. Automatically generating such Skills can improve task performance, yet evaluating a candidate solely from its artifact or final task outcome leaves unresolved which actions the equipped agent will perform and which side effects those actions will produce. We present TRUSS, an evidence guided framework for generating functionally effective and safety reliable Agent Skills. TRUSS first inspects functional claims against source and domain evidence while evaluating the complete artifact under nine predefined safety properties. Candidates admitted by this static gate are loaded by a shadow agent inside a Controllable Execution Environment, where brokered tools expose requested actions to policy enforcement and record their results as provenance preserving execution traces. Functional failures and property violations are linked back to the responsible Skill content and used to guide iterative refinement.
  We evaluate TRUSS on 168 SkillInject artifacts, 155 SkillSafetyBench cases, and all 187 tasks in SkillGenBench. TRUSS achieves 100.00\% precision and recall in vulnerability detection. Repair reduces attack success from 38.71\% to 19.35\% with GPT 5.5 and from 46.45\% to 29.68\% with GPT 5.4, with zero attack regression. For Skill generation, TRUSS raises task effectiveness from 17.11\% without Skills to 52.94\%, while increasing the benchmark Security rate from 50.80\% to 100.00\%. These results show that execution evidence can expose behavioral failures missed by artifact inspection and can guide Skill generation toward jointly verified functional and safety outcomes.

AI.tldr: TRUSS is a framework that automatically evaluates and refines reusable agent ‘Skills’ using both static checks and controlled execution traces to ensure they are functionally effective and safe.
AI.motivation: Reusable Agent Skills can greatly enhance software agents, but existing methods either look only at the skill artifact (code, spec) or only at final task outcomes. This leaves a gap: we can’t reliably know what actions an agent will actually take with a given Skill or what side effects may occur, especially from a safety standpoint. There is a need for a systematic way to both assess and improve Skills so they are simultaneously useful and safe to deploy.
AI.method: TRUSS uses a two-stage, evidence-guided process. First, it performs static analysis: it checks the Skill’s functional claims against source and domain evidence, and evaluates the artifact against nine predefined safety properties. Only Skills that pass this static gate move to the second stage, where a ‘shadow agent’ loads the Skill into a Controllable Execution Environment. In this environment, brokered tools expose the Skill’s requested actions to policy enforcement and log all operations as provenance-preserving execution traces. TRUSS then analyzes these traces to detect functional failures and safety property violations, maps them back to the responsible parts of the Skill, and uses this information to iteratively refine or repair the Skill.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—168 SkillInject artifacts, 155 SkillSafetyBench cases, and 187 SkillGenBench tasks—TRUSS detects vulnerabilities with 100% precision and recall. Its repair process significantly lowers attack success rates for two model versions (from 38.71% to 19.35% for GPT 5.5 and from 46.45% to 29.68% for GPT 5.4) with no new successful attacks introduced. For skill generation, TRUSS improves task effectiveness from 17.11% (no Skills) to 52.94% and raises the Security rate from 50.80% to 100.00%.
AI.conclusion: Execution evidence, in the form of controlled, traceable runs of Skills, reveals behavioral and safety issues that cannot be found from artifact inspection alone. By combining static checks with execution-based analysis and using both to drive iterative refinement, TRUSS can generate and repair Agent Skills that are simultaneously more effective on tasks and safer to deploy, achieving perfect security metrics on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Encoded but Not Actionable: Auditing the Decode-Generate-Steer Gap in Frozen LLMs for Geometric Constraints
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on structured reasoning tasks, but what they encode and whether it informs model behavior remain unclear. We investigate this question through geometric reasoning, using parametric CAD constraints as a controlled testbed for separating local pairwise relations from sketch-level constraint status. By probing the hidden states of six frozen decoder-only LLMs, we examine four properties: linear decodability, forced-choice generation, activation-level influence, and behavioral steerability. Pretraining substantially improves the decoding of local geometric relations, and this advantage persists after accounting for positional cues with shuffled-order controls. In contrast, sketch-level DOF status is already highly decodable from randomly initialized representations and improves only modestly with pretraining, indicating that much of its probe performance is available without learned weights. Further analyses show that decodable information is not always actionable. Generation often fails to express this information, and on the two intervention-tested backbones, activation-restoration effects at the patched entity position vanish while decodability persists across depth. Mean-difference steering also does not reliably control outputs. These results show that decodability, generation, activation-level influence, and steerability can diverge in the tested setting. The audit provides a controlled way to distinguish failures to encode geometric structure from failures to express or control encoded information.

AI.tldr: Study probes what geometric information LLMs encode and whether it actually affects behavior, using CAD constraints as a controlled testbed, and finds that what is decodable from activations does not necessarily steer or control generation.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs perform well on structured reasoning tasks, it is unclear what specific relational and global properties they internally represent, and whether these internal encodings truly drive or constrain model behavior. Prior work often assumes that if information is linearly decodable from hidden states, it is functionally used by the model, but this link has not been systematically tested in a controlled, grounded domain.
AI.method: Use parametric CAD constraint problems as a geometric reasoning benchmark and treat them as a testbed that cleanly separates local pairwise relations from global sketch-level degrees-of-freedom (DOF) status. Probe hidden states of six frozen decoder-only LLMs to evaluate four aspects: (1) linear decodability of local relations and global DOF, including shuffled-order controls to remove positional shortcuts; (2) forced-choice generation accuracy to see whether models express the encoded information; (3) causal influence of activations via activation patching/restoration along depth; and (4) behavioral steerability using mean-difference steering vectors to try to control outputs based on internal representations.
