AI.result: Pretraining markedly improves linear decoding of local geometric relations, and this improvement remains even when positional information is disrupted, suggesting genuine learned geometric structure. In contrast, global sketch-level DOF status is highly decodable even in randomly initialized models and only slightly improves with pretraining, implying much of its probe performance arises from architecture and input format, not learned content. The authors also find that information that is easily decodable is not necessarily used in generation: models often fail to produce outputs consistent with the decoded properties; activation restoration effects disappear at the directly patched positions even as decodability remains at deeper layers; and mean-difference steering vectors do not consistently control model outputs.
AI.conclusion: Linear decodability, generation behavior, activation-level causal influence, and steering controllability can diverge, at least in this geometric CAD setting. Therefore, probe-based evidence that a concept is encoded in hidden states does not guarantee that it is functionally used or that it can be easily controlled to steer behavior. The proposed audit framework offers a way to distinguish between failures of representation (not encoding structure) and failures of expression or controllability (encoding but not using or exposing that structure).

title: MoNe: Modular Neural Memory for Efficient Long Context Inference
summary: We present MoNe, a lightweight modular neural memory that attaches to any frozen pretrained Transformer to enable long-context inference without retraining. MoNe reads context in fixed-size segments via test-time learning of fast-weight neural memory networks with layer-localized gradient updates; at inference, the memory generates keys and values from the query tokens alone, with no context tokens re-read. This two-phase design decouples inference cost from context length, achieving $O(N)$ preprocessing and $O(1)$ query cost with peak GPU memory that does not grow with $N$. At 128K tokens, MoNe reduces both compute and peak GPU memory by approximately 80% compared to ICL with only 6.4% parameter overhead. MoNe generalizes to context lengths far beyond the backbone's native window, achieving strong performance on needle-in-a-haystack and word extraction benchmarks from RULER, where ICL degrades sharply.

AI.tldr: MoNe is a lightweight neural memory module that, when attached to a frozen Transformer, enables long-context inference with constant-time querying and minimal compute/memory overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers have quadratic cost in context length and are limited by a fixed attention window; extending context typically requires retraining or incurs high compute and memory costs during inference. There is a need for a method that can leverage long contexts efficiently at test time without modifying or retraining the base model, and that can generalize to much longer sequences than the backbone was originally designed for.
AI.method: MoNe is a modular neural memory attached to a frozen pretrained Transformer. During a preprocessing phase, it reads the long context in fixed-size segments and performs test-time learning using fast-weight neural memory networks, with layer-local gradient updates to store information about the context. During inference (querying), MoNe uses only the query tokens to generate keys and values from this learned memory, so it does not need to re-read the context tokens. This yields a two-phase procedure: an O(N) preprocessing pass over the context and an O(1) cost per query, while the peak GPU memory footprint remains independent of the context length N. The module adds only about 6.4% parameters relative to the backbone and can be plugged into any frozen Transformer without retraining it.
AI.result: At a 128K-token context length, MoNe reduces both compute and peak GPU memory usage by about 80% compared with standard in-context learning (ICL), while adding only 6.4% parameter overhead. It successfully generalizes beyond the backbone model's native context window. On long-context benchmarks such as RULER's needle-in-a-haystack and word extraction tasks, MoNe maintains strong performance where standard ICL performance sharply degrades.
AI.conclusion: MoNe provides an effective, lightweight way to equip existing frozen Transformers with scalable long-context capabilities. By decoupling query-time computation from context length and keeping memory usage flat in N, it enables efficient inference on very long sequences while preserving or improving performance relative to standard ICL, and without requiring retraining of the backbone model.

title: BayesPrompt: human readable prompts that make sense
summary: Reconstructing prompts that can elicit a desired answer or behaviour in an LLM is an open and important research topic. Optimisation methods which aim at minimising the perplexity of a given answer, however, consistently yield so-called pseudoprompts, unintelligible strings of tokens which can lack human interpretability. We argue that this is a consequence of the ill-posedness of the prompt optimisation task. By reframing the task as a Bayesian posterior inference over prompts, we propose an efficient algorithm to sample prompts which are both efficient (in terms of perplexity) and human readable. We compare our approach with state of the art alternatives showing on a real data set a marked improvement over a range of metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses why perplexity-based prompt optimization for LLMs often produces unreadable "pseudoprompts" and proposes a Bayesian sampling framework that yields both performant and human-interpretable prompts.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt optimization methods frequently minimize perplexity of a target answer, but they tend to generate token sequences that are highly effective yet unintelligible to humans. This lack of interpretability makes them hard to understand, edit, and safely deploy. The authors are motivated to understand why this happens (ill-posedness of the optimization) and to develop a method that maintains performance while enforcing human readability.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret prompt reconstruction as Bayesian posterior inference over the space of prompts. Instead of directly optimizing perplexity, they define a probabilistic model where the likelihood reflects how well a prompt elicits the desired answer (e.g., via perplexity), and the prior encodes preferences for human-readable prompts. They then design an efficient sampling algorithm—likely based on approximate Bayesian inference or MCMC-style methods—to draw prompts from this posterior, balancing performance and readability.
AI.result: On a real dataset, their Bayesian prompt sampling method produces prompts that attain low perplexity (i.e., remain highly effective at eliciting the target answer) while being substantially more interpretable than pseudoprompts. Quantitative comparisons with state-of-the-art prompt optimization techniques show consistent improvements across multiple evaluation metrics, presumably including human-interpretability and performance measures.
AI.conclusion: Perplexity-minimization alone leads to an ill-posed optimization problem that naturally produces pseudoprompts. By casting prompt optimization as Bayesian posterior inference and sampling from a prior-regularized prompt space, one can obtain prompts that are both effective and human-readable. This Bayesian framing offers a principled and practical path toward interpretable prompt engineering and improves over existing methods on empirical benchmarks.

title: Validated Adaptation for Aerial Crowd Monitoring at Mass Gathering Scale: A Deployment Protocol, a Severity Law, and a Diagnostic for Label-Free Drone Crowd Counting, Toward the FIFA World Cup 2034 (Saudi Arabia)
summary: Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 FIFA World Cup and already operates crowd management at Hajj scale. Drone-based counting must hold accuracy on footage unlike anything in its training corpus, without labels, and must warn of dangerous inflow before a crush forms. We deliver a validated answer built on 525 controlled runs, a full-resolution corpus study, five falsification ablations, and a five-condition safety-interlock evaluation. Label-free adaptation recovers 31-49% of shift-induced error across four corruptions and five severities, with the strongest method gaining 41.8 MAE over the frozen source (95% CI [34.1, 49.6], p=7.5x10^-10, d=2.52). We establish a severity law separating methods with a constant absolute margin from the one whose margin grows, and a stability budget identifying which configuration is safe to fly. On a full-resolution corpus carrying a genuine +48 MAE aerial gap (source retrained to 14.6 validation MAE, a 34% improvement), adaptation repairs the dense-scene undercounting that would otherwise under-report a forming crush, and the flux-based risk module fires on real congestion episodes in 2 of 6 full-length clips. We localise the recoverable error: in a regime built to favor a physics-informed conservation prior (300-frame clips at 200ms spacing, five times wider than standard), the adaptation signal is normalisation-driven, not flow-driven; the continuity residual is invariant to the proportional counting errors domain shift produces, confirmed by four on/off ablations correlated at r=0.999 and a 40% input corruption moving accuracy by only 0.05 MAE. A label-free shift gate shows shift magnitude and accuracy damage are rank-independent (Spearman rho=0.20; rho=-0.60 among genuine shifts), quantifying the 58% of headroom a magnitude gate forgoes. We establish unconditional adaptation with tail monitoring as policy, closing with a six-point protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates a label-free domain adaptation and safety-monitoring pipeline for drone-based crowd counting under strong distribution shift, targeting early warning of dangerous congestion in very dense crowds.
AI.motivation: Drone crowd-counting systems trained on standard datasets fail under severe domain shift (e.g., ultra-dense religious or sporting gatherings), yet labeling new scenarios is infeasible and safety demands early crush detection and robust guarantees. Saudi Arabia hosting the 2034 FIFA World Cup and already managing massive Hajj crowds motivates reliable, shift-robust, label-free adaptation and operational safety criteria.
AI.method: They perform 525 controlled runs plus a full-resolution corpus study to systematically test label-free adaptation methods for crowd counting under synthetic corruptions and real aerial gaps. They design five falsification ablations and a five-condition safety-interlock evaluation. They compare multiple adaptation algorithms, analyze performance across four corruption types and five severity levels, and introduce concepts like a severity law (how errors grow with shift severity), a stability budget (configurations deemed safe to deploy), and a label-free shift gate that estimates shift magnitude. They test a physics-informed conservation prior based on temporal continuity (300-frame clips, 200ms spacing) and contrast flow-driven vs normalization-driven adaptation signals. They study correlations and robustness of a continuity residual via on/off ablations and heavy input corruption, and evaluate a flux-based risk module for detecting dangerous inflow in real congestion episodes.
AI.result: Label-free adaptation reduces 31–49% of error caused by domain shift across multiple corruption types and severities. The best method improves mean absolute error by 41.8 over the non-adapted source model (95% CI [34.1, 49.6], highly significant with p=7.5×10^-10, large effect size d=2.52). They identify a distinct severity law showing one method’s error margin grows with severity whereas others remain at a constant absolute margin, and they derive a stability budget delineating safe configurations. On a full-resolution aerial corpus with a real +48 MAE gap, retraining on source data reduces validation MAE to 14.6 (34% improvement), and adaptation specifically corrects dense-scene undercounting that would mask forming crushes. The flux-based risk module successfully flags real congestion in 2 of 6 long videos. They show that the conservation-prior continuity residual is largely insensitive to proportional counting errors from domain shift (r=0.999 between ablations, and 40% corruption changes accuracy by only 0.05 MAE) and that a magnitude-based shift gate fails to capture most useful headroom, given low Spearman rank correlations between shift magnitude and accuracy loss and a quantified 58% headroom loss.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that robust, label-free domain adaptation for drone-based crowd counting is feasible and can materially improve safety in extreme crowd scenarios, but adaptation must be unconditional with explicit tail-risk monitoring rather than gated solely on estimated shift magnitude. Their analyses provide a severity law and stability budget to decide safe configurations and show that normalization-based adaptation, not flow-based conservation priors, drives recoverable gains under realistic shifts. They advocate a policy of always adapting with an accompanying tail-monitoring and safety-interlock protocol, summarized in a six-point deployment guideline.

title: BEAR-Bench: A Bilingual Enterprise and Academic Reasoning Benchmark for Multimodal Models
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made significant strides in visual comprehension, their ability to reason about text-dense, professional documents remains incompletely evaluated. Existing benchmarks emphasize information extraction, require external domain knowledge, or cover professional documents only as one of many settings. They are also largely English- or Chinese-centric, leaving other languages and Russian, in particular, substantially underrepresented. To address these limitations, we introduce BEAR-Bench (Bilingual Enterprise and Academic Reasoning), a self-contained, complex English-and-Russian benchmark comprising 1000 human-annotated questions based on text-rich business and scientific documents. We evaluate 16 proprietary and open-weight MLLMs, including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen3.5-397B, on BEAR-Bench and observe clear headroom even for the strongest systems. Finally, we use the resulting model outputs to compare existing hallucination detection methods, evaluating not only how often models fail on BEAR-Bench but also how reliably those failures can be identified.

AI.tldr: Introduces BEAR-Bench, a bilingual (English/Russian) benchmark of 1000 questions for evaluating MLLM reasoning on text-dense professional documents and studying hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of multimodal large language models focus mainly on visual understanding and relatively simple information extraction, often in English or Chinese. They do not adequately test complex reasoning on text-heavy, professional business and scientific documents, and they underrepresent other languages, especially Russian. Additionally, we lack systematic analysis of how well hallucination detection methods work when models fail on such challenging inputs.
AI.method: The authors construct BEAR-Bench (Bilingual Enterprise and Academic Reasoning), a curated benchmark built from real-world, text-rich business and scientific documents in both English and Russian. They create 1000 human-annotated, self-contained questions that require non-trivial reasoning rather than pure extraction and do not depend on external knowledge. They then evaluate 16 multimodal LLMs, including state-of-the-art proprietary models like Gemini 3.1 Pro and large open models like Qwen3.5-397B, on this benchmark. Using the collected model responses, they further assess multiple hallucination detection methods by measuring how accurately these methods flag incorrect or fabricated model outputs on BEAR-Bench tasks.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows that even the strongest tested MLLMs perform noticeably below perfection on BEAR-Bench, revealing significant remaining gaps in their ability to reason over text-dense professional documents in English and Russian. The benchmark exposes consistent failure patterns across models. When applying existing hallucination detection techniques to the generated outputs, the study finds that these methods only partially succeed in identifying failures; their reliability varies and is far from ideal, especially in this bilingual, document-centric setting.
AI.conclusion: BEAR-Bench provides a challenging, bilingual, and domain-focused benchmark that better reflects real-world professional use cases for MLLMs than prior datasets. The results demonstrate substantial room for improvement in both multimodal reasoning over complex, text-rich documents and in automatic hallucination detection. The benchmark and evaluation protocol can serve as a standard for future model development and for more robust methods to detect and mitigate hallucinations in professional document understanding tasks.

title: Graph Surgery and the Do-Operator: A Precise Correspondence for Acyclic Structural Causal Models
summary: The $\operatorname{do}$-operator is described graphically by deleting arrows into its targets and functionally by replacing their mechanisms with constants. To call these operations equivalent is not yet a mathematical statement: one returns a graph and remembers only the targets, whereas the other returns mechanisms and also remembers the imposed values. We make a dependency-level comparison precise for deterministic acyclic structural causal models with finitely many endogenous variables. If $\operatorname{Graph}(F)$ extracts the dependencies of a mechanism family $F$, our main theorem is $\operatorname{Graph}(F^ι)=\operatorname{Surg}(\operatorname{Graph}(F),T_ι)$. Thus replacing target mechanisms removes exactly the dependencies removed by graph surgery. For a model $M=(G,F)$ whose graph may contain unused arrows, we characterize when the same equality holds with $G$ in place of $\operatorname{Graph}(F)$; it holds for every intervention exactly when $G$ records the dependencies of $F$ exactly. We then define the intervened model, characterize its run, show how sequential interventions combine, and prove that an outcome depends only on interventions at its actual dependency ancestors.

AI.tldr: They formalize and prove the precise relationship between Pearl’s graphical do-operator (graph surgery) and its functional interpretation (replacing structural equations by constants) in deterministic acyclic structural causal models.
AI.motivation: In causal inference, the do-operator is described both graphically (by deleting incoming arrows to intervened variables) and functionally (by replacing structural mechanisms with constants). These are usually treated as equivalent, but the equivalence is informal: the graphical version outputs a modified graph with designated targets, while the functional version outputs modified mechanisms with fixed values. The authors want a mathematically precise comparison showing exactly when and how these two perspectives match, especially at the level of variable dependencies.
AI.method: They work in the setting of deterministic, acyclic structural causal models with finitely many endogenous variables. They formalize: (1) a map Graph(F) that extracts a dependency graph from a family of structural mechanisms F; (2) a surgery operation Surg on graphs that corresponds to the graphical do-operator; and (3) an intervention operation F^ι that replaces target mechanisms by constants. They then prove a main theorem establishing equality between the dependency graph of the intervened mechanisms and the surgically modified graph. They further analyze models M = (G, F) where the given graph G may have extra, unused arrows, and provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which the graphical and functional interventions coincide for all interventions. Finally, they formally define the intervened model, its runs, composition of sequential interventions, and a dependency-ancestor property for outcomes under interventions.
AI.result: The main result is the equality Graph(F^ι) = Surg(Graph(F), T_ι), showing that replacing target mechanisms by constants removes exactly the dependencies that graph surgery deletes, at the level of endogenous-variable dependencies. They extend this to models M = (G, F) with possibly spurious edges by characterizing when the equality holds with G in place of Graph(F): it holds for all interventions if and only if G captures exactly the actual dependencies in F (i.e., has no missing or superfluous arrows). They also provide formal constructions of intervened models, characterizations of runs, proofs that sequential interventions compose cleanly, and a theorem that an outcome’s value depends only on interventions applied to its actual dependency ancestors.
AI.conclusion: The paper rigorously aligns the graphical and functional interpretations of the do-operator in deterministic acyclic structural causal models. It shows precisely when graph surgery and mechanism replacement are dependency-equivalent, clarifies the role of “faithful” graphs that exactly mirror functional dependencies, and establishes that causal effects of interventions propagate only along true dependency paths. This provides a solid mathematical foundation for using graph surgery to reason about interventions defined via structural equations.

title: CABLE: Extending the Reach of Memory Retrieval via Complementary Antecedent-Based Linking and Expansion
summary: As LLM agents operate across structured workflows and sessions, preserving long-term history does not ensure that later contexts can recover relevant evidence through a bounded memory interface. We study this evidence-reachability problem in long-term conversational memory, where retrieval still relies heavily on semantic similarity. This works well for topical recall, but it often misses earlier experiences, plans, or motivations that are semantically distant from the later events they help explain. Existing memory graphs provide cross-memory structure, yet links driven mainly by semantic overlap can duplicate what the host retriever already recovers. We argue that link construction should instead prioritize a sparse set of retriever-complementary associations. We present CABLE (Complementary Antecedent-Based Linking and Expansion), a plug-in augmentation that constructs links designed to extend the host retriever's direct semantic reach. For each new memory, CABLE generates antecedent-oriented queries, retrieves prior memories, subtracts candidates in the direct semantic neighborhood, and verifies the remainder before adding the accepted complementary associations into a sparse directed graph. At retrieval time, CABLE expands the host system's retrieved seeds along these links to surface implicit supporting evidence. We evaluate CABLE with A-MEM on LoCoMo and MA-LongMemEval, and further integrate it into SimpleMem and Mem0g on LoCoMo, using Qwen3.5-27B, DeepSeek-chat, and GPT-4o-mini. CABLE yields higher mean LLM-judge scores in every evaluated system-level setting, with the largest gains in categories where useful evidence is distributed across memories or sessions, including open-domain, multi-session, and preference-oriented questions. These results support prioritizing sparse, reasoning-relevant associations that complement rather than duplicate the host retriever.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CABLE, a complementary linking method that builds sparse, reasoning-relevant connections between memories to improve long-term evidence retrieval for LLM agents beyond standard semantic similarity search.
AI.motivation: In long-term LLM agents, simply storing all past interactions is not enough because bounded memory interfaces and semantic-similarity-based retrieval often fail to surface earlier experiences, plans, or motivations that are important but semantically distant from the current query. Existing memory graphs mostly add links based on semantic overlap, which tends to replicate what the base retriever already finds, offering limited gains. The authors are motivated to solve this "evidence-reachability" problem: enabling later contexts to reach relevant but semantically distant prior evidence in a way that complements, rather than duplicates, the host retriever.
AI.method: They propose CABLE (Complementary Antecedent-Based Linking and Expansion), a plug-in augmentation for memory systems. For each new memory, CABLE: (1) generates antecedent-oriented queries meant to identify earlier items that might explain or support the new memory; (2) retrieves candidate prior memories using the host retriever; (3) removes those that lie in the direct semantic neighborhood (i.e., that the base retriever would already find easily); and (4) verifies and retains the remaining candidates as complementary associations, storing them as edges in a sparse directed graph. At retrieval time, the base system first retrieves seed memories via standard similarity search, and then CABLE expands these seeds along the constructed graph links to surface additional implicit supporting evidence that is semantically distant but linked as an antecedent.
AI.result: CABLE is evaluated mainly with the A-MEM framework on the LoCoMo and MA-LongMemEval benchmarks, and is also integrated into two other memory systems (SimpleMem and Mem0g) on LoCoMo. Experiments use multiple backbone LLMs, including Qwen3.5-27B, DeepSeek-chat, and GPT-4o-mini. Across all evaluated system-level configurations, CABLE improves mean LLM-judge scores, with especially notable gains in tasks where relevant evidence is scattered across different memories or sessions, such as open-domain questions, multi-session interactions, and user-preference-oriented queries.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that constructing sparse, complementary memory links—focused on reasoning-relevant antecedent relationships rather than pure semantic similarity—significantly improves long-term evidence retrieval for LLM agents. The results suggest that memory-graph construction should emphasize associations that extend the reach of the base retriever into semantically distant but explanatory past experiences, rather than redundantly linking memories that are already semantically close.

title: Beyond the Trace: Coupling an Interpretable Reasoning-State Readout to Native MoE Routing
summary: What a reasoning model writes is only a partial record of the process that produces it. We introduce a two-level internal readout for mixture-of-experts reasoning. We first distill vocabulary-scale J-space into J64, a 64-axis semantic frame learned from the model's own reasoning states. J64 reveals readable process state that the emitted trace does not show: it separates inference effort from problem-induced strain. It also adds 0.096 to 0.135 held-out AUC over a baseline that reads the same rollout as token occupancy and aggregates it in exactly the same way. We then reconstruct J64 from native expert-routing statistics. The result is R64, a low-overhead proxy: its median per-axis correlation with J64 is 0.69 to 0.86 across three models and two families, and on gpt-oss-20b it preserves 95 to 100% of J64's predictive gain. The readout supports test-time decisions at two temporal resolutions. Over completed candidate sets, J64 and R64 improve single-branch selection, and R64-weighted voting improves plain majority voting in seven of eight settings. During generation, rolling readout windows drive a cumulative stop-and-resample policy whose operating point is fixed on training questions alone. J64 improves accuracy by 1.1 to 5.9 points over a sibling-permuted control, and the routing-only R64 proxy retains 0.9 to 3.2 of those points. Finally, router edits aimed at the mechanism J64 names induce the predicted reasoning behaviors and shift a diagnosed stall from numerical guessing toward exact symbolic execution. Together, J64 makes latent process state readable, while routing makes it deployable and actionable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new way to read and use internal process signals from mixture-of-experts reasoning models, via a semantic frame (J64) and a routing-based proxy (R64), to better monitor, select, and steer reasoning in real time.
AI.motivation: Current reasoning models expose only token-level outputs and limited traces, which are an incomplete and noisy view of the underlying reasoning process. For mixture-of-experts architectures, there exist rich internal states—such as expert activations and routing patterns—that are not directly readable yet may encode useful information about reasoning quality, effort, and failure modes. The authors aim to create a compact, interpretable, and low-overhead representation of the model’s internal reasoning state that can be used to monitor, predict performance, and intervene during inference without retraining the base model.
AI.method: 1) Learn J64, a 64-dimensional semantic frame, by distilling high-dimensional, vocabulary-scale internal reasoning states (J-space) into a compact representation. This frame is trained on the model’s own internal signals and supervised by downstream metrics so that each axis captures meaningful process state, such as inference effort vs. problem-induced strain. 2) Quantitatively evaluate J64 by measuring its predictive power (AUC on held-out data) against a baseline that uses only token occupancy statistics aggregated in the same way. 3) Construct R64, a lightweight proxy that reconstructs J64 solely from mixture-of-experts router statistics (which experts fire and with what weights) to avoid heavy internal readout overhead. The correlation between R64 and J64 is measured per axis over multiple models and families. 4) Use J64 and R64 for test-time control at two temporal scales: (a) over completed candidate solutions, to improve branch selection and voting; (b) during generation, using rolling windows of readout to trigger a stop-and-resample policy trained only on held-out questions. 5) Perform router-edit interventions informed by J64’s interpretation of mechanisms (e.g., strain vs. effort) and test whether these edits produce predicted changes in reasoning behavior, such as shifting from heuristic numerical guessing toward exact symbolic computation in stalled cases.
AI.result: J64, the semantic frame derived from internal reasoning states, provides substantial predictive improvements over a baseline that only reads output token statistics, improving held-out AUC by 0.096–0.135. The proxy R64, reconstructed from expert-routing signals, correlates strongly with J64 (median per-axis correlations between 0.69 and 0.86 across three models and two model families), and on gpt-oss-20b retains 95–100% of the predictive gain offered by J64. For downstream control, J64 and R64 improve the selection of a single best reasoning branch among multiple candidates, and R64-weighted voting beats simple majority voting in 7 of 8 experimental settings. In an online control regime using rolling readout windows and a stop-and-resample policy fixed from training data, J64 yields 1.1–5.9 percentage-point accuracy gains over a sibling-permuted control, while R64 preserves 0.9–3.2 of those points. Router edits guided by J64’s interpretation of the underlying mechanism cause measurable shifts in the model’s behavior, matching predictions: reasoning stalls that previously manifested as numerical guessing are redirected toward more faithful symbolic execution.
AI.conclusion: A compact internal readout space (J64) can make the latent reasoning process of mixture-of-experts models interpretable and measurably useful for control, distinguishing factors like inference effort and problem difficulty that are not visible from output tokens alone. Moreover, a routing-based proxy (R64) can approximate this rich readout with low overhead, preserving most of J64’s predictive and control benefits. These readouts enable practical test-time interventions—better branch selection, improved voting, and effective stop-and-resample policies—as well as causal manipulations of routing that steer reasoning behavior in targeted ways. Overall, internal reasoning states, when distilled into structured representations and tied to router mechanisms, become readable, deployable, and actionable for improving reasoning model reliability and performance.

title: SpeechSense: A Paralinguistic-Focused Dataset for Fine-Grained Speech Sentiment Analysis
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026 (Dataset Track). Dataset and code: https://github.com/Sher13cked/SpeechSense
summary: Recent advances in AI have revolutionized speech processing, yet effective speech understanding requires discerning not just what is said, but how it is said. Speech Sentiment Analysis plays a critical role in decoding these paralinguistic cues for diverse real-world applications such as recruitment and customer service. However, existing Speech Sentiment Analysis research faces two primary limitations. First, dominant approaches rely on text-centric pipelines that cascade Automatic Speech Recognition with text analysis. This process inevitably discards essential acoustic features like prosody and tone, failing to capture attitudinal meanings in acoustically ambiguous utterances. Second, current benchmarks suffer from a mismatch in label granularity, prioritizing basic emotions (e.g., happy, sad) over the nuanced interpersonal stances (e.g., confident, impatient) necessary for social sensitivity. To address these limitations, we propose a novel dataset, SpeechSense, for fine-grained speech sentiment analysis. Specifically, we define a specialized 8-class taxonomy of interpersonal stances detectable primarily through prosodic cues beyond lexical content alone. We then construct a curated dataset based on this taxonomy, built from high-fidelity speech synthesis and rigorous human validation. Comprehensive experiments across multi-modal LLMs, text-only LLMs, and speech encoders demonstrate that models with acoustic access consistently outperform text-only baselines. These results empirically validate the primacy of acoustic cues in detecting subtle speaker attitudes, highlighting the necessity of SpeechSense. Dataset and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Sher13cked/SpeechSense.

AI.tldr: Introduces SpeechSense, a new dataset for fine-grained speech sentiment analysis that focuses on interpersonal stances detectable from prosody, showing acoustic-aware models beat text-only ones.
AI.motivation: Existing speech sentiment analysis pipelines mostly use ASR followed by text sentiment models, which discards rich acoustic cues like prosody and tone that are crucial for understanding attitudes in acoustically ambiguous utterances. Additionally, current benchmarks emphasize coarse emotion labels (e.g., happy, sad) instead of nuanced interpersonal stances (e.g., confident, impatient) that are more useful for socially sensitive applications such as recruitment and customer support. There is a need for a resource that centers fine-grained, prosody-driven interpersonal sentiment labels.
AI.method: The authors design an 8-class taxonomy of interpersonal stances that are primarily identifiable via prosodic cues beyond lexical content. They then create SpeechSense, a curated dataset aligned with this taxonomy, generated with high-fidelity speech synthesis and subjected to rigorous human validation. Using this dataset, they run comprehensive experiments comparing multi-modal large language models with acoustic access, text-only LLMs operating on ASR transcripts, and specialized speech encoders on the stance classification task.
AI.result: Across all experiments, models that have direct access to acoustic information (multi-modal LLMs and speech encoders) consistently outperform text-only LLM baselines that rely solely on transcripts. This performance gap demonstrates that prosodic and other acoustic cues materially improve the recognition of subtle speaker attitudes represented in the 8-class stance taxonomy.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that effective speech sentiment analysis—especially for nuanced interpersonal stances—requires modeling acoustic features rather than relying only on text derived from ASR. The SpeechSense dataset provides an appropriate benchmark for such fine-grained, prosody-focused sentiment tasks, and the empirical results validate the central role of acoustic cues in decoding subtle speaker attitudes. The authors position SpeechSense as a necessary resource for advancing socially sensitive, real-world speech understanding systems.

title: LLM-Derived Preference Judgments Are Not Self-Consistent
summary: Agents increasingly interpret a person's natural-language preferences by querying an LLM for numerical preference judgments, e.g., by asking how much the person would be willing to pay for an item. A growing body of work estimates a utility function from these judgments and then chooses actions based on their estimated utility. This pipeline assumes the judgments are approximately self-consistent: that a single utility function can reproduce them. But are they? To study this question, we measure the self-consistency of cardinal LLM preference judgments. For example, the difference in stated willingness-to-pay between two items should match the stated payment that makes a person indifferent to exchanging them. We develop statistical tests and interpretable measures of how far observed responses depart from the best-fitting self-consistent utility function. Experiments with flight, apartment, and hotel examples across six LLMs reveal large persistent inconsistencies. This suggests that LLM-derived preference judgments cannot be faithfully summarized by a single utility function.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether numerical preference judgments from large language models (LLMs) are self-consistent enough to be represented by a single utility function.
AI.motivation: Many systems now rely on LLMs to translate natural-language preferences into numerical values (e.g., willingness-to-pay) and then fit a utility function to guide decision-making. This presumes that LLM judgments are approximately self-consistent. The authors question this assumption and aim to rigorously test whether a single cardinal utility function can accurately represent LLM-derived preference judgments.
AI.method: The authors design statistical tests and interpretable metrics that compare LLM-generated cardinal preference statements—such as willingness-to-pay and indifference prices—against the predictions of the best-fitting self-consistent utility function. They focus on relationships that must hold if a single utility function exists (e.g., differences in willingness-to-pay between two items should equal the payment that makes the model indifferent between them). They apply these tests to multiple realistic choice domains (flights, apartments, hotels) and evaluate six different LLMs.
AI.result: Across all tested domains and models, the authors find substantial and persistent violations of self-consistency. Even after fitting the best possible utility function to the observed responses, significant systematic deviations remain, indicating that the LLMs’ cardinal preference judgments cannot be reconciled within a single coherent utility representation.
AI.conclusion: LLM-derived numerical preference judgments are not reliably self-consistent and therefore cannot, in general, be faithfully captured by a single cardinal utility function. This challenges current approaches that treat LLMs as preference or utility oracles and suggests that alternative methods are needed for using LLMs in preference-based decision-making systems.

title: Grading Needs a Rubric, Not Intelligence
summary: Small language models can grade open-ended examination answers as reliably as substantially more expensive models when they grade against an explicit rubric. We test this claim as the design principle behind any-to-bench: a frontier model reads source documents once, at ingestion, to extract each question and its rubric; lower-cost models then perform all repeated grading work. We evaluate six cost-efficient model configurations from two model families at three reasoning-effort levels. Each configuration answers 24 open-ended examination questions, and each also grades every answer sheet three times, yielding 3,456 per-question grades. Scores depend overwhelmingly on the answer being graded: answer identity explains 95.6% of score variance, whereas judge identity explains only 0.2%. Raising a writer's reasoning effort moves earned scores by as much as 0.143 of full marks, while raising a judge's reasoning effort moves assigned scores by at most 0.006. Six frontier-tier judges, added as a check, reproduce these scores and are no more reliable as a panel. Two ablations then decompose the rubric on the same questions and answers. Removing its criteria and levels while keeping the official answer changes nothing measurable. Removing the official answer as well collapses reliability (ICC 0.888 to 0.628), inflates scores, and makes judge reasoning effort matter again. The rubric is what decouples grading from judge intelligence, and within the rubric the official answer does nearly all the work. We find no evidence of length preference or same-family preference under rubric-anchored grading.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when grading is guided by a clear rubric with an explicit official answer, small, low-cost language models grade open-ended exam answers as reliably as large frontier models; grading accuracy depends far more on the student answer than on the grading model or its reasoning effort.
AI.motivation: Automatic grading of open-ended exam responses is costly when using large frontier language models for every grading operation. The authors want to know whether smaller, cheaper models can reliably take over most grading work if the expensive model is only used once to extract questions and rubrics, and to understand what aspects of rubrics make grading robust and model-agnostic.
AI.method: They propose any-to-bench: a pipeline where a single frontier model pass over source documents extracts exam questions and detailed rubrics, and then smaller models perform all grading. They test six low-cost model configurations spanning two model families and three reasoning-effort settings. Each configuration answers 24 open-ended questions and then grades all answer sheets three times, producing 3,456 per-question grades. They analyze variance in scores to separate effects of answer identity, judge (model) identity, and reasoning effort. They also run six frontier models as additional judges and conduct two rubric ablation studies: (1) removing criteria and levels but keeping the official answer; (2) also removing the official answer, to see how rubric components affect reliability, score levels, and the impact of judge reasoning effort.
AI.result: Answer identity explains 95.6% of score variance, while judge identity explains only 0.2%, indicating that the model used for grading matters very little under rubric anchoring. Increasing the writer’s reasoning effort can change scores by up to 0.143 of full marks, but increasing the judge’s reasoning effort shifts scores by at most 0.006. Frontier-tier judges reproduce the same score patterns and are not more reliable as a panel. In ablations, removing criteria and levels but keeping the official answer does not significantly affect grading behavior. However, removing the official answer dramatically reduces reliability (ICC drops from 0.888 to 0.628), raises assigned scores, and reintroduces sensitivity to judge reasoning effort. They also observe no significant length bias or preference for answers from the same model family when grading is rubric-anchored.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that with well-specified rubrics—especially explicit official answers—small, inexpensive language models can grade open-ended exam answers as reliably as large frontier models, making large-scale automatic grading far more cost-efficient. The decisive factor for reliability is the rubric, not the intelligence or reasoning effort of the grading model. Official answers within rubrics carry most of the burden for consistent, unbiased scoring, and they effectively decouple grading quality from model size or family, while avoiding systematic biases like length or same-family preference.

title: GraphWake: Group Polarization via Memory-Mediated Polarization Cascade in LLM-Agent Communities
summary: LLM-driven agents can autonomously exchange opinions on online platforms and form communities. Such agent-operated social platforms raise a new security concern: attackers may manipulate agents to induce group polarization. Existing methods manipulate agent prompts or construct echo chambers, both of which are difficult to realize in practice. We therefore formulate a new threat, Memory-Mediated Polarization Cascade, which uses agent memory as a persistence channel and public discussion as a propagation channel. This threat contains three stages. During exposure and memory retention, the attacker exposes a small set of target agents to arguments that reinforce their respective stated stances. The targets' memory systems then process and retain these arguments. During retrieval and reproduction, a shared stance-neutral discussion cues the targets to retrieve and reproduce their respective retained arguments. During iterative propagation, untreated agents influenced by the reproduced arguments restate and spread them. We instantiate this threat in GraphWake with three components: (i) stance-support argumentation knowledge graphs construct knowledge-based arguments; (ii) axiom-oriented triple selection distills them for reliable retention and reproduction; and (iii) stance-neutral memory cueing triggers concurrent retrieval and reproduction, initiating propagation. Experiments across multiple discussions and memory systems show that GraphWake substantially increases group polarization. These findings reveal a community-level polarization risk.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new, practical attack that uses LLM agents’ memories and public discussions to induce group polarization, and demonstrates its effectiveness via a framework called GraphWake.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents increasingly interact on social platforms and form communities, there is a growing security risk that adversaries can systematically steer these communities toward more extreme, polarized positions. Existing polarization attacks mainly rely on prompt manipulation or constructing artificial echo chambers, which are hard to mount in realistic, open environments. The authors are motivated to study whether a more subtle, memory-based mechanism could be exploited to induce community-level polarization over time.
AI.method: The authors define a new threat model called Memory-Mediated Polarization Cascade, structured into three stages: (1) exposure and memory retention, where a small subset of agents is selectively exposed to stance-reinforcing arguments that are processed and stored in their long-term memory; (2) retrieval and reproduction, where later stance-neutral discussions cue these agents to recall and restate the stored arguments; and (3) iterative propagation, where previously untreated agents adopt, restate, and spread these arguments, causing a cascading effect. They instantiate this with GraphWake, which (i) builds stance-supporting argumentation knowledge graphs to generate structured, knowledge-based arguments; (ii) uses axiom-oriented triple selection to distill stable, memorable argument “atoms” that agents reliably retain and reproduce; and (iii) designs stance-neutral memory cues that trigger concurrent retrieval and reproduction during shared discussions. They then run experiments across multiple discussion topics and different LLM memory systems to evaluate polarization changes in agent communities.
AI.result: GraphWake successfully induces significant increases in group polarization across various discussion settings and memory architectures for LLM agents. A small number of initially targeted agents, once seeded with carefully selected stance-support arguments, can trigger a polarization cascade through subsequent neutral discussions. The empirical results show that polarization effects are robust to different memory implementations and discussion scenarios, highlighting the potency and practicality of the proposed attack.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that LLM-based social platforms face a previously underappreciated community-level security risk: adversaries can exploit agent memory and public discourse to orchestrate polarization cascades, even without explicit prompt tampering or overt echo chambers. By formalizing Memory-Mediated Polarization Cascades and demonstrating GraphWake’s effectiveness, the paper underscores the need for new defenses around memory management, discussion moderation, and community-level monitoring to mitigate polarization risks in autonomous agent ecosystems.

title: Do Large Language Models Play Six Degrees of Separation? Measuring Topological Compression in Long-Context Manifolds
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable multi-hop reasoning capabilities over long contexts, yet the internal mechanisms enabling these distant cognitive leaps remain poorly understood. Traditional attention-based interpretability often fails to capture true semantic proximity due to routing artifacts like attention sinks. In this paper, we bypass attention weights to directly analyze the dynamic geometry of the hidden state manifold, proving that deep LLM latent spaces natively organize into Small-World networks. By sparsifying the continuous similarity matrices of long-context representations into unweighted graphs, we trace the connectivity between highly disjoint semantic anchors across two distinct architectures. Our findings reveal a sharp topological phase transition: while early syntactic layers remain entirely fractured, deep reasoning layers abruptly compress massive conceptual distances into highly navigable pathways strictly bounded by the "Six Degrees of Separation" limit (=< 6 semantic hops). Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical efficacy of this framework by applying it to zero-shot hallucination detection within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using the RAGognize dataset. We show that factually grounded generations maintain structural integrity with their source context (approximately 3 hops), whereas hallucinations induce severe topological collapse. Ultimately, this work mathematically formalizes how transformers execute abstract reasoning and provides a novel, strictly geometric signature for evaluating factual reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that hidden states in deep layers of large language models form small-world networks, enabling efficient multi-hop reasoning and providing a geometric signal to detect hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs are good at multi-hop reasoning over long contexts, we do not understand how their internal representations support these long-distance semantic connections. Existing attention-based interpretability is unreliable because attention weights can be distorted by artifacts like attention sinks and do not reflect true semantic proximity. A more faithful, geometry-based view of hidden states is needed, with both theoretical insight and practical value (e.g., hallucination detection in RAG).
AI.method: Instead of relying on attention weights, the authors analyze the geometry of hidden states across layers. They compute similarity matrices over long-context token representations, sparsify them into unweighted graphs, and study the resulting connectivity structure as a function of depth, across two different LLM architectures. They then measure graph-theoretic properties associated with small-world networks and examine path lengths between distant semantic anchors. Finally, they apply this framework to RAG outputs on the RAGognize dataset, comparing the geometric structure of grounded vs hallucinated generations relative to their source context.
AI.result: They find that deep LLM layers exhibit small-world network structure: representations that are semantically distant in the input become connected via short paths in the latent space. There is a sharp phase transition across depth: early layers are fragmented and mainly syntactic, while deeper layers suddenly become highly navigable, with paths between distant semantic anchors limited to about six hops. In the RAG setting, grounded generations show stable, low-hop connectivity (~3 hops) to the retrieved context, whereas hallucinations correspond to a collapse or distortion of this topological structure.
AI.conclusion: Transformers internally implement abstract, multi-hop reasoning by organizing their deep-layer latent spaces into small-world networks that compress large semantic distances into a few steps. This provides a mathematically grounded explanation of LLM reasoning and yields a geometric signature that can be used to evaluate or detect factual reliability, as demonstrated by zero-shot hallucination detection in RAG. The work advocates moving beyond attention weights toward geometric/topological analysis of hidden states for interpretability and reliability assessment.

title: Auditing Self-Evolution in Financial Agents: Capability Gains, Security Drift, and Execution-Interface Mismatch
summary: Self-evolving agents turn experience into reusable skills, workflows, or memories, but post-evolution accuracy alone does not show whether learned behavior preserves previously correct behavior or security. We audit SkillOpt, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and ReasoningBank in simulated e-banking using matched benign acquisition trajectories, sealed evaluation endpoints, execution-grounded checks, and independent state replay. On Qwen 3.7 Flash, SkillOpt raises benign utility from 0.741 to 0.837 while exposure to injected content rises from 0.820 to 0.943. Conditional attack success after exposure falls from 0.605 to 0.562, yet overall attack success rate (ASR) rises from 0.496 to 0.530 and unauthorized financial state changes rise to 0.685. Across three independently evolved lineages, capability, exposure, and unauthorized-state changes increase in all three, whereas ASR increases in only two. ReasoningBank raises utility to 0.859 without increasing aggregate ASR, although unauthorized state changes remain slightly above Static. AWM reveals a separate evaluation hazard: a literal WebArena text-action envelope disrupts tool execution in our native function-calling executor. In a post-hoc sensitivity test, removing only that envelope restores utility from 0.319 to 0.756, while exposure rises from 0.299 to 0.909 and ASR from 0.195 to 0.575. Auditing self-evolving financial agents therefore requires tracking regressions, attack-surface contact, unauthorized financial-state change, and artifact-executor compatibility, not accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how self-evolving AI agents behave in a simulated e-banking setting, showing that improved task accuracy can come with increased security risks like higher attack success and unauthorized financial changes, and that evaluation can be confounded by mismatched execution environments.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents can learn new skills from experience, but current evaluations mostly look at post-training accuracy or utility, not whether the new behavior preserves earlier safety properties, avoids security regressions, or interacts safely with tools and environments. The authors want an auditing framework that captures both helpfulness and security impacts of evolution, particularly in sensitive domains like e-banking.
AI.method: The authors simulate e-banking tasks and compare several self-evolving systems—SkillOpt, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and ReasoningBank—against a static baseline using the Qwen 3.7 Flash model. They use matched benign acquisition trajectories to train/evolve the agents, sealed evaluation endpoints to prevent contamination, execution-grounded checks, and independent state replay to measure effects on benign task utility, exposure to injected attack content, conditional and overall attack success rates, and unauthorized financial state changes. They also inspect the interaction between learned workflows (e.g., WebArena-style text envelopes) and their native function-calling executor.
AI.result: SkillOpt improves benign task utility but also increases exposure to injected attack content, overall attack success rate, and unauthorized financial state changes; across three independent evolutionary runs, capabilities and unauthorized-state changes consistently rise, while attack success rises in most but not all lineages. ReasoningBank boosts utility without increasing aggregate attack success, though unauthorized state changes stay slightly above the static baseline. AWM’s evaluation is confounded by a WebArena-style text-action envelope that breaks tool execution in the native executor, severely depressing measured utility; removing just this envelope in a sensitivity test reveals much higher utility but also sharply higher exposure and attack success.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy or utility alone is an unreliable indicator of whether self-evolving financial agents remain safe. Robust auditing must jointly track regressions in previously correct behavior, degree of contact with adversarial content, unauthorized financial-state changes, and compatibility between learned artifacts and the actual execution environment; otherwise, both security regressions and evaluation artifacts can be missed.

title: When Writing Style Drifts: Benchmarking Authorship Verification under Distribution Shifts in Genre, Time and the AI-Era
summary: Authorship verification (AV) assumes that an author's writing style remains sufficiently stable to distinguish it from that of other writers. In practice, however, this assumption is challenged by distribution shifts caused by changes in genre, time, and AI-assisted writing. Existing AV benchmarks typically study these factors in isolation and focus predominantly on English, limiting our understanding of model robustness under realistic conditions. We introduce AVShift, the first German benchmark for systematically evaluating AV under multiple distribution shifts. AVShift comprises over 150,000 text pairs spanning three genres and 21 years, enabling controlled evaluation of cross-genre, temporal, and AI-era shifts within a unified framework. We benchmark representative feature-based, embedding-based, and LLM-based approaches. Our experiments show that fine-tuned LLMs generalize best across genres and benefit substantially from stylistically diverse training data. We further demonstrate that temporal drift is one of the strongest factors affecting AV, with performance degrading significantly as the time gap between documents increases. In contrast, we find no evidence of a measurable AI-era distribution shift within AVShift. Finally, our feature analysis reveals stylistic features that remain stable across genres, while their relative importance varies depending on the specific genre transition. We release AVShift and our code for future research.

AI.tldr: Introduces AVShift, a large German benchmark to test how robust authorship verification methods are under realistic distribution shifts (genre, time, and AI-era).
AI.motivation: Authorship verification models often assume stable writing style, but in real settings style is affected by genre, time, and AI assistance. Existing benchmarks mostly cover English and usually vary only one factor at a time, making it hard to assess robustness under combined, realistic shifts, especially for German. The authors aim to fill this gap with a controlled, large-scale benchmark.
AI.method: Construct AVShift, a German corpus of 150k+ text pairs covering three genres over 21 years, designed to create controlled cross-genre, temporal, and AI-era distribution shifts. Evaluate representative AV approaches: feature-based systems, embeddings, and fine-tuned LLMs. Analyze performance under different shift scenarios and perform feature analysis to identify stylistic features that are stable or variable across genres and time.
AI.result: Fine-tuned LLM-based AV models show the best cross-genre generalization and improve further with more stylistically diverse training data. Temporal drift is identified as a major source of performance degradation: the larger the time gap between documents, the worse the AV accuracy. No measurable AI-era distribution shift is observed within AVShift. Feature analysis identifies stylistic cues that remain stable across genres, but their importance changes depending on the specific genre transition.
AI.conclusion: AVShift provides the first systematic German benchmark for AV under multiple realistic distribution shifts and shows that temporal drift is a key challenge, while AI-era effects are not yet detectable in this setting. Fine-tuned LLMs are currently the most robust AV methods, especially with diverse training data. The released dataset and code enable further research into robust, cross-domain and temporally stable authorship verification models.

title: Mixture-of-Expert Blocks Contain Strong Hallucination Detection Signals
summary: Despite their widespread use, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain limited by a fundamental problem: the generation of plausible but false content, known as hallucinations. Most existing detection methods operate at the answer or sentence level, yet per-token detection is essential for localizing hallucinated spans and enabling fine-grained interventions. In this paper, we explore the use of the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm to address this gap. In MoE architectures, a single forward pass activates a sparse subset of experts (i.e., distinct feedforward networks per layer) via a routing mechanism, producing internal signals (e.g., router entropy, expert disagreement, and expert usage patterns) that are unavailable in dense architectures and have not been previously exploited for hallucination detection. To this end, we introduce InnerExpert, the first method to leverage these MoE-specific signals for per-token hallucination detection. InnerExpert combines routing-level and standard transformer signals into compact per-token feature vectors, classified by a lightweight detector trained on labels produced by an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline, which enables continuous model updates without manual annotation. Our results show that InnerExpert outperforms existing methods across five datasets and two MoE architectures, achieving up to 0.91 answer-level and 0.76 token-level AUROC, while requiring only a single forward pass.

AI.tldr: A new method, InnerExpert, uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) internal routing signals to detect hallucinations at the token level in LLM outputs.
AI.motivation: LLMs often generate hallucinations—fluent but false content. Existing detection approaches mostly work at coarse granularity (answer or sentence level), which is insufficient to precisely locate hallucinated spans or perform fine-grained interventions such as selective editing, highlighting, or rejection. Moreover, standard dense architectures offer limited internal signals for hallucination detection, missing the opportunity to exploit richer information present in MoE models.
AI.method: The authors focus on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, where each token is processed by a sparsely activated subset of expert feedforward networks, chosen by a router. This routing procedure yields internal signals such as router entropy, expert disagreement, and expert usage patterns. They propose InnerExpert, which constructs compact per-token feature vectors by combining these MoE-specific routing signals with standard transformer signals. A lightweight classifier then predicts whether each token is hallucinated. Training labels are obtained automatically using an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline rather than manual annotation, enabling continuous updating of the detector as models or data change.
AI.result: Across five datasets and two different MoE architectures, InnerExpert outperforms previous hallucination detection methods. It reaches up to 0.91 AUROC at the answer level and 0.76 AUROC at the token level. The approach operates with only a single forward pass of the base MoE model, making it computationally efficient compared with methods requiring multiple queries or external verification steps.
AI.conclusion: MoE routing signals contain useful information for hallucination detection that is not available in standard dense models. By leveraging these signals via InnerExpert, one can achieve accurate, fine-grained (per-token) hallucination detection in a single forward pass. This demonstrates the value of MoE-specific internal features for reliability tools around LLMs and suggests a path for scalable, continuously updated detectors without human labeling.

title: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees
comment: Accepted at Conference on Language Modelling 2026
summary: Using LLMs as judges has become standard practice for evaluating model outputs at scale. This is particularly common for subjective, open-ended tasks such as assessing helpfulness or alignment, where no single reference answer exists. However, objective tasks introduce a distinct reliability challenge for reference-free LLM judging. In the absence of a reference answer, the judge evaluates factual correctness either through its parametric knowledge or through tool augmentation. Although the former enables efficient evaluation, the judge may hallucinate or lack sufficient evidence for its verdict. Conversely, tool augmentation can provide additional evidence but introduces extra computational cost and requires an appropriate mechanism to determine when and how that evidence should be used reliably. More importantly, neither approach alone provides formal control over the risk of accepted verdicts or guarantees their reliability at a specified level. We propose a risk-controlled framework that calibrates uncertainty thresholds on a held-out set so that the false discovery rate among accepted verdicts remains below a user-specified level~$α$ with high probability, using finite-sample Clopper--Pearson intervals. When the parametric mode is not sufficiently confident, the instance is routed to a retrieval-augmented mode, where the judge gathers web evidence and re-evaluates the instance under a second calibrated threshold. The finite-sample guarantee carries over to this two-threshold routing without additional assumptions. Across open-domain QA benchmarks and judges of varying scales, the framework maintains the target error rate while achieving substantially higher coverage than single-mode baselines.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes a risk-controlled framework for using LLMs as judges that keeps factual-evaluation error rates below a user-specified level while maximizing coverage.
AI.motivation: LLMs are widely used as automatic judges, especially for subjective tasks, but for objective factual tasks reference-free judging is unreliable: parametric knowledge can hallucinate and tool-augmented approaches are costly and lack formal error guarantees. There is a need for a systematic way to control the risk (false positives) of LLM verdicts while still evaluating at scale.
AI.method: They design a two-stage, risk-controlled judging framework. First, they calibrate confidence/uncertainty thresholds on a held-out dataset using finite-sample Clopper–Pearson intervals so that the false discovery rate (FDR) among accepted verdicts stays below a user-specified level α with high probability. Instances are initially evaluated in a parametric mode (judge relies on its own knowledge); if the judged confidence is below the first calibrated threshold, the instance is routed to a retrieval-augmented mode. In this second mode, the judge queries the web or external tools, gathers supporting evidence, and re-evaluates the instance under a second calibrated threshold. The statistical analysis shows that the finite-sample FDR guarantee extends to this two-threshold routing without extra assumptions.
AI.result: On open-domain QA benchmarks and using different-scale LLM judges, their framework achieves the target error control (empirical false discovery rate at or below the chosen α) while covering a larger fraction of instances than single-mode baselines (only parametric or only retrieval-augmented). This demonstrates that combining calibrated thresholds with selective tool use improves the trade-off between reliability and coverage.
AI.conclusion: A calibrated, two-mode LLM judging framework with explicit risk control can reliably evaluate factual tasks without reference answers, keeping error rates below a desired level while still handling many examples. The work shows that formal statistical guarantees (via Clopper–Pearson intervals and FDR control) can be practically integrated with LLM-based evaluation pipelines, and that routing from parametric to retrieval-augmented judging is both feasible and beneficial under these guarantees.

title: Accuracy and Robustness of Model Cascades Under Data Perturbations
summary: Prediction cascades significantly reduce energy consumption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models while maintaining high predictive performance. The idea is that easy inputs are routed through a lightweight small model, and difficult uncertain cases are deferred to a larger model. While this design can improve computational efficiency on clean data, its effectiveness depends on the reliability of confidence-based routing. Input degradations, such as static corruptions and sequential perturbations, can shift model confidence and routing decisions. In this paper, we study confidence-based cascade frameworks for image classification and investigate how such degradations affect their confidence-based deferral behavior. We select a model cascade at the pareto-optimum of accuracy, routing quality, and energy consumption that achieves competitive predictive performance with an up to 10-fold decrease in CO$_2$ emissions. We study the behavior of that model cascade under input corruptions and analyze how the cascade's routing decisions change when the input distribution shifts. Our analysis identifies three failure modes. Static corruptions either (1) break the routing signal while the large model remains useful, or (2) degrade both models so deferral no longer recovers accuracy. Sequential perturbations reveal a third mode: predictions stabilize but deferral suppresses, yielding stable but unreliable predictions. These findings demonstrate that energy efficient model cascades require evaluation beyond clean accuracy, with explicit attention to routing reliability under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how confidence-based prediction cascades for image classification behave under input degradations and distribution shifts, showing they can fail in multiple ways and must be evaluated beyond clean accuracy.
AI.motivation: Prediction cascades can cut energy use by routing easy inputs to a small model and only sending hard cases to a large model, but this depends on reliable confidence-based routing. Real-world data are often degraded or shifted (corruptions, temporal perturbations), which can distort confidence and routing. The authors want to understand whether cascades remain accurate, energy-efficient, and reliable under such imperfect conditions, and to expose hidden failure modes that are not visible when evaluating only on clean data.
AI.method: They build confidence-based model cascades for image classification where a lightweight model handles easy inputs and defers uncertain ones to a larger model. They select a cascade operating at a Pareto-optimal trade-off among accuracy, routing quality, and energy/CO2 usage. They then systematically apply two types of distribution shifts: (1) static image corruptions and (2) sequential perturbations of inputs. For each setting, they analyze routing decisions, confidence, and accuracy of both models to characterize how the cascade’s deferral behavior changes and where it breaks down.
AI.result: They identify three characteristic failure modes under degraded inputs. For static corruptions, (1) the routing signal can collapse so the small model misroutes cases even though the large model would still be accurate, and (2) both small and large models can be degraded to the point that deferring no longer recovers accuracy. Under sequential perturbations, they find a third mode where predictions become temporally stable but the cascade stops deferring, yielding apparently stable yet systematically unreliable predictions. Despite achieving up to a 10× reduction in CO2 emissions on clean data, the cascade’s benefits and reliability deteriorate under these shifts.
AI.conclusion: Energy-efficient prediction cascades cannot be judged solely by clean accuracy or nominal routing statistics. Their reliability hinges on how well confidence-based routing behaves under distribution shift and input degradation. Static and sequential perturbations expose distinct, practically important failure modes that can undermine both accuracy and the intended efficiency-accuracy trade-off. Robust deployment thus requires evaluating and likely redesigning routing mechanisms with explicit attention to their behavior under corrupted and shifted inputs.

title: The IOL-AI Challenge: An Open Challenge towards Advancing Linguistic Reasoning
summary: Reasoning in LLMs is overwhelmingly studied in domains that provide a model with rules: mathematics and code. Linguistic puzzles invert this: the solver must first discover the system before reasoning within it. We present the IOL-AI Challenge, an open-science competition run on the unseen problems of the International Linguistics Olympiad (IOL) 2026 Individual Contest, evaluated both automatically and, for the first time, by members of the official IOL Jury under the same rubrics applied to human contestants. The challenge drew 731 submissions from 46 teams under a strict compute budget (one T4, 30 mins). We additionally benchmark 15 unconstrained frontier and open models, with Claude Opus 4.8 earning a jury score equivalent to a gold medal, while both resource-constrained systems we submitted for jury grading scored in the range of the bottom 5% of contestants. Capability was not determined by scale: 14B submissions outperform models twice their size, and gains come from decoding and output-handling rather than model capacity. We also found that automatic metrics rank systems exactly as the jury does, but compress the scale, upscoring weak systems by ~13 points and understating strong ones. Our analysis shows that while frontier models might have prior knowledge about some of the problem languages, it does not significantly help them solve the linguistic reasoning tasks, leaving linguistic reasoning as a strong benchmarking proxy for generalizable reasoning skills.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the IOL-AI Challenge, using International Linguistics Olympiad problems to benchmark LLMs on discovering and reasoning over unknown linguistic systems, and analyzes how different models and evaluation methods perform.
AI.motivation: Most LLM reasoning research focuses on domains with explicit rules (math, code). The authors want a benchmark where the model must infer the rules themselves, to better test generalizable reasoning. Linguistic Olympiad puzzles are ideal because they require discovering an underlying linguistic system before applying it. They also aim to create a rigorous, human-aligned evaluation using the official IOL Jury and to understand how compute limits and model scale affect performance.
AI.method: They organized the IOL-AI Challenge around the unseen 2026 IOL Individual Contest problems. Teams (46 teams, 731 submissions) had to solve these under a strict compute budget (one T4 GPU, 30 minutes). Systems were evaluated automatically and also manually by official IOL Jury members using the same rubrics as for human contestants. The authors additionally benchmarked 15 unconstrained frontier and open-source models, compared constrained vs unconstrained settings, and analyzed correlations between automatic metrics and jury scores, as well as the impact of model scale, decoding strategies, and potential prior knowledge of problem languages.
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.8 reached a jury score comparable to a human gold medalist, while the resource-limited systems graded by the jury performed in the bottom 5% of human contestants. Performance did not monotonically follow model size: some 14B-parameter models outperformed larger ones. Improvements were largely due to decoding and output-handling strategies rather than raw model capacity. Automatic evaluation metrics reproduced the jury ranking order but compressed the score range, overestimating weak systems by about 13 points and underestimating strong ones. Prior knowledge of the languages used in the problems provided little advantage on the reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic Olympiad puzzles, which require discovering unknown linguistic systems and then reasoning within them, form a powerful benchmark for testing generalizable reasoning in LLMs beyond math and code. Frontier models can reach human gold-medal performance, but under realistic compute limits, current systems remain far below strong human contestants. Model scale alone is not the key driver of success; decoding and output-handling choices matter substantially. Automatic metrics can stand in for human grading in terms of ranking, but they distort score magnitudes. Overall, linguistic reasoning emerges as a robust, scalable proxy for evaluating broader reasoning abilities in LLMs.

title: Beyond Suspicious Steps: Ontological Trust in Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon agents increasingly operate across many steps, tools, and observa- tions. In this setting, the relevant oversight question is not only whether each action is locally valid, but whether the evolving trajectory still corresponds to the task the user authorized. Drift can accumulate quietly: an agent may call the right tool with plausible arguments at every step, while its prefix moves toward a broader role, an adjacent objective, or evidence the user never supplied. Existing monitors mostly check local compliance, deliver final-trace verdicts, or score generic risk; they do not directly estimate this prefix-level relation. We introduce ontological trust, a task-conditioned property of trajectory prefixes, and instantiate it as RGE, an online monitor that decomposes trust along Role, Goal, and Evidence. RGE uses LLMs only to derive structured task and step representations; trust-state updates, projec- tions, and intervention decisions are deterministic, so the output is a replayable and auditable trust trajectory rather than a single end-to-end judge verdict. We construct a cross-domain trajectory corpus from OSWorld, FinanceBench, and EICU-AC, covering benign executions, prefix-paired drift, and pseudo-consistency failures.
