On this corpus, RGE outperforms adapted rule-, judge-, and shield-style baselines on prefix-paired drift detection. With the two larger estimator models, it exceeds 93% Drift F1 on every benchmark while keeping benign coverage at or above 95.8%. Pseudo-consistency is harder: detection depends on whether task completion is externally visible, a structural limit we characterize empirically.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces ontological trust and RGE, a monitor for long-horizon agents that tracks whether an agent's trajectory remains aligned with the user-authorized task, detecting drift at the prefix level.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents act through many steps and tools, where each individual action may look valid but the overall trajectory can drift away from the user-authorized task. Existing monitoring focuses on local checks or final-trace assessments and fails to capture evolving task drift along the trajectory.
AI.method: Define ontological trust as a task-conditioned property of trajectory prefixes and implement it via RGE, which decomposes trust into Role, Goal, and Evidence dimensions. RGE uses LLMs only to build structured representations of tasks and steps; the subsequent trust-state updates, projections, and intervention decisions are done deterministically to yield a replayable, auditable trust trajectory.
AI.result: The authors build a cross-domain trajectory corpus using OSWorld, FinanceBench, and EICU-AC, containing benign runs, prefix-paired drift, and pseudo-consistency failures. On drift detection, RGE outperforms adapted rule-based, judge-style, and shield-style baselines, achieving over 93% Drift F1 on all benchmarks while maintaining at least 95.8% coverage on benign traces. Pseudo-consistency failures are more difficult and detection performance varies based on whether task completion is externally observable.
AI.conclusion: RGE provides a structured, auditable way to monitor long-horizon agents for task drift at the prefix level via ontological trust over Role, Goal, and Evidence. It improves drift detection over baselines but faces inherent limits on pseudo-consistency detection, especially when task completion lacks clear external signatures.

title: Chain-of-Experience for Continual LLM Improvement
comment: H.T. and Y.F. contributed to this work equally
summary: Humans continuously learn from experience, whereas conventional large language model (LLM) evaluations ignore the models' ability to improve through inference-time interaction. In this paper, we study how LLMs learn from iterative experience at test time, a setting we refer to as Chain-of-Experience (CoE), where models accumulate experiential traces through iterative interactions with self or environmental feedback to form a continual improvement loop beyond zero-shot inference. We instantiate CoE with diverse feedback mechanisms, including model self-feedback and environmental signals such as correctness or public coding test pass rates, and evaluate across math, coding, and knowledge domains using 8 LLMs, including GPT-5, Gemini-2.5 Pro, Claude-4.5 Sonnet. Our study shows that leveraging iterative experience consistently outperforms feedback-free baselines, achieving substantial gains with self feedback alone, alongside a 5.6% overall improvement and 19% lower API cost across tasks and models. We further show that combining complementary feedback channels (e.g., model and correctness signals) yields additional gains, and that CoE delivers higher accuracy per token than existing test-time strategies. We observe a positive correlation between LLM base ability and improvement capacity, and show that models remain robust under weak or spurious feedback, with different feedback contributing to distinct improvement aspects and most gains emerging early in the iterations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates Chain-of-Experience (CoE), a test-time learning framework where LLMs iteratively improve by accumulating and using feedback from prior interactions.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM evaluation treats models as static zero- or few-shot predictors and ignores their capacity to learn from ongoing interaction and feedback at inference time. The authors aim to understand and quantify how much LLMs can improve performance by leveraging iterative experience, similar to how humans learn, rather than only relying on pretraining and fine-tuning.
AI.method: They define Chain-of-Experience (CoE), where an LLM interacts over multiple iterations on tasks while collecting experiential traces (e.g., its prior answers, feedback, and performance signals) and using them as additional context in subsequent attempts. They instantiate CoE with several feedback mechanisms, including self-generated feedback (the model critiques or refines its own outputs) and external environmental feedback such as correctness labels and public coding test pass rates. They test multiple variants and combinations of these feedback channels. Experiments are run on math, coding, and knowledge benchmarks using 8 different LLMs (e.g., GPT-5, Gemini-2.5 Pro, Claude-4.5 Sonnet). They compare CoE to feedback-free baselines and to other test-time strategies, and analyze how performance and cost evolve over iterations, how base model strength affects gains, and how robust the method is to weak or noisy feedback.
AI.result: Across domains and models, CoE consistently improves performance relative to feedback-free baselines. Even using only self-feedback yields substantial gains. Overall, CoE delivers an average 5.6% performance improvement and 19% reduction in API cost compared to baselines, and achieves higher accuracy per token than existing test-time methods. Combining complementary feedback sources (e.g., self-feedback plus correctness signals) leads to further gains. The experiments also reveal that stronger base models tend to benefit more from CoE, and that most performance improvements occur in the earlier iterations.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time, experience-based learning via CoE is an effective and efficient way to boost LLM performance without retraining, enabling continual improvement over iterative interactions. The approach is robust even under weak or partially misleading feedback, different feedback types contribute to different aspects of improvement, and gains largely materialize early in the interaction process. This suggests that future LLM evaluation and deployment should explicitly consider and exploit test-time learning from experience rather than treating models as static predictors.

title: Evaluating the Diversity of AI-Generated Content with Diversity Profiles
summary: Diversity is a fundamental criterion for evaluating generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems, yet its measurement remains inherently ambiguous. Existing approaches typically represent generated samples in an embedding space, compute pairwise distances or similarities, and aggregate them into a single scalar score. Such scalar summaries are convenient, but they often encode different inductive biases and may yield contradictory rankings of the same sample sets. In this paper, we argue that diversity evaluation for AI-generated content is intrinsically under-specified when reduced to a single number. We first review representative diversity metrics, and then diagnose their limitations from two complementary perspectives: an axiomatic analysis showing that no representative scalar metric satisfies all desirable properties simultaneously, and an empirical analysis showing that high-dimensional representation spaces can induce concentrated, modality-dependent distance distributions. To address these issues, we propose diversity profiles: curve-valued, condition-aware summaries that evaluate a parameterized diversity family across a range of thresholds, scales, exponents, or orders under a specified representation and distance or kernel function. Diversity profiles reveal whether a comparison is robust across resolutions or instead depends on an arbitrary parameter choice. We instantiate profiles for several representative metric families and demonstrate their practical use in generative AI evaluation. Overall, diversity profiles provide a more transparent and resolution-aware framework for comparing the diversity of AI-generated content.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that diversity in generative AI cannot be meaningfully reduced to a single scalar metric and proposes ‘diversity profiles’—curve-valued summaries over parameter ranges—as a more transparent, robust way to compare diversity.
AI.motivation: Diversity is a key quality dimension for generative AI outputs, but current evaluation practices compress complex distributional information into a single scalar derived from distances in an embedding space. Different scalar metrics embed different inductive biases and can rank the same sample sets inconsistently, while high-dimensional representations further distort distance distributions. This ambiguity and inconsistency motivate a more expressive and diagnostically rich framework for assessing diversity.
AI.method: The authors first survey existing diversity metrics and conduct an axiomatic analysis to show that no common scalar metric can satisfy all reasonable, desirable properties at once. They complement this with an empirical study of distance distributions in high-dimensional representation spaces, revealing concentration and modality-dependent effects that undermine simple scalar summaries. To address these issues, they introduce diversity profiles: for a chosen representation and distance/kernel, they evaluate a whole parametric family of diversity measures across a continuum of thresholds, scales, exponents, or orders, yielding curve-valued, condition-aware summaries rather than single numbers. They instantiate these profiles for several representative metric families and show how they can be computed and visualized in practice.
AI.result: The analyses demonstrate (1) theoretical incompatibilities between desirable axioms for scalar diversity metrics and (2) empirical artifacts in high-dimensional distance distributions that can mislead scalar-based comparisons. The proposed diversity profiles successfully expose when comparisons between sample sets are stable across parameter choices versus when they flip depending on thresholds or scale parameters. Case studies with generative AI systems show that profiles can differentiate systems in a way that makes the dependence on representation, metric family, and parameterization explicit.
AI.conclusion: Scalar diversity scores are fundamentally under-specified and can be misleading for evaluating generative AI systems, due to conflicting axiomatic requirements and distortions in high-dimensional representation spaces. Diversity profiles, which chart metric families over parameter ranges under fixed representational conditions, offer a more transparent, resolution-aware, and diagnostically robust framework. They help practitioners see whether diversity judgments are stable or parameter-sensitive, improving the interpretability and reliability of diversity evaluation in generative AI.

title: Language Has Two Parameters: Narrative-Induced Semantic Plasticity and Phase-Sensitive Interpretation
summary: Language has two parameters. Count how often words occur together and you estimate amplitude, the strength of association. Word embeddings and attention weights refine that count, which sums every writer in the corpus together. This paper claims a second parameter, phase, which signed weights learned from a corpus do not supply. Phase exists only between meanings: it determines how coactivated meanings combine, and it can reverse what a meaning contributes while that meaning stays fully present. A speaker can set phase in the signal through linguistic form; encounters install phase relations and history distributes them. Population averaging deletes history-indexed phase: agent-deindexed corpora identify the population marginal state and determine no individual or dyadic state, at any scale. The standard transformer has no explicit representation for phase in frozen inference, and the interpretability program measuring progress by monosemanticity is optimizing against it: the coexistence it treats as a defect is the condition of allusion, irony, and quotation. Six predictions test whether a suppressed meaning stays active, whether encounter order changes what a phrase does, whether marking the signal changes how a shared phrase is taken, and whether a model given a history is changed by it or only informed about it. The claim defended is the weak version: interpretation requires a second relational parameter, signed, persistent, and indexed to individuals and dyads. Quantum probability is one notation for the parameter; nothing in the formalism claims quantum processes in the brain. The strong version, that the quantum calculus constrains these phenomena as signed classical models do not, rests on an encounter-order constraint not yet derived. The architecture the theory calls for is a language model with agent-indexed, phase-bearing semantic states.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current language models capture only one parameter of meaning (amplitude/association strength) and miss a crucial second parameter (phase), which encodes how multiple meanings interact for phenomena like irony and allusion.
AI.motivation: Existing distributional semantics and transformer-based models represent meaning via co-occurrence statistics and signed weights, effectively capturing how strongly words and senses are associated (amplitude). However, these models struggle with context-dependent interpretive phenomena such as irony, quotation, allusion, and meaning reversals that depend on speaker history, encounter order, and interpersonal relationships. The author is motivated to explain these failures and to propose a theoretical parameter that can model how simultaneously active meanings combine and sometimes invert their contribution without disappearing.
AI.method: Conceptual and theoretical analysis: (1) Distinguish amplitude (association strength) from a proposed second parameter, phase, defined relationally between meanings. (2) Argue that standard embeddings, attention weights, and transformer architectures—especially when trained on agent-deindexed corpora—cannot represent history- and agent-indexed phase. (3) Relate phase to quantum probability formalism as a convenient notation, while explicitly avoiding claims about physical quantum processes in the brain. (4) Formulate six empirical predictions about suppressed-but-active meanings, encounter-order effects, signal-marking effects, and how models should change when given histories rather than merely being informed about them. (5) Sketch an architecture for language models with agent-indexed, phase-bearing semantic states.
AI.result: The abstract does not report empirical or quantitative results. Instead, it claims: (a) that existing models only encode amplitude, not phase; (b) that population-averaged, agent-deindexed corpora necessarily erase individual- and dyad-specific phase information; (c) that the standard transformer has no explicit representation of phase during frozen inference; and (d) that interpretability efforts focused on monosemanticity are at odds with the coexistence of multiple phase-related meanings needed for irony, allusion, and quotation. It proposes testable predictions to evaluate the theory but does not present tests or outcomes here.
AI.conclusion: Meaning interpretation requires a second, relational semantic parameter—phase—that is signed, persistent, and indexed to individuals and dyads, in addition to amplitude. This phase governs how coactivated meanings combine and can reverse their contributions without removing them. Standard transformer architectures and current interpretability goals are structurally misaligned with this requirement. A more adequate language model architecture would maintain agent-indexed, phase-bearing semantic states, and quantum probability offers a formalism to express this, though it does not imply that cognition is physically quantum. A stronger claim that quantum calculus uniquely constrains these phenomena is left for future work pending a derivation of an encounter-order constraint.

title: Neuro-symbolic learning over OWL 2 DL via consequence-based compilation to differentiable circuits
summary: OWL 2 DL ontologies, grounded in the description logic $\mathcal{SROIQ}$, express large knowledge bases in biomedicine and the Semantic Web. Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) learners over description logics either embed the ontology in a continuous space, abandoning classical entailment, or restrict to the Horn fragment $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$, which has a single canonical model. We present Baobab, which compiles a $\mathcal{SROIQ}$ ontology with a finite ABox into a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD): it saturates a propositional core under a consequence-based calculus and instantiates the remaining $\mathcal{SROIQ}$ features (nominals, number restrictions, and the role axioms) over the active domain. The SDD's evidence-conditioned weighted model count then trains a perception network to recognize real images under partial ABox supervision: on an ontology that exercises every distinctive $\mathcal{SROIQ}$ feature, a CNN learns to read MNIST digits coupled by a successor relation and recovers latent ontology concepts that an independent perception leaves at chance. When the supervision admits several ontology-consistent completions, an independent perception collapses onto one, a reasoning shortcut: we show that a mixture indexed by the query's justifications can represent the calibrated posterior no independent perception can, and that seeding it from the circuit's enumerated completions attains the Bayes-optimal posterior on a real-image MNIST task where single-WMC and learned mixtures (the BEARS-ensemble hypothesis class) do not: to our knowledge the first to characterize and mitigate reasoning shortcuts in a non-Horn description logic. Soundness of the compiler and the representation result are machine-checked in Lean 4. Code is available at https://github.com/bio-ontology-research-group/baobab.

AI.tldr: Baobab compiles expressive OWL 2 DL (SROIQ) ontologies into Sentential Decision Diagrams to enable sound probabilistic neuro-symbolic learning with images, avoiding Horn restrictions and exposing reasoning shortcuts.
AI.motivation: Existing neuro-symbolic learners over description logics either relax logic into continuous embeddings and lose classical entailment guarantees, or restrict to the Horn fragment EL++ which is far less expressive than full OWL 2 DL/SROIQ. This limits the use of rich biomedical and Semantic Web ontologies, particularly those using nominals, number restrictions, and complex role axioms. Moreover, current approaches suffer from reasoning shortcuts where perception models latch onto one ontology-consistent completion instead of representing full calibrated posteriors when supervision is partial or ambiguous. The paper aims to support full SROIQ reasoning in a neuro-symbolic setting while characterizing and mitigating such shortcuts.
AI.method: The authors introduce Baobab, a compiler from SROIQ ontologies with finite ABoxes into Sentential Decision Diagrams (SDDs). They first saturate a propositional core of the ontology using a consequence-based calculus, then instantiate remaining SROIQ features (nominals, number restrictions, role axioms) over the active domain, yielding a propositional theory compiled into an SDD. They use weighted model counting (WMC) on the SDD, conditioned on observed evidence, as a differentiable objective to train a perception network (e.g., CNN on MNIST images) under partial ABox supervision. To address reasoning shortcuts under supervision with multiple ontology-consistent completions, they define mixture models indexed by logical justifications of queries: mixtures over completions enumerated from the circuit, and show these can represent the Bayes-optimal posterior that independent perception models cannot. They machine-check the soundness of the compiler and representation results in Lean 4, and run experiments on MNIST digits linked via successor relations and SROIQ constructs, comparing against single-WMC and learned mixture baselines (BEARS-ensemble).
AI.result: Baobab successfully compiles SROIQ ontologies with all distinctive features (nominals, number restrictions, role axioms) into SDDs and supports evidence-conditioned WMC for training perception networks. On a constructed ontology over MNIST digits with successor relations, a CNN trained with Baobab recovers latent ontology concepts that a purely perceptual baseline leaves at chance level. In settings where supervision is ambiguous and multiple ontology-consistent completions exist, independent perception collapses onto one completion, exhibiting reasoning shortcuts. The proposed justification-indexed mixture model, initialized using completions enumerated from the SDD, achieves a calibrated, Bayes-optimal posterior on a real-image MNIST task. This outperforms single-WMC approaches and learned mixture baselines (BEARS-ensemble) that fail to match the true posterior.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that full SROIQ (OWL 2 DL) ontologies can be compiled into tractable probabilistic circuits (SDDs) to support sound neuro-symbolic learning, without restricting to Horn fragments or abandoning classical entailment. By using evidence-conditioned WMC and justification-indexed mixtures over ontology-consistent completions, Baobab both exposes and mitigates reasoning shortcuts that arise with independent perception under partial supervision, achieving Bayes-optimal inference on challenging MNIST tasks. The approach is formally verified in Lean 4, and the released implementation provides a practical tool for neuro-symbolic learning with expressive ontologies in domains like biomedicine and the Semantic Web.

title: TokEval: A Tokenizer Evaluation Suite
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026; Library hosted at https://github.com/cimeister/tokenizer-intrinsic-evals
summary: Language model tokenizers are typically selected with minimal evaluation, despite the fact that their design choices directly impact model capabilities. This can be partly attributed to a limited understanding of which tokenizer properties affect which aspects of downstream performance. We introduce TokEval, a framework of tokenizer evaluation metrics that goes beyond standard measures like fertility and compression rate to capture linguistically and structurally meaningful properties, e.g., UTF-8 character boundary integrity and digit place-value boundary alignment for mathematics. To validate whether these metrics are predictive of downstream model performance, we conduct controlled language model pretraining experiments, varying solely the tokenizers' training data mixture, pretokenization strategy, and training algorithm. We evaluate the resulting models on bits-per-byte (a tokenizer-agnostic version of perplexity) and several benchmarks, spanning linguistic understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Our experiments suggest that different intrinsic properties have different impacts on model abilities: information-theoretic metrics predict language modeling abilities (Spearman rho up to 0.80), while structure-sensitive metrics, such as those measuring digit and line-break handling, correlate with task accuracy. We hope TokEval enables more principled tokenizer evaluation, replacing pretraining sweeps with intrinsic measurement wherever the two agree.

AI.tldr: TokEval proposes intrinsic tokenizer evaluation metrics and shows they predict different aspects of downstream LM performance, enabling more principled tokenizer choice without full pretraining sweeps.
AI.motivation: Tokenizer choice strongly affects language model capabilities, but practitioners typically select tokenizers with little systematic evaluation because it is unclear which tokenizer properties influence which downstream behaviors. Existing simple metrics like fertility and compression rate miss many linguistically and structurally relevant aspects of tokenization, leaving a gap in principled tokenizer design and selection.
AI.method: The authors design TokEval, a suite of tokenizer evaluation metrics that extend beyond standard information-theoretic measures to include linguistically and structurally meaningful properties (e.g., respecting UTF-8 character boundaries and aligning tokens with digit place values or line breaks). They then run controlled language model pretraining experiments where they vary only tokenizer-related factors—training data mixture, pretokenization, and training algorithm—while holding the rest of the LM setup fixed. They evaluate the resulting models using bits-per-byte (a tokenizer-agnostic perplexity metric) and performance on diverse downstream benchmarks covering language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. They compute correlations (e.g., Spearman rho) between TokEval metrics and downstream performance to assess predictive power.
AI.result: Intrinsic information-theoretic TokEval metrics (like compression-related statistics) correlate strongly with general language modeling quality, achieving Spearman correlations up to 0.80 with bits-per-byte. Meanwhile, structure-aware metrics targeting things like digit tokenization and line-break handling show meaningful correlations with accuracy on tasks that rely on those structures, such as math and code. Different classes of metrics thus map onto different capability dimensions, indicating that tokenizer properties are differentially predictive of specific downstream skills.
AI.conclusion: TokEval provides a more comprehensive and diagnostic way to evaluate tokenizers, capturing both information-theoretic and structural/linguistic properties. The study shows that some intrinsic tokenizer metrics are strongly predictive of downstream language modeling and task performance, suggesting that practitioners can often select or refine tokenizers via intrinsic evaluation rather than expensive pretraining sweeps, at least in regimes where intrinsic and downstream metrics agree.

title: The Curious Case of Exploding DecPOMDPs: Containing the Fire through Policy Counting
comment: Full version including appendix of a paper accepted at the 17th International Conference on Scalable Uncertainty Management (SUM2026) under the same name
summary: Decentralised partially observable Markov decision processes (DecPOMDPs) provide a general framework for modelling multi-agent decision making under uncertainty. However, DecPOMDPs are known to suffer from exponential complexity in the number of agents. One way to combat this intractability in agent numbers is to look at partitions of agents that exhibit a form of symmetry among agents, allowing for a compact encoding by counting. However, a challenge arises as the policy space explodes, even though the model complexity and evaluation cost reduce to a polynomial dependence. In this paper, we redirect our focus from counting agents to counting policies, which actually enables tractability in agent numbers for so called policy-counted DecPOMDPs. Further, we present policy-counted dynamic programming using the compact representation to solve policy-counted DecPOMDPs efficiently.

AI.tldr: They propose a new way to exploit symmetry in multi‑agent DecPOMDPs by counting policies instead of agents, leading to tractable planning in the number of agents and an efficient dynamic programming algorithm.
AI.motivation: DecPOMDPs are a powerful but intractable framework for multi‑agent decision making because complexity grows exponentially with the number of agents. Existing symmetry-based methods reduce model size by grouping and counting similar agents, but the policy space still explodes, preventing true scalability. The paper is motivated by the need for an approach that remains tractable as the number of agents grows, not just in model representation but also in policy search.
AI.method: They introduce the notion of policy-counted DecPOMDPs, where the state and decision process are represented in terms of counts of distinct policies rather than counts of individual agents. Building on this representation, they develop a policy-counted dynamic programming algorithm that operates over these compact policy-count statistics, achieving polynomial dependence on the number of agents while still computing optimal or high-quality joint policies.
AI.result: The authors show theoretically that representing DecPOMDPs by counting policies instead of agents yields tractability in the number of agents for the defined class of policy-counted DecPOMDPs. They provide an efficient dynamic programming procedure whose computational complexity depends polynomially on the number of agents, overcoming the traditional exponential blowup, while preserving the benefits of DecPOMDP modelling under uncertainty and partial observability.
AI.conclusion: By shifting from agent-counted to policy-counted representations, the paper demonstrates that one can make certain DecPOMDPs tractable in the number of agents. The proposed policy-counted dynamic programming exploits this compact structure to solve large multi-agent decision problems more efficiently, suggesting a promising direction for scalable multi-agent planning under uncertainty.

title: Multi-Agent AI System for Radiology Report Structuring and Quality Assurance with Independent Radiologist Evaluation
summary: Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. A multi-agent AI pipeline was developed to perform report structuring and quality assurance (QA). The system structured the report into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regex rules and local large language models. It also detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections, or within sections; gender-anatomy conflicts; and undocumented communication of critical findings. Two board-certified radiologists independently evaluated a 45-report subset. Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 (14.1%) reports, most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%). In the radiologist evaluation, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%) were correctly restructured, 2 reports (4%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on the remaining 12 reports (27%). Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" or "good" in 84% of the evaluated reports, with the remaining reports rated as "fair". Conclusion: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow. The system demonstrated favorable performance in radiologist evaluation. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice.

AI.tldr: They developed and tested a local multi-agent AI system that automatically structures radiology reports and performs quality checks, showing good performance and no clinically relevant errors in a subset review.
AI.motivation: Radiology reports are often unstructured and variable in format, which can make them harder to read, search, and analyze. Quality issues such as inconsistencies between Findings and Impression, gender-anatomy errors, or missing documentation of communicated critical results may go unnoticed in busy clinical workflows. There is a need for automated, locally deployable tools that can both standardize report structure and assist with quality assurance without altering clinical content or creating hallucinations.
AI.method: The authors performed a retrospective study on 638 CT chest/abdomen/pelvis reports from 15 board-certified radiologists. They built a locally deployed multi-agent AI pipeline that combines rule-based (regex) components with local large language models. The system: (1) parsed and restructured the Findings section into standardized anatomical subsections at the sentence level, preserving original wording; and (2) ran several QA checks, including detection of mismatches between Findings and Impression or within sections, gender–anatomy conflicts, and missing documentation of critical results communication. Two radiologists independently reviewed a subset of 45 flagged reports, judging restructuring correctness, presence of omissions or hallucinations, and overall QA performance.
AI.result: The system successfully structured all 22,270 sentences from the Findings sections of the 638 reports into the predefined anatomical format while preserving original content. It flagged 90 reports (14.1%) for potential quality issues, predominantly section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%). In the 45-report subset review, both radiologists agreed that 31 reports (69%) were correctly restructured and 2 (4%) incorrectly restructured, with disagreement in 12 (27%). They agreed that no clinically relevant information was omitted and no fabricated content was added. Overall QA utility was rated as "excellent" or "good" in 84% of the evaluated reports, with the remainder rated as "fair."
AI.conclusion: The study shows that a locally deployed multi-agent AI pipeline can simultaneously standardize the structure of radiology reports and provide automated quality assurance checks within one workflow. The system performed well in expert evaluation, introducing no clinically important omissions or hallucinations in the tested subset. Such an approach has potential to improve consistency of reporting and to support routine QA processes in radiology departments, especially when deployed on local infrastructure that addresses data privacy and integration concerns.

title: D$^2$ACCI: A Dual-Loop Diagnostic Protocol for Evidence-Preserving Agent Memory
summary: Memory is a key capability of LLM agents. Persistent memory extends this across sessions---enabling recall, revision, and personalization. Yet its multi-stage pipeline (ingestion, retrieval, filtering, generation) makes failures difficult to localize: end-to-end evaluation reveals that an error occurred, but not which stage caused it. Existing evaluations often report aggregate performance without paired statistical comparisons, slice-level non-regression checks, or stage-level diagnostic traces. We propose D$^2$ACCI (Diagnostic-Driven Artifact-based Closed-loop Controlled Iteration), a dual-loop protocol whose outer diagnostic gate promotes, feature-flags, or rejects memory interventions based on paired evidence, protected-slice monitoring, and trace-level localizability. We further introduce DCR, a graded observability metric that measures whether failures remain localizable, and D$^2$ACCI-Eval, a reusable artifact for gate replay. We instantiate the protocol in MemStack and evaluate on three public benchmarks, achieving 93.59% on LoCoMo, 90.93% on LongMemEval, and 57.20% on PersonaMem-V2. Five paired ablations show that supplement extraction, session-memory retrieval, and Forget Guard yield statistically significant gains (+1.9 to +3.7pp, all p $\le$ .003). In contrast, BM25/RRF is retained as a monitored feature flag---a distinction invisible to aggregate-only evaluation. A diagnostic audit shows enriched traces substantially improve root-cause agreement over result-only relabeling. Diagnostic artifacts reach 98--100% DCR@3 versus 0% for results-only logs. These results establish that robust memory-system iteration demands traceable, statistically grounded, and regression-aware evidence---exactly the gap D$^2$ACCI fills.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces D^2ACCI, a diagnostic protocol for evaluating and iterating LLM memory systems, emphasizing traceable, statistically grounded, and regression-aware evaluation, and demonstrates its effectiveness on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents rely heavily on memory, especially persistent memory across sessions, but the multi-stage pipeline (ingestion, retrieval, filtering, generation) makes it hard to pinpoint where failures occur. Existing evaluations are mostly aggregate, lack paired statistical tests, do not protect specific data slices from regression, and provide little stage-level diagnostic information. This creates a gap for reliable, interpretable, and safe iteration on memory systems.
AI.method: The authors propose D^2ACCI (Diagnostic-Driven Artifact-based Closed-loop Controlled Iteration), a dual-loop evaluation and iteration protocol. An outer diagnostic gate decides whether to promote, feature-flag, or reject memory-related interventions based on (1) paired comparisons, (2) protected-slice monitoring, and (3) trace-level diagnostic artifacts that allow localization of errors to specific stages. They also define DCR, an observability metric quantifying how localizable failures are, and D^2ACCI-Eval, a reusable artifact that allows replaying evaluation traces. They instantiate this framework in a memory system called MemStack and perform controlled ablations on its components (e.g., supplement extraction, retrieval variants, Forget Guard, BM25/RRF) with statistical testing and trace analysis.
AI.result: Using the D^2ACCI protocol with MemStack, they achieve strong performance on three public benchmarks: 93.59% on LoCoMo, 90.93% on LongMemEval, and 57.20% on PersonaMem-V2. Paired ablation experiments show that several components, such as supplement extraction, session-memory retrieval, and Forget Guard, deliver statistically significant performance improvements of +1.9 to +3.7 percentage points (p ≤ .003). BM25/RRF retrieval, however, does not show clear benefits in aggregate and is therefore retained only as a monitored feature flag, illustrating that trace-based diagnostics expose distinctions invisible in aggregate metrics. Diagnostic audits reveal that enriched traces greatly improve agreement on root-cause attribution compared with result-only relabeling, and diagnostic artifacts achieve 98–100% DCR@3 versus 0% for results-only logs, demonstrating substantially better failure localizability.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that iterating on LLM memory systems in a robust and safe manner requires evaluation that is traceable, statistically grounded, and regression-aware, rather than relying solely on aggregate, end-to-end metrics. D^2ACCI provides a concrete protocol and artifacts to meet these needs, improving both performance and diagnostic power. The high DCR scores and the ability to distinguish useful from non-useful interventions (like BM25/RRF) show that diagnostic-driven iteration is essential for advancing persistent-memory pipelines in LLM agents.

title: Grounding Healthcare LLMs in a Causal Knowledge Graph: Framework, Metrics, and a Cardiovascular Pilot
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for healthcare decision support, but their evaluations still reward single-answer accuracy rather than reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. We propose a reproducible, graph-centered evaluation framework for intervention-oriented LLM behavior in healthcare and stress-test it in a cardiovascular pilot. The framework has four components: (i) a domain causal knowledge graph in which assertions are first-class, provenance-preserving nodes with stable identifiers; (ii) a scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction step that, given any clinical scenario, retrieves the relevant reified-assertion subgraph; (iii) four controlled grounding conditions that vary how the retrieved subgraph is composed into the model's context (ungrounded C1, knowledge-graph C2, causal-graph C3, integrated C4); and (iv) an automated scoring pipeline, anchored on assertion identifiers, that computes intervention accuracy, and other evaluation measures on a single pass. To test the framework, we built a category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes and instantiated it on a cardiovascular graph. The metric panel discriminates conditions along interpretable, non-redundant axes: C4 obtains the strongest causal edge F1 (0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and unsupported claim rate (0.114), while C1 obtains the highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) with no measurable causal or evidential grounding.

AI.tldr: Proposes and pilots a graph-centered framework to evaluate how LLMs reason about clinical interventions, not just give single best answers.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of LLMs in healthcare focus mostly on single-answer accuracy (e.g., correct diagnosis or treatment) and ignore the quality of underlying reasoning about interventions, causal mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. This is problematic because clinical decisions require understanding of causal structures and evidence, not just point predictions. The authors aim to build a more realistic and reproducible way to probe and compare LLM behavior in this intervention-focused, causally grounded setting.
AI.method: They design a four-part, graph-centered evaluation framework: (i) construct a domain-specific causal knowledge graph where clinical assertions are explicit, provenance-preserving nodes with stable identifiers; (ii) for any given clinical scenario, automatically extract the relevant subgraph of these reified assertions; (iii) define four grounding conditions that differ in how this subgraph is provided to the LLM: C1 with no graph grounding, C2 with a knowledge graph view, C3 with an explicitly causal graph, and C4 with an integrated representation; and (iv) implement an automated scoring pipeline that leverages assertion identifiers to compute intervention accuracy and additional metrics in a single pass. They then build a category-balanced scenario generator spanning eight types of reasoning failures, instantiate the framework on a cardiovascular knowledge graph, and measure LLM performance under each grounding condition.
AI.result: The evaluation metrics clearly distinguish the four grounding conditions along meaningful, non-overlapping dimensions. The integrated condition C4 yields the best performance on causally and evidentially grounded metrics: highest causal edge F1 (0.838), highest adverse-effect F1 (0.833), highest evidence accuracy (0.738), and the lowest rate of unsupported claims (0.114). In contrast, the ungrounded condition C1 achieves the best raw intervention accuracy (0.948) but shows no measurable grounding in causal or evidential structure.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based causal and evidential grounding substantially changes and improves how LLMs reason about clinical interventions, even if raw answer accuracy can appear highest without grounding. The proposed framework offers a reproducible, interpretable way to evaluate intervention-oriented LLM behavior along multiple, non-redundant axes beyond single-answer accuracy. This can better stress-test models in realistic healthcare scenarios and guide the development of systems that reason more safely and transparently about interventions, harms, and evidence.

title: StartupBench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Agents on Market-Validated End-to-End Workflows
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models(LLMs) and agents have substantially improved the ability of AI systems to execute complex tasks. Yet existing benchmarks largely rely on researcher-selected tasks, leaving uncertain whether such progress extends to the work that real-world users actually demand from AI systems. We introduce \textbf{StartupBench}, an E2E agent benchmark grounded in market-validated AI startup products. Rather than defining tasks from pre-defined assumptions about useful agent capabilities, we systematically study AI products with demonstrated adoption, together with their product workflows and users, to identify real-world tasks for which AI has established practical demand across diverse professional domains. We translate these workflows into complete deliverable-oriented tasks and evaluate them with fine-grained rubrics capturing their complex requirements. Across representative models evaluated under a unified agent harness, even the strongest model successfully completes only approximately 30\% of StartupBench, despite making substantial partial progress on many tasks. Further analysis identifies aspects like complex instruction following and domain-specific expertise as major sources of failure. Our results reveal that many market-validated workflows remain beyond the reliable capabilities of current general-purpose agents, establishing StartupBench as an empirical measure of progress toward E2E completions of real-world user tasks.

AI.tldr: StartupBench is a benchmark of end-to-end agent tasks derived from real, market-validated AI startup products, showing that even top LLM agents reliably solve only ~30% of these realistic workflows.
AI.motivation: Most existing LLM/agent benchmarks are based on researcher-curated tasks that may not reflect what real users actually need. As a result, it is unclear whether apparent progress on benchmarks corresponds to genuine progress on solving end-to-end real-world workflows that have proven market demand. The authors want a way to measure how well general-purpose AI agents can execute the kinds of complex, multi-step tasks that successful AI products already perform for users across professional domains.
AI.method: The authors construct StartupBench by first identifying AI startup products that have demonstrated real user adoption (“market-validated”). They then analyze these products’ workflows, the tasks they automate, and their target users, to extract representative, end-to-end tasks with concrete deliverables. These workflows are translated into benchmark tasks with detailed, fine-grained evaluation rubrics designed to capture complex requirements and allow partial credit. Under a unified agent harness, multiple leading LLM-based agents are run on all tasks, and their outputs are graded using the rubrics. The authors further conduct error/failure analysis to categorize where and why agents fail, focusing on patterns such as instruction following and domain-specific reasoning gaps.
AI.result: Across a set of representative state-of-the-art LLM agents evaluated on StartupBench, the strongest model fully and successfully completes only about 30% of tasks. However, models often achieve partial progress, indicating non-trivial ability but insufficient reliability for full end-to-end automation. The detailed rubrics expose systematic weaknesses: agents frequently struggle with following complex, multi-layered instructions and with tasks requiring specialized domain knowledge. These patterns hold across a variety of professional domains represented in the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that despite recent advances, current general-purpose LLM agents are far from reliably executing many real-world workflows that are already validated by the market. StartupBench thus provides a more realistic, end-to-end assessment of agent capabilities and can serve as an empirical yardstick for future progress. The benchmark highlights that closing the gap will require improving complex instruction following, integrating or acquiring deeper domain expertise, and better handling of multi-step, deliverable-oriented tasks common in real user products.

title: ARASH: Adaptive Retrieval And Shot Selection for Tabular Prediction
summary: Tabular prediction is a critical task across numerous applications. The recent success of large language models has sparked various approaches for adapting them to the tabular domain. A prevalent strategy involves training or fine-tuning specialized Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) such as TabPFN. However, TFMs require substantial computational resources, and frequent model retraining is often impractical. In-context learning (ICL), specifically, few-shot prompting, offers a resource-efficient alternative to enhance performance. Yet, identifying the most relevant rows to serve as shots remains a challenge for tabular data. This paper introduces ARASH (Adaptive, query-specific Retrieval And Shot selection), a method that improves TFM efficiency by selecting optimal shots based on local neighborhood analysis within the training set. Our results demonstrate that ARASH reduces the prompt length and memory usage of TabPFN by 1261.5$\times$ and 2.56$\times$, respectively, while providing comparable accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes ARASH, a query-specific retrieval and shot-selection method that makes Tabular Foundation Models like TabPFN far more efficient while keeping similar accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tabular prediction is important but training or fine-tuning specialized Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) like TabPFN is computationally expensive and often needs retraining. In-context learning with few-shot prompting is cheaper, but it is unclear how to choose the best example rows (shots) for tabular data. There is a need for a principled, efficient way to select informative shots tailored to each query to reduce cost without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: Introduce ARASH (Adaptive, query-specific Retrieval And Shot selection), which selects shots for in-context learning by analyzing the local neighborhood of the query within the training data. For each new query row, ARASH retrieves training rows that are locally most relevant and uses them as few-shot examples in the prompt to a Tabular Foundation Model like TabPFN. This adaptive retrieval and selection mechanism aims to minimize prompt length and memory usage while maintaining predictive performance.
AI.result: When applied to TabPFN, ARASH reduces prompt length by a factor of 1261.5× and memory usage by 2.56× relative to the baseline, yet achieves comparable prediction accuracy. This indicates that many shots in standard prompting are redundant and that carefully chosen local examples suffice.
AI.conclusion: ARASH offers an efficient, query-specific shot selection mechanism for tabular in-context learning that substantially reduces computational and memory costs of Tabular Foundation Models such as TabPFN while retaining similar accuracy. This makes TFMs more practical in resource-constrained and dynamic settings where frequent retraining is infeasible.

title: AutoResearch: Insight In, Hallucination Out
summary: Autonomous research systems are increasingly capable of executing long research workflows, yet automation alone does not ensure that the resulting process remains scientifically grounded. We introduce AutoResearch, a two-stage system that connects Idea Generation with Idea Execution to address both how research ideas are formed and how they are reliably established through experimentation. In Idea Generation, AutoResearch continuously integrates emerging research signals with accumulated domain knowledge, identifies transferable mechanistic insights, and uses multi-model generation and cross-review to produce grounded, testable research plans. In Idea Execution, coordinated agents decompose these plans into experiments, iteratively implement and diagnose them, and employ independent evidence-based review before accepting research conclusions. Across representative settings in cross-modal retrieval, systems optimization, and benchmark-driven machine learning, AutoResearch turns generated ideas into measurable progress, detects and corrects unreliable experimental results, and makes evidence-conditioned decisions to continue, revise, or terminate research directions. For example, on RSICD benchmark, an AutoResearch-generated idea improves mean Recall from 32.84 to 34.69, while recording only 5 audit-confirmed issue events compared with 11-27 for other autonomous research systems. These results demonstrate a research process in which meaningful insight is grounded before experimentation and conclusions are grounded before acceptance: Insight In, Hallucination Out.

AI.tldr: AutoResearch is a two-stage autonomous research system that grounds both idea generation and experimental execution to reduce hallucinations and produce reliable scientific progress.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous research systems can run long, complex workflows, but they often lack mechanisms to ensure that generated ideas are scientifically grounded and that experimental results are trustworthy. This leads to unreliable conclusions and hallucinated progress. The paper aims to design a full-stack research pipeline—spanning from idea formation to experimental verification—that systematically constrains and audits autonomy so that it yields genuine, measurable research advances.
AI.method: The authors propose AutoResearch, a two-stage architecture: (1) Idea Generation: the system continuously integrates new research signals (e.g., recent papers, benchmarks) with stored domain knowledge to identify mechanistic insights that can transfer across problems. It uses multiple models to generate candidate research plans and cross-review them, filtering for grounded, testable hypotheses. (2) Idea Execution: a team of coordinated agents decomposes selected plans into concrete experiments, implements them iteratively, diagnoses failures, and submits results to an independent, evidence-based review process before accepting any conclusions. Throughout, AutoResearch logs issues, audits anomalies, and can decide whether to continue, revise, or terminate a research direction based on collected evidence.
AI.result: In case studies across cross-modal retrieval, systems optimization, and benchmark-driven machine learning, AutoResearch transforms autonomously generated ideas into measurable performance gains. For example, on the RSICD benchmark, an idea produced by AutoResearch improves mean Recall from 32.84 to 34.69. The system also shows improved reliability: it records only 5 audit-confirmed issue events, versus 11–27 for comparison autonomous research systems, while still making competitive or superior progress.
AI.conclusion: AutoResearch demonstrates that combining structured, grounded idea generation with rigorously audited, evidence-based execution can significantly reduce hallucinations and unreliable findings in autonomous research. By enforcing grounding both before experimentation and before accepting conclusions—captured in the slogan “Insight In, Hallucination Out”—the system yields more trustworthy, reproducible research progress and provides a template for designing safer and more effective autonomous scientific agents.

title: Adaptive Policy Portfolios for Robust Markov Decision Processes
summary: Robust Markov decision processes optimize one policy against a set of plausible transition functions. This can be conservative when the unknown dynamics are fixed and become partially identifiable after deployment. We study adaptive policy portfolios: finite sets of memoryless randomized policies synthesized offline and paired with a lightweight online selector. Robust regret is a natural measure of portfolio quality: for each plausible environment, it measures the loss of the best portfolio member relative to the policy that would have been optimal had that environment been known. Related regret objectives were studied by Ghavamzadeh et al. (2016) with an emphasis on approximations and relaxations for safe policy improvement. We give a complexity-theoretic account of portfolio certification and synthesis. Certifying a given portfolio is $\forall\mathbb{R}$-complete already for deterministic portfolios in acyclic (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs. Synthesizing a portfolio of unary-bounded size is $\exists\forall\mathbb{R}$-complete for general rational polytopes, even with fixed discount and acyclic dynamics. The single-policy case is already hard, both combinatorially and algebraically. Finally, we present an offline portfolio construction that is amenable to runtime specialization.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to design and certify small sets (portfolios) of policies for Robust MDPs so that, after deployment, one can adapt among them with low worst-case regret, and shows that both certifying and synthesizing such portfolios are computationally very hard.
AI.motivation: Classical robust MDPs choose a single policy that must perform well against all plausible transition models, which tends to be overly conservative when the true dynamics are fixed and can be partially identified from data collected after deployment. The authors want a framework that allows some adaptation to the realized environment while still offering robustness guarantees. Regret with respect to the environment-specific optimal policy is a natural way to measure the quality of such adaptive strategies.
AI.method: They introduce adaptive policy portfolios: finite sets of memoryless randomized policies computed offline, plus a light online selector that chooses between them during execution. They formalize robust regret as the performance gap between the best policy in the portfolio (for each environment in the uncertainty set) and the environment-optimal policy. Using this formalization, they perform a complexity-theoretic analysis of two main decision problems: (1) portfolio certification—checking if a given portfolio guarantees a regret bound for all environments in a given uncertainty set; and (2) portfolio synthesis—constructing such a portfolio of bounded size. They study these problems over various classes of robust MDPs, focusing on (s,a)-rectangular uncertainty sets represented as rational polytopes, with assumptions like acyclicity and fixed discount factors, and characterize their complexity using real-number quantifier complexity classes (e.g., ∀ℝ-complete, ∃∀ℝ-complete).
AI.result: They prove that the certification problem is ∀ℝ-complete even for deterministic portfolios in acyclic, (s,a)-rectangular robust MDPs. For the synthesis problem, they show that constructing a portfolio of size bounded by a unary-encoded number is ∃∀ℝ-complete for general rational-polytope uncertainty sets, even when the discount factor is fixed and the dynamics are acyclic. They also demonstrate that these hardness results already appear in the single-policy case, indicating that the difficulty is inherent, not merely due to portfolio combinatorics. Finally, they propose an offline portfolio-construction procedure that admits efficient runtime specialization by the online selector.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive policy portfolios offer a principled way to mitigate the conservatism of classical robust MDPs while keeping robustness guarantees, by enabling post-deployment specialization to the realized environment. However, both verifying that a given portfolio satisfies a robust regret bound and synthesizing such a portfolio are computationally intractable in a strong sense—already hard in simplified, single-policy settings. This positions robust regret minimization in RMDPs as a fundamentally difficult problem and motivates approximate or problem-structure–exploiting methods for practical deployment, while their offline construction scheme illustrates one such direction amenable to online adaptation.

title: EvoTS-Agent: A Self-Evolving LLM Agent for Financial Time Series Change Point Detection
summary: Financial time series exhibit non-stationary and heterogeneous statistical properties, making change-point detection challenging because no single unsupervised algorithm performs consistently across assets and market regimes. Conventional workflows consequently depend heavily on expert-driven model selection, feature design, and hyperparameter tuning, limiting their scalability and adaptability. We propose EvoTS-Agent, a validation-guided self-evolving LLM agent for autonomous financial time-series change-point detection. EvoTS-Agent first performs curated exploratory data analysis to characterize dataset properties and initialize candidate detection models. It then evolves executable experiment trajectories through three complementary operators: \textit{Revision} exploits the current best solution, \textit{Alternative Strategy} explores fundamentally different modeling directions when progress stagnates, and \textit{Recombination} synthesizes complementary evidence from high-performing trajectories. Validation feedback guides trajectory evolution throughout the search, enabling the agent to adapt its detection pipeline to the statistical characteristics of each dataset while preserving reliable optimization. Experiments across four benchmark datasets demonstrate that EvoTS-Agent consistently outperforms existing LLM-based agents while maintaining a 100\% execution success rate across all evaluated backbone LLMs.
