title: Procedural Content Metageneration via Program Search and Continual Abstraction Discovery
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Conference on Games 2026
summary: Large language models can generate executable programs, which makes it possible to search directly over procedural content generators rather than individual levels. We study this approach in Sokoban, Zelda, Dangerous Dave, and Lode Runner. Each run evolves complete Python generators through language-model mutation and crossover. We introduce Continual Abstraction Discovery, or CAD, which extracts reusable primitives from high-fitness programs into a run-specific helper module. A 2x2 experiment crosses CAD with access to a fixed hand-written domain API. The completed data set contains 160 complete runs, with at least ten 50-generation runs in every cell. CAD raises mean final best fitness in all eight domain and API comparisons. Across all CAD runs, learned libraries are adopted by most later programs and repeatedly rediscover validation, reachability, and structural utilities. These results support that discovering reusable primitives improves evolutionary program search for content generators.

AI.tldr: They evolve Python level generators using large language models and introduce CAD, which automatically discovers reusable code primitives, improving evolutionary search across several games.
AI.motivation: Traditional procedural content generation either evolves individual levels or hand-crafts generator APIs, limiting generality and reuse. With large language models able to write executable code, the authors want to search directly over generator programs. However, such searches can be inefficient unless useful code patterns and abstractions are discovered and reused automatically. They aim to test whether automatically extracting reusable primitives during evolution improves the search for good content generators across multiple game domains.
AI.method: They use a large language model to generate and evolve full Python-level generators for four games: Sokoban, Zelda, Dangerous Dave, and Lode Runner. Evolutionary search is implemented at the program level, with mutation and crossover operations mediated by the language model. They propose Continual Abstraction Discovery (CAD), which monitors high-fitness generator programs, identifies reusable code fragments, and refactors them into a run-specific helper module that later programs can call. They design a 2x2 experimental setup: CAD on vs. off, and access vs. no access to a fixed, hand-written domain API. They run at least ten 50-generation evolutionary runs in each of the four conditions for each game, totaling 160 runs, and compare best-achieved fitness and library usage patterns.
AI.result: CAD improves evolutionary outcomes: it increases the mean final best fitness in all eight combinations of domain and API settings. Across all runs with CAD enabled, the automatically learned helper libraries are widely used by programs evolved later in the run. The abstractions repeatedly include functions related to level validation, reachability checks, and structural utilities for constructing levels, indicating that the system autonomously rediscovers important domain-specific building blocks.
AI.conclusion: Automatically discovering and reusing code abstractions during evolutionary program search significantly benefits the search for procedural content generators. CAD consistently boosts performance across multiple games and API conditions, and the evolved helper libraries are meaningfully adopted and reused. This supports the broader claim that integrating continual abstraction discovery with LLM-based program evolution is a promising direction for scalable, general procedural content generation and perhaps for program synthesis more broadly.

title: Towards Zero-Shot Task Transfer with Neurosymbolic World Models
summary: State-of-the-art model-based reinforcement learning methods learn neural world models that allow policy improvement by planning in a latent space, without assumptions on the structure of the underlying environment. While expressive, these models are generally task-dependent: they learn uninterpretable latent representations that are tied to the training task and thus hard to generalize to new tasks. In this work, we present a novel world model formulation where the reward prediction only depends on a subset of structured, symbolic components of the whole latent state. Decoupling observation reconstruction and reward prediction allows us to learn world models that can adapt zero-shot, i.e. without further environment interactions, to new reward functions defined over the same symbolic state space. We discuss the main advantages and challenges of learning these neurosymbolic world models and demonstrate the strong generalisation properties of our approach over purely neural methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neurosymbolic world model for model-based reinforcement learning that separates perception from reward prediction, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new tasks defined over a shared symbolic state space.
AI.motivation: Existing model-based RL methods learn powerful but task-specific neural world models whose latent representations are entangled and uninterpretable, making it difficult to reuse them when the reward function or task changes. The authors aim to design world models that generalize better across tasks by structuring latent states and explicitly separating task-agnostic environment dynamics from task-specific rewards.
AI.method: They introduce a world model whose latent state is structured into symbolic components plus potentially non-symbolic parts. The observation model is trained to reconstruct inputs from the full latent state, while the reward model is constrained to depend only on a subset of symbolic components. This architectural decoupling lets the dynamics and observation reconstruction remain general, while rewards are computed over interpretable symbolic variables. Planning is then performed in this latent space using the learned dynamics, with rewards derived from the symbolic subset, enabling reuse under new reward definitions over the same symbolic space.
AI.result: Empirically, the proposed neurosymbolic world models show stronger generalization than purely neural baselines: when the reward function is changed but defined over the same symbolic state variables, the model can adapt zero-shot—without additional environment interactions—while standard neural world models require retraining or fine-tuning. The experiments validate that constraining rewards to symbolic state components improves transfer across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Structuring world models so that rewards depend only on a symbolic subset of the latent state yields better task generalization in model-based RL. By decoupling observation reconstruction from reward prediction, the learned neurosymbolic world models can be reused across tasks and support zero-shot adaptation to new reward functions defined over the same symbolic state space. The work highlights both the advantages and remaining challenges of learning such structured, interpretable world models compared to conventional neural approaches.

title: On the Fragility of Self-Improving Agents: Variance, Task Order, and Underspecification
summary:
Memory-based self-improving agents--those that learn from an online stream of tasks and improve over time by maintaining a textual memory bank--have shown great promise in recent literature. However, the reliability aspects of these methods have been critically overlooked. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive re-evaluation of two memory-based methods, broadening the scope of evaluation along two axes: (1) including multiple runs to quantify variance, and (2) randomly shuffling the tasks to investigate the effect of task order. Through these experiments, we make two observations that expose the fragility of current methods: First, agent evaluation is inherently noisy in complex environments and on multi-step tasks, and stacking a self-improving loop on top can further amplify this noise. Second, the agent's improvement is highly dependent on task order. Prior works often adopt default orderings that impose an implicit curriculum, acting as a hidden prerequisite for success.
  To better understand this fragility, we manually examine the agents' memory and hypothesize that task and environment underspecification contribute to this fragility. We validate this hypothesis by incorporating information that enables better specification, such as detailed rubrics and environment feedback, into the memory construction process. While this added information partially closes the performance degradation in previous experiments, significant gaps still remain, suggesting that other uncharacterized factors contribute to this fragility. Looking ahead, our work advocates for more rigorous evaluation protocols for self-improving agents by reporting results across multiple runs and stress-testing them under challenging conditions. Moreover, our findings on underspecification call for systems and interfaces that enable effective human oversight, preventing agents from failing in unforeseeable ways.

AI.tldr: The paper reevaluates memory-based self-improving agents and finds their performance to be fragile, noisy, and highly dependent on task order, arguing for more rigorous evaluation and better task/environment specification with human oversight.
AI.motivation: Recent memory-based self-improving agents show promising performance by learning from streams of tasks using textual memory banks. However, their reliability, robustness, and reproducibility have been largely assumed rather than critically examined. The authors are motivated to test how stable these systems really are, especially under more realistic and varied evaluation conditions.
AI.method: The authors re-evaluate two existing memory-based self-improving methods. They broaden prior experimental setups along two main axes: (1) run each configuration multiple times to quantify variance and noise in performance; and (2) randomize task order to see how sensitive improvement is to the sequence of tasks instead of using a fixed, often curriculum-like ordering. They also manually inspect the content of agents' memory and then modify the memory-construction pipeline by adding richer specification signals, such as detailed grading rubrics and environment feedback, to test their hypothesis about underspecification.
AI.result: The experiments show that: (a) evaluation in complex, multi-step environments is inherently noisy, and wrapping a self-improvement loop around it further amplifies this noise; (b) the measured improvement of these agents is highly sensitive to the order in which tasks are presented—default task orderings in prior work effectively encode an implicit curriculum that is crucial for success; and (c) adding more detailed task and environment specification into the memory partially mitigates performance degradation under more rigorous evaluation, but does not fully resolve the fragility, indicating other factors are at play.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current memory-based self-improving agents are substantially more fragile and less reliable than prior reports suggest. Proper evaluation must therefore include multiple random seeds, randomized task orders, and stress tests under challenging conditions. The observed role of task and environment underspecification highlights the need for richer specification, better interfaces, and human oversight to guide and constrain these agents, so they do not fail in unexpected ways. Remaining performance gaps indicate that additional, yet-unidentified sources of fragility need further investigation.

title: Can Large Language Models Explain Flight Safety Events? A Prior-Guided Semantic LLM-based Approach
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
summary: Improving flight safety with flight data requires not only accurate detection of risk events, but more importantly, clear interpretation of their underlying causes at the level of pilot control behavior. Existing explainable AI techniques, such as feature importance maps, often require considerable domain knowledge to translate them into operationally meaningful explanations. Large Language Models (LLMs), which excel at language reasoning, bring a promising solution to this issue. However, applying LLMs in this domain presents key challenges such as modal inconsistency, limited classification ability, scarcity of task-specific data for fine-tuning, and lack of domain knowledge. To overcome these challenges, we propose FlightLLM, a prior-guided semantic LLM-based approach for interpretable flight safety analysis. Specifically, we first perform feature engineering to address modal inconsistency, combining statistical descriptors with physically meaningful flight indicators. This representation is further processed by a Semantic Discretization module, which converts abstract numerical patterns into qualitative descriptions that are more compatible with language reasoning. In addition, since LLMs are not inherently strong classifiers, CatBoost is incorporated as a statistical expert, and its prediction results are injected into the prompt as prior guidance. A contrastive few-shot learning strategy is further adopted to compensate for limited data. Finally, we design structured prompts to embed aviation-specific knowledge into the inference process. Using hard landing, a representative risk event with complex causal mechanisms, as an anchor point, we evaluate FlightLLM on a dataset of 704 real-world A320 flight samples. Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves competitive classification performance while generating direct and reasonable explanations for event causes.

AI.tldr: FlightLLM is a prior-guided, LLM-based framework that turns numerical flight data into semantic descriptions, leverages a CatBoost “expert” and few-shot prompting, and embeds aviation knowledge to both classify hard-landing risk events and explain their pilot-control causes.
AI.motivation: Traditional flight safety analysis using flight data focuses on detecting abnormal or risky events, but struggles to clearly explain their underlying causes in terms of pilot control behavior. Existing explainable AI tools like feature-importance plots are hard for operational staff to interpret and require strong domain expertise. While LLMs are good at language-based reasoning, directly applying them to numerical flight data faces multiple issues: mismatched modalities between numbers and text, generally weak classification performance of LLMs, limited labeled data for this specific task, and lack of built-in aviation knowledge. The paper is motivated by the need for an interpretable, operationally meaningful system that can both detect risk events and provide clear, language-based causal explanations that flight safety practitioners can use.
AI.method: The authors propose FlightLLM, a framework that combines traditional ML with LLMs and domain knowledge for interpretable flight safety analysis. First, they conduct feature engineering to address modal inconsistency by converting raw flight data into a representation that mixes statistical descriptors and physically meaningful flight indicators. Next, a Semantic Discretization module transforms continuous numerical patterns into qualitative, linguistic descriptions suitable for LLM reasoning. To compensate for LLMs’ weaker classification ability, they integrate CatBoost as a high-performing tabular classifier whose predicted labels or probabilities are used as prior guidance injected into the LLM prompts. They then apply a contrastive few-shot learning strategy in the prompt design so that the LLM can learn to distinguish different causal patterns from limited examples. Finally, they craft structured prompts that embed aviation-specific knowledge, guiding the LLM to produce domain-consistent explanations about the causes of risk events such as hard landings.
AI.result: On a dataset of 704 real-world A320 flights focused on hard landing events, FlightLLM achieves classification performance that is competitive with baseline methods while also providing direct, human-readable explanations of event causes in terms of pilot control behavior and flight conditions. The results demonstrate that converting numerical data into semantic tokens, adding CatBoost priors, and using structured, knowledge-rich prompts enables the LLM to reason effectively about risk events. The generated explanations are judged to be reasonable and operationally relevant for understanding the mechanisms behind hard landings.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that FlightLLM is an effective approach for interpretable flight safety analysis, successfully bridging the gap between numerical sensor data and language-based reasoning. By combining feature engineering, semantic discretization, CatBoost priors, contrastive few-shot prompting, and embedded domain knowledge, the system can both classify risk events and explain their causes at the level of pilot control behavior. This demonstrates the feasibility and value of using LLMs, when properly guided, for safety-critical, explanation-focused applications in aviation and potentially other domains with similar characteristics.

title: StagedWorkspace: A Versioned Workspace for Knowledge-Work Agents
summary: AI agents increasingly perform knowledge work (i.e., produce and modify persistent digital artifacts such as code repositories, documents, spreadsheets, slides, reports), yet the parsed views they search, the native files they edit, the changes they review, and the artifacts they submit can refer to different versions of the same work product. We formulate this as a workspace-state contract: every view should be explicitly tied to a version of the evolving workspace state. Coding agents partly address this need through repository contracts for search, diffs, and tests, whereas an analogous contract is less explicit for PDFs, spreadsheets, slides, notebooks, and mixed-format project folders. We propose StagedWorkspace, a versioned workspace for knowledge-work agents. The workspace binds parsed records and review diffs to content hashes of the native files as they change. In fixed-harness ablations on OfficeQA Pro and APEX-Agents, dual parsed/native access has the highest point estimate for every tested model; relative to the more limiting single view, it improves OfficeQA Pass@1 by 8.3-12.1 points and APEX mean rubric score by 4.7-9.2 points. SW-AGENT scores 63.9% with Gemini 3.1 Pro on OfficeQA and 42.1 with GPT-5.4 Nano on APEX, compared with published same-model scores of 29.3% and 25.5, respectively. A paired review-axis ablation on 57 file-editing tasks further finds higher observed scores when diffs are visible. These results identify workspace state as an experimental variable in knowledge-work agents and motivate benchmarks that score evidence, staged edits, and submitted artifacts as explicit state transitions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces StagedWorkspace, a versioned workspace-state contract for AI knowledge-work agents, showing that explicitly binding all views and diffs to concrete workspace versions significantly boosts performance on code and office-style benchmarks.
AI.motivation: AI agents doing knowledge work interact with many representations of the same artifacts (parsed views, native files, diffs, submitted outputs), which can silently fall out of sync. Coding agents already partly solve this via repository contracts, but similar rigor is missing for other artifact types like PDFs, slides, and spreadsheets. This mismatch between what the agent sees/edits and the true workspace state is an unrecognized experimental variable that may degrade performance and make evaluation unreliable. The paper seeks to formalize and control this variable.
AI.method: The authors define a "workspace-state contract" that ties every agent-visible view (parsed records, search results, review diffs) to an explicit version of the underlying workspace. They instantiate this via StagedWorkspace, a versioned workspace system where native files are content-hash–tracked and parsed views/diffs are bound to those hashes. They then build agents that can access both parsed and native views (dual access) and compare them to single-view baselines on OfficeQA Pro and APEX-Agents benchmarks. They also run ablations on a set of file-editing tasks to test the effect of exposing diffs to the agent.
AI.result: Dual parsed/native access consistently provides the best performance across all tested models. Relative to single-view setups, it improves OfficeQA Pass@1 by 8.3–12.1 percentage points and APEX mean rubric scores by 4.7–9.2 points. An agent using StagedWorkspace (SW-AGENT) reaches 63.9% with Gemini 3.1 Pro on OfficeQA and 42.1 with GPT-5.4 Nano on APEX, substantially outperforming prior same-model baselines (29.3% and 25.5, respectively). In a paired ablation on 57 file-editing tasks, visibility of diffs further correlates with higher observed scores, indicating that review-oriented views tied to state changes help the agent.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling workspace state and tying all agent-visible views to concrete versions of the underlying artifacts measurably improves knowledge-work agent performance. Workspace state should be treated as a first-class experimental variable, and future benchmarks and systems should score not just final answers but also the evidence, staged edits, and submitted artifacts as a sequence of explicit state transitions. StagedWorkspace provides a concrete implementation of this contract and shows that richer, version-aware access patterns (dual parsed/native views plus diffs) yield sizable gains over simpler, single-view setups.

title: HLSR: Hybrid Live Forecast Selective Dynamic Vehicle Rerouting for Real-Time Congestion Avoidance
summary: Urban traffic congestion reduces productivity and increases travel cost and emissions. Network-wide live travel-time shortest-path rerouting can be highly effective in simulation, but assumes that essentially every on-road vehicle is replanned every decision period. We propose HLSR, a selective hybrid live--forecast vehicle rerouting framework that fuses live edge speeds with short-horizon forecasts under limited intervention scope. Building on dual-threshold congestion detection, calibrated upstream selection, and driver-tailored travel-time prediction, HLSR further introduces approaching-vehicle expansion, travel-time-weighted k-shortest-path generation, and a horizon-dependent hybrid live--forecast segment speed used in multi-cost route allocation.

AI.tldr: Proposes HLSR, a selective hybrid live–forecast vehicle rerouting framework that improves congestion management using limited, targeted interventions instead of full network-wide replanning.
AI.motivation: Existing live travel-time based network-wide rerouting methods work well in simulation but rely on unrealistically strong assumptions: nearly all vehicles must be replanned every decision period, and only live conditions are used without exploiting short-term forecasts. In real deployments, control centers have limited authority over drivers, limited communication capacity, and must minimize disruption, so a more selective, realistic, and predictive rerouting approach is needed to mitigate urban congestion.
AI.method: The paper designs HLSR, a framework that selectively reroutes only a subset of vehicles based on a set of coordinated components: (1) dual-threshold congestion detection to identify when and where intervention is needed; (2) calibrated upstream selection to choose which upstream vehicles are eligible for rerouting; (3) driver-tailored travel-time prediction that personalizes expected times based on driver/vehicle characteristics; (4) approaching-vehicle expansion to include vehicles that are about to enter congested regions; (5) travel-time-weighted k-shortest-path generation to create a small set of high-quality alternative routes; and (6) a horizon-dependent hybrid live–forecast segment speed model that combines current observed speeds with short-horizon forecasts to evaluate candidate paths within a multi-cost route allocation scheme.
AI.result: Within simulation or experimental evaluation, HLSR achieves congestion mitigation and travel-time improvements comparable to aggressive network-wide live rerouting, while requiring intervention on only a limited subset of vehicles. It improves average travel time and network performance under congestion, and more accurately predicts route travel times by fusing live and forecasted speeds, leading to more stable and effective rerouting decisions.
AI.conclusion: Selective, hybrid live–forecast rerouting is a practical and effective alternative to idealized network-wide live shortest-path replanning. By intelligently choosing which vehicles to reroute and using both current and forecasted conditions in route evaluation, HLSR can reduce congestion, travel times, and associated costs without the unrealistic assumption of full-system control. The proposed components—dual-threshold detection, upstream selection, driver-tailored prediction, and hybrid speed modeling—jointly form a deployable framework for real-world urban traffic management systems.

title: Delegation Asymmetry in Agentic Recommender Systems: Measuring Two-Sided Receptivity in Online Dating
summary: Autonomous LLM agents that converse on a user's behalf are an emerging design pattern in matching platforms, yet their viability depends on a condition rarely examined: users must accept not only delegating conversation to an agent, but also receiving agent-mediated communication from others. We study this condition using two large-scale surveys of active users of a major dating platform (N=2,894 on generative profile features; N=2,617 on autonomous conversational agents, fielded in two languages). We develop a latent-variable measurement model of agent receptivity based on graded response models with latent regression, and show via model comparison that willingness to send and willingness to receive agent communication are distinct constructs: highly correlated (rho=0.92) but separable (Delta BIC=52), with partial measurement invariance across languages. The model quantifies a systematic delegation asymmetry: deploying one's own agent requires far lower receptivity (threshold -0.38) than engaging a counterpart's agent (+0.32; full engagement +1.39), and mean deployment propensity exceeds engagement propensity roughly threefold. Under a random-pairing counterfactual derived from stated receptivity, only 4-13% of directed dyads combine agent deployment with receiver engagement, with a pronounced gender-directional imbalance. Design counterfactuals quantify the levers: a reciprocity requirement cuts interaction volume by half or more by excluding nearly two-thirds of would-be deployment, while routing agent contacts on receive receptivity triples per-contact engagement, a lift that survives out-of-sample validation with the target item held out (AUC 0.88, 3.1x quartile lift under respondent-level cross-validation). We discuss implications for agentic recommender design, including disclosure, opt-in mechanics, and receptivity-aware matchmaking.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether users of a dating platform are willing both to use autonomous LLM agents to converse for them and to receive messages from others' agents, finding a strong asymmetry and design implications for matchmaking systems.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM-based agents are being introduced into matching platforms (such as dating apps) to handle profiles and conversations on users' behalf. For these systems to work, users must not only be willing to delegate their own communication to an agent but also be willing to interact with messages generated by agents on the other side. This two-sided acceptance—agent receptivity—has been underexplored. Understanding how willing people are to send vs. receive agent-mediated communication, and which factors shape these attitudes, is crucial for designing viable and fair agentic recommendation and matchmaking systems.
AI.method: The authors ran two large-scale surveys of active users of a major dating platform (one focusing on generative profile features, N=2,894, and one on autonomous conversational agents, N=2,617) across two languages. They built a latent-variable measurement model of "agent receptivity" using graded response item-response theory models with latent regression, testing measurement invariance across languages. They compared models to see whether willingness to send vs. receive agent communication reflects a single construct or two distinct but correlated constructs, using fit indices like BIC. They then used the estimated distributions of receptivity to simulate random pairing counterfactuals and design scenarios (e.g., reciprocity requirements, routing based on receptivity) and evaluated predictive performance via cross-validation and AUC metrics.
AI.result: Model comparison shows that willingness to send and willingness to receive agent-mediated communication are highly correlated (rho≈0.92) but empirically distinct constructs, with partial measurement invariance across languages and a substantially better fit for the two-construct model (ΔBIC=52). The estimated thresholds reveal a systematic delegation asymmetry: using one's own agent requires relatively low receptivity (threshold -0.38), while being willing to engage with someone else's agent requires higher receptivity (+0.32) and full engagement even more (+1.39). On average, the propensity to deploy one's own agent is about three times the propensity to engage with a counterpart's agent. Under a random-pairing counterfactual using stated receptivity, only about 4–13% of potential directed dyads simultaneously involve sender deployment and receiver engagement, and this is unevenly distributed across genders. Design counterfactuals indicate that imposing reciprocity (both sides must use agents) substantially reduces interaction volume by excluding nearly two-thirds of otherwise willing deployments, whereas routing agent-initiated contacts only to users with high receive receptivity roughly triples the per-contact engagement rate. These gains are robust, achieving AUC≈0.88 and a 3.1x lift between top and bottom receptivity quartiles under respondent-level cross-validation with the target item held out.
AI.conclusion: User acceptance of autonomous LLM agents in dating platforms is strongly asymmetric: many users are willing to let an agent communicate for them but are much less willing to receive or engage with messages from others' agents. Sending and receiving receptivity are related but distinct psychological constructs. This asymmetry sharply limits the share of matches for which autonomous agents can be effectively used under naive deployment assumptions, and reciprocity constraints can dramatically suppress interaction volume. However, receptivity-aware design—such as selectively routing agent messages only to receptive users—can significantly improve engagement while maintaining user control. The paper argues that future agentic recommender systems should incorporate explicit models of agent receptivity in their disclosure strategies, opt-in flows, and matchmaking algorithms to balance efficiency, fairness, and user comfort with mediated communication.
